With the exception of two, every one of those hon. members, who sit around him, was elected on that manifesto. One of those two is the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. J. F. Reid), who was elected as an Independent . and who, therefore, has a perfect right to choose where he will sit in this House, and the other is the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), who was elected at a byelection in October, 1919, and who, as admitted by himself, sits in this House today as an instructed delegate of fifteen men who hold his signed resignation. I want to know where these hon. gentlemen, who are going to vote on this amendment, got their mandate, bias ever one of them gone back to his constituents and asked for an endorsation of the position he holds in this House? Not one of them, not even their leader, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), has done so. They have no mandate for the position they hold; yet, they expect to vote for this amendment, to vote a want of confidence in this Government and to say, that we who are supporting this Government have no mandate from our constituents to do so.
During the last two years we- in Western Canada have been looking for redistribution. If we get redistribution, the four western provinces will likely be I'epresent-ed in this House by twenty more members. .Saskatchewan should have five new members, and I know the people in my constituency want redistribution. I do not know what the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), whose constituency is next to mine, thinks on the subject, but I know a very large number of the people in his constituency want redistribution, because his constituency is very large and unwieldy. I was surprised the other day when the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), speaking about redistribution^ said that he would be afraid to leave that matter to this Government to handle; that there would be gerrymandering. That is an old political party cry that we have heard for years and years, and I thought this new party was above all that; that it was blazing a new trail in this country and dropping all the old party cries, and' that we would hear no more of them. I believe this Government is quite as capable of giving us redistribution as any other Government that could be elected in Canada.

The other night the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) discussed the question of freight rates. The people of the West have no objection to paying their way, of paying their fair share of whatever it costs to run our railways, but we object to paying more than our share. I believe the sooner we can have a readjustment of those rates, the better it will be for the whole country and much better for the western provinces.
Let me now take up the question of the much-abused Wheat Board, and let me say right here that if any Government in Canada has ever passed a piece of legislation that has been of benefit to the farmers of Western Canada, it is the legislation constituting the Wheat Board. But when the Wheat Board was appointed, it was not accepted in that way. I will not say that our papers in Western Canada were unanimous in condemning, but the great majority of them condemned this Government from Monday morning until Saturday night for constituting the Wheat Board. They even went so far as to say that, in regard to those participation certificates-"anticipation certificates" they called them-they advised the farmer to get rid of them, dispose of them, sell them at anything he could get for them; that after this Government got rid of the Wheat Board, all the money that went into the farmers' pockets would never enrich them. The sad part of the matter is that many farmers disposed of their participation certificates at five, seven, ten cents a bushel to speculators, who reaped fortunes by buying them out. The other night, when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) was speaking, he was asked what his attitude was during his election campaign with reference to the Wheat Board. He said that the Wheat Board was not in existence during his campaign, and he was supported in that by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg).
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I did not make the statement the hon. gentleman alleges.

All I have to do is to turn up Hansard. Here it is:
Mr. Cowan: Is it not true that at the election in which the hon. member was elected he and every part of his constituency were opposed to the existence of a Wheat Board; that he fought it from beginning to end and that he was elected as an opponent of the Wheat Board?
Mr. Gould: That is another bugaboo. I do not think the hon. gentleman can find in Assiniboia any sentiment whatever in that direction.
I will give to the House this evidence-

Mr. Cowan: That is not the point at all. The point is that my hon. friend was elected straight on that platform and nothing else.
Mr. Maharg: There was no Wheat Board in existence then.
Mr. Cowan: Yes, there was.
Mr. Maharg: Not on your life.

My point of order was
that the hon. gentleman alleged J said there was no Wheat Board in existence.
I made no such statements and Hansard proves it.

I will continue the quotation:
Mr. Gould: The hon. gentleman is mixed as to his facts. I might tell the House that not on any of the many platforms on which I stood during my whole election was the Wheat Board mentioned-
Hear, hear.
I say that to-night as an hon. member of this House.

When we look up the records of that election we find that the Wheat Board was one of the burning questions before the people of that constituency. They were told that this Government had appointed the Wheat Board and that the farmers were losing in consequence anywhere from ten to forty cents a bushel on their wheat. That was in October, 1919. What were they saying in 1920 about the Wheat Board? All hands were up for a Wheat Board in 1920, after the Board had gone out of existence. As my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) used to say, it was a case of "You're damned if you do, and damned if you don't."
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he can produce any evidence to support his statement that the Wheat Board was made an election issue in my campaign? I absolutely deny it.

I am not prepared to say whether, had the Wheat Board been in existence this year, it would have made any difference in the price of wheat at the terminal elevators. But one thing I do know, and that is it would have stabilized the price at the country elevators. When the Wheat Board was in existence, after the farmer had done this threshing he knew how many bushels of wheat he had, knew what grade it was, and knew to a cent what it was worth at his station. He could go to his banker and say: I have so many bushels of wheat out on my farm, and I want so much money to carry it till the ground freezes, so that I can get on
with my fall work; when I market my wheat I will pay you off. But how coufd that be done this year? There was no Wheat Board in existence this year. Take my own little city of Swift Current. Nine miles west of us is Beverley with two elevators. Now I have seen farmers haul their wheat past Beverley into Swift Current and make fifteen cents a bushel. Then nine miles south is Dunelm on the Vanguard line. I have seen farmers haul their wheat past Dunelm into Swift Current, and make eighteen cents a bushel on the same grade of wheat.
Then, there is the question of trackage price and street price. When I sold my wheat there was eleven cents difference between the trackage price and the street price. Now all the elevator man had to do when a man came in with a load of wheat was to pay eleven cents less for it than it was worth on the track. The farmer must sell his wheat, because he must have money to buy coal and provisions for his family. The elevator man would pay him eleven cents less than it was worth on the track, and the next day he would put it through the elevator and load it on the car and sell it for eleven cents more than he paid for it. These are the things which are disturbing the farmers of the West. We are not satisfied with our grain handling system, and we are asking that the Government appoint a commission to investigate the whole matter and take control not only of the terminal elevators but of all the individual elevators up and down the line. We want to know how many hundreds of thousands of bushels of No. 1 Northern the elevators buy, and how many they sell. We want to know that with respect also to No. 2, No. 3, No. 4 and No. 5. We want to know how much they make out of what they call the promotion of grade. We want to know how many thousands of bushels they have left in their elevators at the end of the season, and what becomes of it. If you take up any of the reports of the elevator companies, you will not find the overages mentioned, and there is nothing to show what they have made by the promotion of grade. What we are asking the Government to do is to appoint a commission to make a thorough investigation of the wheat handling system, and ascertain the best system of handling wheat from the time it leaves the producer until it gets to the consumer.
Mr. JOHN A. CAMPBELL (Nelson) : Mr. Speaker, before I commence my re-



marks on the Address I wish to extend, as others have done before me, my very sincere personal congratulations to the Prime Minister in having attained the highest office in the gift of the people. In some respects I may differ from him in matters of policy, but personally I sincerely congratulate him and wish him every success. I also wish to extend my felicitations to the mover and the seconder of the Address. I had not the pleasure of listening to their remarks, but according to statements made regarding them their speeches were not only a credit to themselves, but did honour to their constituencies.
I have listened to a number of the speeches on both sides of the House in this debate, and have read some others, and I have been struck by the fact that there has been very little in the way of enunciation of party policies in any of the speeches so far delivered. That applies not only to the speeches of the leaders, but to those of their followers. The speech from the Throne contained a clause, outlining the Government's policy on the tariff question. For what purpose that was inserted I do not know. However, I do not think it was a bad idea. Probably the Government thought they might get some idea of where the members of the House stood on this question before they brought down their policy in connection with the Budget. If that was the idea, they must have been disappointed for there has been very little definite statement of tariff views so far. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. King), followed the seconder of the Address, and ignored the tariff problem, in fact, ignored practically everything that was in the speech from the Throne. He raised the question of a great constitutional crisis, and claimed the Government had no mandate to continue in office. The Prime Minister, in reply, devoted his attention entirely to rebutting and refuting, in his opinion at any rate, the statements made by his opponent. Shortly afterwards, the leader of the Progressive party discussed the points already raised, and to some extent outlined his policy and that of his party. Up to that time his speech was the only one in which the policy of any of the parties had been outlined to any extent. The followers of the different parties naturally took their cue from their leaders, and the result is that the definite laying down of party policies has hitherto been notable by its absence.
I gather from the speeches already delivered that there were in the main two
[Mr Campbell.]
questions raised; first, the question of confidence or otherwise in the Government, and secondly, the tariff question. Before discussing these questions, I should like to direct attention of the House for a moment or two to my position in this House.
It may possibly not have escaped your attention, Sir, that since last session I have crossed the green carpet and now occupy a position on the side opposite the Government. I do not know that that fact is of any particular significance. I have not changed my policy nor my ideas politically by doing so. It may be simply a question of expediency or form. For the first year of the term I occupied a position directly in front of you, Sir. I chose what subsequently became known as the cross benches, in the first instance, for physical reasons, because it was a position from which I could both see and hear better than I could from any other part of the floor available, for neither my sight nor my hearing is particularly good. During that session the work of the Gove moment was entirely or almost entirely concerned with carrying on the war, and I supported it throughout. Before the second year commenced the war had fortunately ended, and during that year not only was the Government concerned with questions arising out of the war, but it took up some matters which might be considered as having no direct connection with the war. That may be a matter of opinion. However, one such matter was the tariff and another the question of taking over certain railways. In this connection I found that it was necessary for me to differ from the Government, because I did not approve of their policy so far as the tariff was concerned. And subsequently, in the second session when the matter of railway legislation came up and we were considering the taking over of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, while I approved of the policy- there seemed to be nothing else to do under the circumstances-still I felt compelled to differ from the Government in one respect, namely, as to certain of the terms of the agreement, in which connection I moved an amendment. I am satisfied that my atitude was right, and I have every reason to believe that some at least of the members of the Government were thoroughly in accord with me. It was during that time that the cross benches began to take on political significance. Some of those' who held similar

views to mine were there, and others of like mind joined us, while some of those who did not share our opinions moved away. Then we came to this Chamber, where the seats are differently arranged and last year I occupied a seat on the other side. So far as I can recollect the only question of moment on which I really differed from the Government was the question of policy involved in the Budget;
1 found that I was not in accord and had to vote against them. So this year, on coming to the House I decided that it was but fair not only to myself but to the Government that I should take up a position somewhat apart and act in such a way as I thought would be advisable in the interests of the country.
This does not mean that I differ from the Government now any more than I did in the past. It is quite probable however that my ideas will be found to be at variance with those of the Government in connection with the tariff. It may be that in the Budget to be brought down certain amendments may be made which will enable me to vote for the proposals. I can only say that I shall give them the benefit of any doubt. I am quite unrepentant so far as votes I have given are concerned. I am satisfied that they were right, and in some cases my stand will be shown to have been right. In other instances there is and always will be room for debate. I have no desire to see a change in government just at the present moment that would produce unnecessarily chaotic conditions.
As I mentioned before, the question of the tariff has been introduced in a clause in the Address. This, I understand, is somewhat unusual. It was intended, presumably, that the matter should thereby be open for discussion and it was a case of the Government's nailing its colours to the mast. I am not in favour of the principle of protection; I do not mind making that statement strongly and emphatically. It might be argued from that assertion that it would be necessary for me to oppose the Government and support the amendment to the motion which is now before the House. What I shall do remains to be seen; but I do not think that such is a necessary inference from my statement. At this particular time it is proper for us all to get away as far as possible from terminology and technicalities and try to get at the heart of things; and so far as I can make out the terms in connection with t]ie tariff are not well defined, and

people may and do think alike who are under different banners and call themselves by different names. The principle of protection, is not the main question before the House at this time; I make that statement, although I may be misunderstood in doing so. I had almost said it was not an issue; I am not prepared to go so far, but it is not an issue of immediate concern. I do not wish to be misunderstood and I shall therefore try to make my position perfectly clear. When the debate on the railway question was in progress, I had the temerity to state that the question of public ownership was not an issue at that time. I thought so then and I think so now. I am satisfied that there were members on the Government side who all supported the Government's stand in that respect who were absolutely opposed to the principle of public ownership. That was a case where of necessity the Government had to do something; they had to become public owners whether they wished to do so or not; and therefore I say that the fundamental principle was not really at stake. I was satisfied at that time that if members of the Government had had placed before them any kind of reasonable offer from any private concern to take over those railways, that offer would have been accepted with celerity. And I think so yet.
In this case I am not prepared to go so far; but I say that the main business of the House at the present time is not to decide the principle of protection, but to deal with the tariff as it stands with a view to simplifying it, removing certain irregularities and passing upon certain matters in connection therewith regarding which, I think, not only those opposed to the principal of protection but those who are in favor of it are agreed. There are on the other side of the House and on the Opposition side to my right, members who, I think, have policies in this connection ranging all the way from free trade to moderate protection if that is a proper term. I do hot know that there are any absolute free traders in the House, though theoretically there may be; but there are some who come pretty near it; so, eliminating the high protectionists, of whom there are some on both sides of the House, the remainder go all the way from free trade to moderate protection. I have been talking to some recently who have been known as strong protectionists all their days, and I was surprised to learn that they thoroughly agree with me, or I with them as the case may be, as to what is necessary

and advisable, in the interests of the country, to do with the tariff' at the present time; and there are many things upon which this House can agree in regard to the tariff before we come to the question of disposing of the absolute principle. For instance, we might direct our attention to the elimination of the duties in connection with industries that do not really need the benefit of any tariff at the present time; and there are such in Canada.
There are other industries which, even from their own standpoint, do not need as much protection as they are receiving at the present time, a fact that is well known.
Then comes the question of reducing the tariff on necessities and on the instruments of production to the minimum and, in some cases, the elimination altogether of the existing duties. This involves the question of giving the most encouragement to those industries which are indigenous to Canada, as against those of an adventitious nature, thus helping to develop the natural resources of which we hear so much.
The question, Mr. Speaker, is where does the House stand in respect to these matters? The position of the Prime Minister is clear and distinct-he is emphatically out for protection presumably similar to what we now have. The leader of the Opposition has not, this year, stated what his policy is; but one of his followers this afternoon announced that the Liberal party was standing on the platform of 1919. It is pretty clear what that platform is, but there is sometimes a question in my mind whether all the members of the Opposition to my right are supporting it in its entirety. The leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) has enunciated his platform on the tariff and I think that it is also clear and distinct. In connection with the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) on the tariff, the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) took the ground that the leader of the Progressive party had not clearly stated his position. Well, that is a matter of opinion. Personally, I am inclined to think that my hon. friend from Marquette made a very clear-cut statement. At any rate, I am satisfied that I know where he stands, just as well as I know what the policy of the Prime Minister is on this question. But I must say that my hon. friend from Macdonald did not state his own views on this particular problem. Now I have been informed that the hon. member for Macdonald had some part to play in the formation of the platform on which the leader of the Progressive 
party now stands. That being so, I presumed that my hon. friend was thoroughly familiar with the Progressive platform; in fact that he supported it himself; but tha< appears not to be the case. If I am mis taken in this assumption, my hon. friend from Macdonald will correct me.
As I stated previously, some of the members of this House who are pronounced protectionists have intimated to me that the tariff is running amuck; that the present schedules are not really operating in the interest of those Canadian industries which it is intended to protect and foster. I am inclined to agree with these hon. gentlemen in that respect.
In connection with amendments proposed consideration should first be given to duties on the necessities of life. As already pointed out, there is not much difference of opinion as to the desirability of doing this, and there should be none. The duties on these necessities should be reduced to a minimum and in many respects eliminated altogether. The duties on textiles have often been discussed in this Chamber. I will not do more, at the present time, than refer to the enormous profits which the Dominion Textile Company has been able to make during the last few years. That company should need no assistance from the people.
A couple of days ago a memorandum was given to me with respect'to an industry in Canada, the product of which might properly be classed as a necessity. I refer to the paint industry. The memo in question was given to me by a strong protectionist, a Conservative. I will only read part of it:
Sherwin-Williams Co. Optimistic about Paint Industry.
The sales of Sherwin-Williams Co. for the fiscal year ended Aug. 31 show a total of $75,952,000 which is a gain of $22,000,000 over the banner year of 1919. Comparison of the sales of $'51,817,000 for the American Companies alone with the $36,992,000 of the previous year shows a gain of 40 per cent.
According to the balance sheet the company has current assets of $27,679,859 compared with current liabilities of $6,636,738. It has $992,855 in the cash account, and inventory of $15,814,260. During the year a stock dividend of 50 per cent was declared so that the surplus account shows $4,481,667 this year compared with $7,175,311 a year ago.
Attached to the memo is a clipping from a newspaper. It contains a New York despatch intimating that there is a combine between the white lead men in connection with the output of paint.

speechtext:
Is the hon.
gentleman quoting the figures .of the

Sherwin-Williams Paint Company of United States, or the Sherwin-Williams Paint Company of Canada? They are of course two different companies.

The figures I have
given from the quotation seem to include both companies. The point I wish to make
