speechtext:
My hon. friend
must know that the two companies are quite different, and I hope he will have the justice to say, when he is quoting such figures, whether they relate to the American or the Canadian company. As my hon. friend quoted the figures, the House would be led to believe that they had reference to the Canadian company.
I did not know, Mr. Speaker, that the two companies are entirely and distinctly separate. I understood they were affiliated companies, and that one was merely a branch of the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.

I understood in quoting the figures of the business done that they related not only to the American but also to the Canadian company. However, the point I wish to make is this: The paint industry seems to be very prosperous both in the United States and in Canada, and this particular company is doing a very large and extensive business, and realizing excellent profits, in both fields of activity. In my opinion, as well as in the opinion of the well informed gentleman who handed me this memo, the protection which is afforded to this company is beyond all bounds and a great deal more than what is necessary to fully protect the industry even if such protection were advisable.
There remains for me to deal with the question of the removal of the duties, or at any rate a very material reduction in the duties, on the instruments of production. I shall confine my attention at the present time merely to those required for the agricultural and mining industries. It was mentioned in a speech the other day that the average tariff on agricultural implements is very low. Again in this House this afternoon it was stated that generally speaking the average tariff is very much lower than it has been. ,	. ~
I am not concerned very much, Mr. Speaker, regarding average tariffs; I do not think that is a fair way of arriving at their incidence. To my mind the better way is to take specific instances, and then
we know exactly where we are at. Re- ' garding agriculture, notwithstanding the statement that the average tariff is very low-I forget the figures quoted-I find that some implements used in connection with agriculture are taxed as follows: Harvesters, partly complete, 121 per cent; ploughs, cultivators and drills, 20 per cent; grain crushers and fanning mills, 25 per cent; gasoline engines, 27 or 30 per cent-I am not quite sure which; the humble wheel-barrow pays a duty of about 30 per cent; Ford cars and carriages are subject to a duty of 35 per cent. With respect to the Ford car, I do not think any hon. member will say that it is a luxury; at any rate, it has not hitherto been looked upon as such; but the duty of 35 per cent is certainly excessive and should be materially reduced, if not eliminated altogether. Agricultural producers have the above handicaps to contend with.
Contrary to what has been ferquently stated, mining machinery and utensils intimately connected with mining are not free. It is true that mining machinery and such utensils as I have mentioned are free when they are used in connection with iron and steel and associated industries. But why they should be admitted free when used by any particular industry and be subject to duty when not so used passes my comprehension. This is a matter which I simply wish to draw to the attention of the Government. In some cases machinery is admitted free. For instance, machinery for dredging gold is on the free list, as are also briquetting machinery, machinery for the manufacture of rifles, machinery for the manufacture of ship plates, and other kinds of machinery; but when we come down to the tools of the prospectors who make the original discoveries of our natural resources, we find there is a duty ranging from 22! to 30 per cent. This duty, it is true, is not exacted when machinery and tools in connection with mining are imported for universities, endowed or otherwise, but when the ordinary prospector, who is not by any means a man of means, desires to buy tools for his work he has to pay the duties I have mentioned. Then I wish to draw the attention of the Government to the rates of duty on complicated and newly invented machinery, and I will mention only two or three varieties:	Gyrating
crushers, 27! per cent; machinery for removing the overburden in connection with

mineral deposits, very important in mining', 271 per cent; gasoline locomotives, also very important instruments in mining development, 35 per cent. I submit to the Government that if they are anxious to relieve the burdens on the people at the present time, and to encourage that development of our natural resources about which we hear so much, such duties as I have named should be either removed altogether or reduced to the very minimum.
The other question to which the attention of this House has been directed for some time is that of the confidence or othe>
wise which this Parliament and the country have in the Government. I may not be a constitutional authority, but so far rs I can see this Government, constitutionally, cannot be called usurpers; they are rot in the position of overholding tenants by any means. Constitutionally, they are entitled to hold office just as long as they have a majority in this House, which will be put to the test shortly. However, there are two other points involved; one is as to the agreement or understanding reached by the members of the Government at the time the Coalition Government was formed in 1917, and the other is the present attitude and feeling of the people towards the Government.
I agree with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean)-a former member of this Government-who spoke a few days ago. The hon. gentleman was on the inside in connection with the formation of the Coalition Government; I was very much on the outside. He knew exactly what transpired, and he has given his report in respect to that, and his opinion as to what should be done, and I see no reason why I should take issue with him thereon. As to my position, there was no contest in the constituency of Nelson, and with the exception of a few speeches of a semi-political nature at the time of nomination we heard none in the constituency during the period of the campaign, and I did not take part in the campaign in any other constituencies. However, I gained the impression at that time that the Government was formed for the period of the war and for such time thereafter as would be necessary" to clear up matters particularly pertaining to the war, and I think my constituents had the same idea. It is true that, technically, the Coalition Government did come to an end when the new Government headed by the right, hon. the new Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) was formed, but I can only consider his Government as the

direct successor of the Coalition Government.
However, in my opinion, the question is larger than that presented by speakers who have preceded me. I am inclined to think that it is not simply a question of whether the Government should give up office at the present time or not, but whether the whole Parliament should come to an end. We see statements in the papers that this Parliament-I do not refer to one side or the other, but to both sides of the House-is unrepresentative, unresponsive, moribund and stale. These expressions may be somewhat exaggerated, but nevertheless there is an element of truth in them. Any election within the near future would mean a great change not only on the Government side, but on this side of the House. Many hon. members who were elected in 1917 were urged to give their services solely on account of the fact that a peculiar situation had arisen, and that it was necessary to get a certain type of men to take office. These hon. members now think their mandate has expired. Certain other hon. members who were then elected have been referred to as "compromise" candidates and were placed in the position which they now occupy by their electors with the distinct idea that when the term mentioned had elapsed political conditions would revert to normal.
In another respect, however, I differ very materially with the argument and statements made by my hon. friend from Halifax, in that I contend that redistribution is a very important matter to be considered at the p resent time. While I am of opinion that there should be an election, not immediately, but before another session of the House, this should not be held until redistribution has taken place. There should be an election soon, but there should be redistribution sooner. The hon. member for Halifax gave his case away- perhaps inadvertently-when he said that the question of redistribution involved an increase of representation in certain parts of the country, and it necessarily followed that the representation would decrease in other parts of the country. I do not know that that necessarily follows, but in all probability it will be the result of increased representation in any one part of the country.
Without redistribution there will not be proper representation. For instance, let us assume that there are two constituencies of equal population, and that within ten years one half of one of those constituencies

should move into another:	If there were
no redistribution, it would necessarily follow that the votes of the electors left in the first constituency would have three times the value of the votes of the electors in the second constituency. Of course, that may be a far-fetched case, but there are instances where such results obtain in Canada. I know constituencies which have fifty thousand or sixty thousand electors and others with only twenty thousand or thirty thousand.
It is generally the case, Mr. Speaker, that when changes are suggested, hon. members look for precedents. If we are to look for precedents for the holding of an election on or about the time of the taking of the census -the decennial period-we find that during the last three decades elections have taken place without such redistribution, very close to the times at which the census returns were made. I refer to the following elections: March 5, 1891; November 7, 1900; September 21, 1911. These precedents, perhaps, are against my contention, but the fact is they are such that we do not wish to follow them at the present time or at any time in the future. They are precedents that it is a good thing to get away from; I cite them merely to point out that they should not be followed. In these instances a great injustice was perpetrated on certain parts of the country by the holding of elections at these particular times.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is a local reason why I think there should be redistribution before an election. The constituency of Nelson is very large. It is approximately
200,000	miles in extent, being about four times as large as all the rest of Manitoba put together. It is in two separate and distinct parts: the southern part, by far the smaller portion, namely, the Swan River Valley, is composed almost entirely of fertile agricultural lands and settled by prosperous farmers, and the northern part, the great stretch of the northland, where almost every industry but farming is carried on. I might say here that this district has capabilities for farming, but these have not yet been brought into operation. Between the centre of the Swan River District and the southern edge or gateway to the great north, between the town of Swan River and The Pas, there is a stretch of railway of two hundred miles-we have to go out into Saskatchewan and back into Manitoba. The electors in the different ends of the constituency think they have no community of interest; they think that in the interests of the whole constituency they should be placed
in different ridings. I am here to represent the views, as far as possible, of those who sent me here. I simply place this matter before the House, not as the main reason, but as an incidental and important reason why I think as I do in this connection.
Now, I propose to place before this House a concrete proposal. I think there is a way whereby we can have both a redistribution and an election. The last speaker intimated that the electors in his district were very strong for redistribution. I think that is a feeling which prevails throughout the whole of the West, also, that the West is pretty strongly in favour of an election; I can come to no other conclusion, notwithstanding statements made here to the contrary, and I am now inclined to think that the East largely entertains the same view. What I suggest, then, is that this House proceed with the necessary business of the session; that it pass whatever legislation may be in the interests of the country at this time; that an adjournment be then made until early fall, and that in the meantime the census be expedited, especially in respect to such returns as are absolutely necessary for the Redistribution Bill. When the House meets in the fall the Redistribution Bill could then be put through, and, as soon as might be thereafter, an election should be held. This would cover the objections raised by various parties to an election without redistribution. With this whole scheme in view, I shall take up the different suggestions in. a little more detail.
I say that the House should proceed with the business of the session; by this I mean not only the extremely urgent business, but such business as may be necessary at this time in the interests of the country. I would not exclude the amendments to the tariff which the Government, I understand, intend to bring down. In fact, I think that it is very important that these tariff proposals should be submitted. If they are brought down-and that is another reason why I wish things to continue as they are for the time being, at any rate-we shall have something definite and concrete in the way of a tariff placed before the House; we shall get a definite idea as to where the different members on both sides really stand. I am not afraid of the issue, and I do not know that any other hon. member is afraid of it. It has been suggested that some are not travelling exactly under the right colours. However, if certain definite proposals are placed before us we shall

know absolutely where the different parties stand; the House and the country will know the policy of the Government, of the Opposition, and of the Progressive party.
I have suggested that after the necessary legislation is put through there should be an adjournment until early fall, not another session. There are precedents for that also. Long adjournments of the Canadian House are mentioned in Bourinot as follows: 1867 to 1868, from the 21st December to the 12th of March, to enable the Government to consider and complete measures. No more important issues were at stake then than are before us at .the present time.	There was an
adjournment in 1873, from the 23rd of May to the 13th of August, to receive the report of the Royal Commission on the Canadian Pacific Railway scandal. The fact is that the House prorogued on the 13th of August without receiving the report; but that does not alter the precedent in any way. The House adjourned from the 23rd of December, 1880, to the 4th of January, 1881, in connection with certain issues relating to the Canadian Pacific contract. In 1911 there was an adjournment from the 19th of May to the 18th of July to enable Sir Wilfrid Laurier to attend the Imperial Conference and the coronation. Notwithstanding the fact that the question of reciprocity was very strongly before the people at that time, the House adjourned for two months. These, precedents are very much to the point, and I think it is fair to say that the issue before the House at present is fully as important as the issues which gave occasion for any of these adjournments. There is in connection with the last adjournment mentioned another degree of similarity, namely, that the Prime Minister and his associates wish to attend the Imperial Conference very shortly. In order that this session may continue at the time I have mentioned, it may be necessary to expedite to some extent the compiling of such portions of the census returns as are necessary for the purpose of bringing down a Redistribution Bill, not generally speaking to quicken up the returns. I am advised by the census authorities that by September sufficient data can be gathered to allow of a Redistribution Bill being drafted, and by the time that this House will need to meet all the returns will be ready. At a reasonable time after the redistribution Bill has been dealt with and passed, a dissolution of Parliament may take place and an election

be held before another session. In his speech the other day the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) accepted the challenge of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) saying in effect: "We are not afraid of an election we desire it as much as you, but we want redistribution first." In fact, I think the general tenor of the remarks of hon. gen-tlement opposite was that they would be glad to have an election, to meet the party to my right or my left, at any time provided redistribution comes first. My proposition would thus appear to be a solution of the difficulties of hon. members on all sides of the House; it is sound, sane, feasible, and, if I may use a word which is somewhat overworked, constructive, and also it is what the country is looking for just now. In order, therefore, to put the matter into definite shape before this House, so that the House will have an opportunity to pass upon it, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis), an amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition as follows:
That all words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Existing political conditions call for redistribution, and a general election at an early date thereafter, and that this Parliament should proceed forthwith to pass such legislation as may be necessary, at this time, in the interests of the country and then be adjourned to the earliest date at which the census returns will be available, for the purpose of making the necessary changes in the Representation Act; and that a general election be held as soon thereafter as possible; and, further, that the work of taking the census and completing such returns as may be necessary for the redistribution for the representation be expedited so far as practicable.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not call in question the form of the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member (Mr. Campbell), but put it to the House subject to more careful inquiry during the dinner hour.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it is necessary for me to take up the time of the House in further congratulating the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) on his elevation to that high office. I have already done that personally. I would, however, like to add my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the Address on the able manner in which they performed their duty.
My intention in taking part in this debate is to touch upon two matters, both of which

are of political importance to Western Canada. The first to which I wish to refer is the matter of bringing on a general election at this time. In the year 1911 an election was sprung upon us just as the census figures were being completed, and for six years, from 1911 to 1917, the province from which I come was represented in this House by seven members instead of twelve, and a similar condition would no doubt arise again if an election were held before redistribution took place. The mover of the amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been recently through the West, and I think he will agree with me when I say that, as leader of his party, he has very little to hope for from the West. To bring on an election at this time would be taking an unfair advantage of particularly the four western provinces. Of recent months, I have been through my constituency a number of times, and I must admit there has been a demand for an election, but only from those who were opposed to this Government in the first place, and particularly from those who were opposed to this Government's war policy. I have not heard of a demand for an election from the Liberals who supported me and who were many; I have not heard of it from the Conservatives who supported me, and there were many of them too. The fact of the matter is that the people in the province of Alberta are not wasting very much time in thinking about party politics; they are attending to their business and going ahead as best they may.	.
The question which I want to deal with particularly and which seems to me of greater importance to the three Prairie Provinces than anything that has as yet been discussed in this House, is the matter of handling the farmer's grain. I need not state that agriculture is now and probably always will be the great industry of those three provinces, and grain growing is the most important branch of agriculture. At the outset I want to say that I agree with the remarks and the suggestions made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) in the latter part of the speech which he made in this House the other day. Everything he said in connection with that subject is the truth, but I want to remind the hon. member that he did not, by any means, tell the whole truth. Indeed, I do not know that there is in this House a member who is fully and well-enough informed upon the subject of handling grain and the disabilities under which the farmers operate to be capable of telling
the whole story. We get small threads of it here and there; we hear rumours, many of which are no doubt true; but they have not been established, and they have not been referred to particularly in this House. Of course, any disability under which the farmer suffers pertains somewhat also to the consumer; but, as is most other lines, the man who is at the primary point of production is the first man to suffer from those injustices. I regret many of those who represent constituencies in the eastern pro-inces are not more fully acquainted with the methods by which grain is handled in Western Canada.
I would like to speak particularly on how completely the farmer is at the mercy of the grain dealer. When you consider that his grain is threshed and harvested and marketed, sometimes as far east as Fort William, in the course of a very few weeks, you can see that a good deal of the work that is done cannot be closely supervised, and the first opportunity the grain dealer has to " get " the farmer is the minute he drives his wagon load of wheat upon the scales of the country elevator. These scales are owned and controlled by the grain dealer, and are operated by one of his employees. A few days before I left my home, my nearest neighbour drove off the scales of a well-known elevator company in our town to the scales of another elevator company, and found there was a difference of eight bushels between the time he left the one company and got to the other. Now that eight-bushel loss means that the farmer was losing from ten to twenty per cent of his wheat, and at this point there will probably ,be marketed this year $1,500,000 of grain. So if all the companies are as dishonest as the one to which I refer attempted to be, there will be a loss of anywhere from $100,000 to $300,000 for the farmers in that way alone, at that one point; and that is only one of thirty-five shipping points in the constituency I represent.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the
House rose at six o'clock I was referring to the methods of some of the grain companies that are operating at country points in the Prairie Provinces. I had mentioned the fact that it had been reported to me that a farmer had driven his load of grain

from one elevator to another and found in doing so that it had increased some eight bushels in weight. That meant probably from 10 to 20 per cent of the value of the whole load of grain, and at the point where I live and market my grain it would mean from $100,000 to $300,000 per year that would be taken out of the farmers of that immediate district. There are in the riding in which I represent some 35 shipping points on the different lines of railway; so that it will be seen that if the Government proposes to do anything towards investigating this condition, the place at which to begin is the beginning, at the country elevators.
It would seem to me that a method could be easily devised to take the weighing away from the elevator companies and place the handling of it under the control and direction of Government officials. In addition to the weighing of the grain at the country elevators, the operator of the local elevator is also charged with the grading of grain under certain conditions, and this is where the small farmer particularly is squeezed. The small farmer who has less than a car-load of grain to ship drives up to the country elevator and is at the mercy of the operator, not only as regards the weighing of the grain, but so far as the grading as well is concerned. Grain sold in this way is refered to as street wheat, and as stated by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Argue), there is no reason why there should be much difference between street wheat and track wheat offered on the market at Fort William. But at one point on one of the lines of railway in my riding there was a difference of as much as 47 cents a bushel between the street wheat and track wheat on one particular day this fall, and at a point within 35 miles of this very place on another line of railway some of the same companies were operating and paying for street wheat only about 20 or 22 cents less than track wheat. There was a combine undoubtedly amongst the elevators operating at the first point-there can he no question in the world about that-and that combine existed for the purpose of killing competitive buying. At the other point the ordinary methods of competitive buying were practised, and the farmers there were coming from greater distances, delivering their wheat and getting a square deal.
There is another phase of the question to which I want to refer, and that is the position in which the operator of the country elevator finds himself. He is an em-

ployee of these large companies, some of them very large indeed, and he is engaged on a salary and put under heavy bonds. He is charged with the responsibility of taking in the grain, weighing it out and grading it, and in many instances paying for it. If there is a bank, payment is made by 'cheque, and if there is not he has to pay in currency. He loads his wheat or other grain into the cars; it is delivered at Fort William and weighed from the cars into the terminal elevators. It is never made known to him during the whole operating season how the cars weigh out. They may be short or over, but the facts are never made known to him, and frequently at the end of the year, after everything is closed up, a representative of the elevator company comes along and without giving particulars, without telling him how these things happened, informs him that he is short, two, or three, or five hundred bushels, as the case may be, and the operator is ordered to make good the shortage. You can see the temptation that is placed in the way of an operator of a country elevator. If he desires to be honest he has the knowledge that this club may be continuously swung over his head. _
I might remind the House that during past sessions we have heard about screenings or dockage, and we got some rather interesting information a session or two ago before a special committee of this House known as the Cost of Living Committee. I would like to explain that if these screenings are under three per cent at Fort William they become the absolute property of the terminal elevator. If they are over three per cent they become the property of the farmer. Now the farmer pays for the threshing of the wheal; that he delivers to the country elevator and he pays there a cent and three quarters a bushel for handling it. He also pays the elevator a commission and he pays the freight. Yet at Fort William, when the screenings are three per cent or under the terminal elevator gobbles the whole thing without having paid one cent in the matter of production, transportation or anything else.

Who pays for the
cleaning of the screenings?

The terminal elevator, but
I would be very glad to go into the terminal elevator business myself if I could get such a concession as I have described. As I say, the farmer pays every other charge, and in two crop years during the war the.

price at the terminal elevator of these screenings was $35 a ton. That is a higher price than is being paid on the market to-day for No. 2 C.W. oats.

Who regulates the
screenings; who makes the recommendations in connection with that matter?

It is perfectly legal, as
I understand, for the terminal elevator to take the three per cent.

My question was, who
makes the recommendation?

I do not know that that
matters. The point is that we want the whole thing investigated in order to bring out the facts. Now as to the matter of overages. That has been fully dealt with by the member for Macdonald (Mr. Hen-ders), and I do not propose to say much upon the subject. I have heard it argued that the terminal elevator should get the overages because it must pay for the shortages. Now I do not know of any more convincing way to answer that argument than to say that such a contention amounts to this:	Because the terminal
elevators pay for what they are caught stealing they should be allowed to get away with what they are not detected in stealing.
A great deal has been sa'id with respect to the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. Properly and honestly conducted, a grain exchange cannot be objected to. It is a legitimate place for buyers and for sellers, just as in the case of other commodities. But the Winnipeg Grain Exchange has become practically the whole channel through which our western wheat reaches the eastern miller and the buyer overseas. One rule that I believe exists with the Winnipeg Grain Exchange is objectionable. The member for Macdonald explained how the prices are fixed at country places. These prices are sent out by the North West Grain Dealers' Association each day, after having been fixed by an officer of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, and the rule to which I refer declares that any member of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange who is found paying a higher price than that authorized by its officer is doomed to expulsion from the organization.
I have had personal experience in this matter. On one occasion I sold three carloads of oats to a member of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. He signed a contract on a certain date and I had the privilege of shipping these oats later on. When I was ready to ship the oats the price had
dropped. They were loaded through the elevator of a well-known grain company and immediately these oats were shipped they wrote and asked me why I had not sold my oats to them. I replied that I had been able to get a higher price than they were willing to pay me.
I immediately got a request for all papers and documents in connection with this transaction, but I refused to comply with the request and, so far as I know, the matter was dropped. But the point I want to make is that if these people are able to penalize the man who goes out into the open competitive market and buys from the farmer at a higher price than the price authorized at Winnipeg, they will do so if they can find a way.
I now want to say a word or two with reference to the Wheat Board. Like every other public institution that Board at one stage of its existence was extremely unpopular, and at another stage it became extremely popular. I am quite sure that if I had been in the hands of fifteen committee men in my riding in the year 1919 they would have enforced my resignation from this House. I am just as sure that if my resignation had then taken place, my successor would also have been re-called last fall because the Wheat Board was not re-established. The fact of the matter is that the unpopularity of the Wheat Board was the result of the persistent and systematic agitation carried out by men who wanted to knock this Government by any means they could employ for the purpose. These men went about the country and told the' people that the participation .certificates or the "anticipation" certificates were next to valueless, and I know one man in my own neighbourhood who, as a result of Hie agitation, took his certificates home and threw them into the stove. Other men sold them in great numbers for a price not greater than twenty-one cents a bushel. Eventually these certificates were redeemed by the Wheat Board at forty-eight cents a bushel. These agitators-and some of them were paid agitators-who went through the country working up this agitation for the sole purpose of knocking the present Government, through the Wheat Board, caused a loss to the farmers which aggregated hundreds and thousands and perhaps millions of dollars. They told the farmers that this Government was their enemy, but they awakened one day to find out that their real enemy was to be found right in their own organization. The Wheat Board rendered efficient and valuable service to the farmers of Western Canada, and I have

here a testimonial which I think ought to bear some weight with the members of this House. This testimonial was given by a member of the Wheat Board, it was given by the man who is the President of the United Farmers of Alberta, Mr. H. W. Wood; it was given at a public meeting attended by some two thousand farmers and the report of the proceedings appeared in a paper which is not always friendly to the present Government, the Edmonton Bulletin. This is a verbatim report from the Edmonton Morning Bulletin:
The Canadian Wheat Board during its existence saved the Canadian farmer 50 millions of dollars and I am certain that if it continues to sell their grain along the same lines as before its abolition by the Government that it would save the farmers of this country several millions more.
The Wheat Board in the past has rendered efficient service and there is no reason why it cannot be continued along efficient operative lines providing you get the right kind of men on the Board. But let me tell you this, just as soon as you get politics and inefficiency mixed up with it then give me the open market.
Now, I want hon. members to note the significance of Mr. Woods' statement. He stated that in handling the wheat crop alone $50,000,000 was saved to the farmers of Western Canada in one year. If the same efficie'ncy and the same good results had been secured from handling all the other grain, that is, the oats, flax, barley and rye, another $50,000,000 would have been saved; that would he $100,000,000, according to the testimony of Mr. H. W. Wood, who is not politically a friend of this Government. I want to emphasize that the ordinary charges made by the Wheat Board for commission, handling, freight, storage and insurance were not less than those under ordinary conditions. So it follows that, if the statement is correct, the farmers of Western Canada this year might have been saved an equal amount, and that in other years they were deprived of this amount of money by the grain dealers.
I think it would be well for the Government to investigate the means of marketing the Western grain when the saving may be so great as $100,000,000 a year. We have got into the habit of thinking in big figures, but let us consider for one minute what $100,000,000 would do. It would pay almost the interest on the national debt; it would build 400,000 miles of rural telephone line-that is worth considering-it would build 2,000 miles of railway; it would put under cultivation 10,000,000 acres of raw prairie land; it is more money than has already been loaned by the Soldiers Settlement Board and it

would pay the duty on all the agricultural implements imported into the Dominion in a period of sixty years.
I have referred to the spread between the street and track wheat and other grain. I have talked to some of those who are of the type I referred to at the beginning of my remarks, and who want an election. They will say that there was not much spread at points on the Canadian Pacific Railway-and they are not altogether wrong in saying so-but that generally speaking the spread was greater on the Grand Trunk Pacific and at Canadian Northern points. But I have the word of the president of one of the largest grain firms in Winnipeg to the effect that both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National handled the western grain this last year better than it had ever been handled before, considering the volume of wheat that was going out. And again I am afraid that there is a little touch of politics in this criticism. It is a curious thing that the men who are to-day damning the Canadian National system are the' men who damned the Canadian Pacific for forty years. They have at last come to the conclusion that the Canadian Pacific Railway is a pretty good institution and that the Canadian National is all wrong.
I want to urge most strongly on the Government that they investigate every phase of the marketing of wheat and other grains from the time the farmer drives his wagon on the scales at the country elevator point to the time the grain reaches Liverpool or until it is handed into the mills in Eastern Canada. I have heard more complaint about the way our grain has been handled this last year, and especially since the farmers got acquainted with the efficiency of the Wheat Board, than I have heard concerning any other phase of the economic life of Western Canada, and I feel sure that if the Government conducts a thorough investigation to find out where the abuses are, and the remedy for those abuses, it will do a greater service to the grain growers of Western Canada than any other action that this Government has taken or can take or that any Government in the past has taken. Certainly the Government will render a greater service to the farmers of these three provinces than anything that has been suggested by our friends in either Opposition party. I hope that such an investigation as was proposed by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) will be proceeded with and that it will have concluded its labours in time to have the

results formulated before the next season's crop is harvested and ready for the market.

Mr. Speaker, this being the eleventh day of the debate on the motion for the adoption of the Address and the amendment offered by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), I feel that so much has been said in support of the amendment that there remains but very little for me to add unless I repeat the arguments already advocated. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition asked by what authority my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and the members of his Ministry presumed to carry on the Government. No reason has as yet been given by the Government and its supporters. It is unnecessary for me to repeat certain points at issue, they having been so well put before this House by my hon. friends the leader of the Opposition and the hon. members for Beauce (Mr. Beland), Gaspe and Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), Brome (Mr. McMaster), St. James (Mr. Rin-fret), Wright (Mr. Devlin), Rimouski, (Mr. D'Anjou), Bellechasse (Mr. Fournier), and Halifax (Mr. Maclean), who have thoroughly explained every phase of the situation. I merely wish to state that I fully endorse all that these gentlemen have said, and I will therefore direct my remarks to other questions.
For a number of years past we have been told by social agitators from their soap boxes and even by so-called statesmen from their places in Parliament or on the public platforms that public ownership of utilities was the panacea for all the ills that affect the body politic. This theory was held up to us as being the greatest advance made in generations by a democratic government towards the full enjoyment by the people of their rights and privileges under the constitution. It may be, Sir, that public ownership in certain countries has increased the control of the people over their natural heritage, but I submit that in this country we have found that the taking over of the railways by the Government has had the contrary effect. In practice, instead of being for the benefit of democracy, public ownership has immeasurably increased the powers of autocracy. We have had a board appointed by the Government, without consultation of the people, and clothed with powers higher and more formidable than those enjoyed by the ministers themselves, answerable to no one, and in the present instance not only incapable of understanding the public mind but of taking part in the progressive ideas of the people. We cannot insist that one of its members be removed for incompetency; we cannot urge upon it that large sections of the country are being badly served by the national railway; we are not permitted to show that it is inefficient in organization and extravagant in operation. It can be proven beyond a shadow of a doubt that contracts are given to favorites of the directors, to the detriment of the railway; that certain sections of the country are granted privileges denied to other sections where the traffic receipts are higher; that in the only province wherein, as a matter of fact, the Government railroads can and do earn more than the cost of maintenance, we are treated with a total disregard of the convenience of the population with respect to returns and service. I shall touch upon this point a little later, Mr. Speaker.
I say that a Government controlled by a body such as this is not democratic, because we have placed ourselves in the hands of a body of men who are not now answerable and, if the intention of the Government is to be followed, never will be answerable to the people,-who may if they will, and do as a matter of fact, carry on the administration of this most important of our national undertakings with inefficiency, incompetency, extravagance and neglect, and that even though the people be groaning under the weight of repeated deficits. It is impossible for us to remove these gentlemen and so in some degree alleviate our financial embarrassment.
May I refer to Mr. Hanna's order preventing railway employees from becoming candidates in elections or taking any part in politics? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that order is absolutely unfair to the railway employees. These men were compelled by the Government to become its employees when it took over the different railways; therefore it is through no fault of theirs if they are now in the employ of the Government, or of the Canadian National Railways. I fail to see why they should be now disfranchised by the Government or its creatures-and you will admit, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Hanna and other officials of the

National Railways are the Government's own creatures.
I said a few moments ago that certain sections of this country were granted privileges denied to other sections where the income is great. I shall refer to one division in particular, take the Montreal and Mont Joli division of the Intercolonial Railway; that division is showing a surplus while the other divisions on the same road are showing deficits. I may say that I repeatedly asked the construction of three subways under railway crossings at very dangerous places in my riding, and was refused all three-one at St. Octave, at a sharp curve; one at Little Metis Station, and one at Ste. Florence. If the officials would only take the trouble to have these places inspected, they would immediately see the justice of my requests.
Further, I asked certain officials of the Intercolonial Railway to prevent certain lumber merchants from piling lumber in the railway yards immediately east of the railway station at Amqui. My reason for making the request was because there were quite a number of residences in the immediate vicinity, the owners of which had to pay premiums for the insurance on their buildings at the same rate as that applicable to the lumber yards. That request also, was refused. Then, on the Montreal and Mont Joli division, why should we not have some men on the dining cars who can speak the French language? We are being asked repeatedly by travelling salesmen and others why we as members of the House cannot have this condition remedied.
The taking over of the railways was forced through this House by the Unionist Government and against the will of the Liberals comprising. His Majesty's loyal Opposition. We contended that Canada was practically bankrupt as a result of our participation in the Great War-and I will say, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's participation in the war did not create such a great national financial liability as did the railway policy involved in the creation of a national railway system. The war cost Canada about $1,800,000,000, while the outstanding indebtedness of the Canadian Northern, [DOT] Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific is admitted to be $1,000,000,000, but is really much more. To this must be added $300,000,000 for the National Transcontinental, and $150,000,000 for the Intercolonial, and then there are such other systems as the Hudson Bay Railway and the smaller non-paying roads. If interest on investment was computed and added, the total

cost of the National system to Canada would equal Canada's expenditure in the Great War. Canada has certainly paid for its railway debauch, but the worst is yet to come. Within three years the capital expenditure necessary for connecting links, replacements and equipment will absorb another hundred million dollars, adding six million more to the annual sixty million dollar deficit which the country must pay for its Government ownership fad. It is costing more to pay railway deficits than it did to run the whole government twenty-five years ago. No one has suggested a feasible solution. The Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk and Intercolonial as one system with a capital not exceeding $250,000,000 might, under efficient management, be made a selfsustaining organization, but load them with the Grand Trunk Pacific and other roads, and the result would be immediate bankruptcy.
To-day, Mr. Speaker, if the truth was known, I believe it would be found that the Government is seeking to unload its pet system of public ownership of railways which was imposed on the Canadian people through the exercise of .closure in the House of Commons, as I predicted on the floor of this House in 1919. Such a government is not giving the public justice, particularly a government which refuses to dissolve Parliament and give the country an opportunity to select a government of the people, by the people and for the people.
In figurative language we say that we liquidate a situation when we set things back in order, when all is arranged for the best and we come back to normal conditions. The war, which had brought about a disorganization of the economic, social and national life of the nation, is over. The treaties have been signed, and even though peace has not altogether been restored, the nations are all doing their best towards effecting a reconstruction of the political as well as the general domestic conditions. We have thus seen England, France, Italy and the United States renew their Parliaments and governments. Peace brought on a new state of affairs and new men were called upon to establish it .
Let us consider what is going on in the economic world and in the social domain. Industry liquidates; commerce liquidates; groupes replace one another and take their pre-war positions; and while, of course, all this does not take place without some contradiction and friction, this reconstruction is for the best, because it is only in this way that in those domains normal con-

ditions will reappear. Why should conditions he different in the political domain? In Canada, the political situation will not be improved until after liquidation, that is to say, when things and men shall have taken their pre-war places, and, Mr. Speaker, it is only by a dissolution of Parliament and a general election that the necessary liquidation will be accomplished. It is known throughout the world to-day, except by a few non-believers, that the Prime Minister is in the position of what "Le Maitre de la Theologie Catholique" calls a usurper, "qui per ambitionem et proceumque illicito modo potestatem adip-iscitur"-"a man who came into power through ambition and by illicit means."
My right hon. friend does not hold his "would-be" mandate from any national group or from any political party except his own self-constituted party, namely, the "National-Liberal Conservative Party," if I may call it such. Therefore, it behooves my right hon. friend, in order to do justice to the people of this country, to dissolve Parliament and to give the electors an opportunity of either ratifying or rejecting his self appropriated mandate.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make any lengthy remarks in this debate; but since the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) has brought forward a request asking that the Government appoint a commission to make a thorough investigation into the handling of grain from the time it leaves the farmers' hands until it * reaches its final destination, I feel that I would be negligent in my duty to my constituents if I did not say something regarding it. I am not going to relate any incidents that have come to my knowledge whereby the farmers have not been getting a fair deal. We have heard several incidents cited by former speakers, and what is common at one point occurs throughout the West.
We have heard a great deal, Mr. Speaker, in this chamber about the discontent and unrest that exists among the farmers of Canada. I believe the key to this unrest and discontent which at present exists, will, if an investigation is made, be found in large measure within the operations of the Canada Grain Act. I know the farmers of my constituency, and they are, in my opinion, reasonable; they are willing to live and let live; all they want is a square deal; but under the conditions under which the grain is at present handled,
they know, if I may be pardoned for using a slang expression, that they are being "trimmed at every turn."
We have also heard in this chamber statements made as to the money paid in duties to this Government by farmers of the West. I believe the money paid in duties by the farmers of the West, in comparison with the money lost through the present method of handling grain, is a mere bagatelle. I would strongly endorse the request of the hon. member for Macdonald, that this Government appoint a commission to investigate the grain trade, and do it at the earliest possible moment, so that the farmers of the West may be able to take advantage of it during the coming year.
There is another matter that I wish to bring to the attention of the Government, Mr. Speaker, and that is winter grazing on the forest reserves. At the present time ranchers living in the vicinity of these reserves have the privilege of getting a permit to graze cattles or horses on them, these permits being good for six months, from May 1 to October 31. I believe the rate charged is seven cents per head per month, and is_ charged for the six months. In the^ past this six months' regulation wa3 not rigidly enforced, and ranchers who lived on the edge of the reserve and those who were surrounded by it and who had secured their land before the reserve was set aside, let their cattle graze on these lands later than October 31. Last summer the department issued strict instructions that winter grazing was not to be permitted, with the result that these ranchers who lived on land adjoining the reserve or within its boundaries found themselves in the position that they had nowhere to run their cattle during the winter months. I believe the regulations were changed in the early months of the winter, allowing ranchers who were in this position to obtain special permits to run their cattle as in former years, but they were informed that in future these special winter permits would not be continued.
What I ask is that the Government allow winter grazing on these forest reserves. The ranchers are willing to pay the additional fees, if any, and I am sure that the Government will find use for the money so collected. If there was a lack of grass on these reserves, I could see the wisdom of not allowing winter grazing, but there is plenty of grass at present; in fact, I do not think there are fifty per cent of the cattle in this district that there were two

years ago. On account of the dry year and the high prices for cattle in 1919, the ranchers sold everything that was salable; the winter of 1919-20 was very severe, and the loss to the ranchers was from 10 to 30. per cent. I am not speaking from hearsay; I was oyer parts of the reserve last fall, and I may say that I never saw more grass on it, at that time of the year, than I did then. I have received from the ranchers several letters regarding winter grazing, one of which contains certain statements that I would like to put on Hansard. It is from George Porter, of Maycroft, Alberta:
In taking up this question of winter grazing upon the Forest Reserves you will understand that we are not discussing the reserves as a whole, but just that section in which ourselves and a few other ranchers are interested, namely the porcupine Hills and part of the Rocky Mountain Reserves.
Ourselves and a few others have been running stock in this district for close on to twenty years, some much longer. We realize other reserves have different conditions. Some have no ranchers located within their boundaries, others are only used as summer grazing ground, as, for instance, the Gap Country behind the Livingstone range. On account of the depth of snow and the different quality of the grass, all the average winter cattle would perish if left there. With us in the foothills conditions are entirely different, as, on account of the grass curing and open water, cattle and horses do well in the winter.
We, along with a few others, are located in practically the middle of the reserve, and in our case we have leaseholds scattered throughout the reserve which were acquired before there was any reserve. Since the reserve was formed we have been surrounded, and if you deprive us of winter grazing you force us to discontinue as we have no place else to run our stock, our leases being so mixed up with the grazing on the reserve that it is impossible to use one without the other. Considering the state of the stock industry to-day, we feel sure once you are aware of the facts in connection with our case it would not be the policy of the Government to close us out.
Unlike the farmer and the man residing on the outside of the reserve who have other lands upon which to run their stock in the winter, and, other interests, such as grain farming, our sole business is the raising of live stock.
We settled here many years ago when very few people would think of living this far away from civilization ; in fact, it is still considered about the jumping off place.
This part of the reserve is an exceedingly rough country, broken up by high ridges and deep ravines; also a big percentage is not available for grazing on account of being covered with poplar-and willow brush, as the topographical map of this district will show. The coulees running up towards the ridges have numerous poisonous plants growing in them, such as larkspur, water hemlock, wild parsnip, etc., etc., so the stock has to be kept out of these places in the spring, but as the plants are harmless in the fall and winter we use that grass then, also the high ridges up toward

the timber, for in the summer the bull-dog and black flies are so bad there that it is impossible to keep stock there, and they stay on the flats. From this you will see that there are only parts of the country available for summer use. It is a kind of law of nature where she reserves certain parts for fresh grass during the fall and winter. A peculiar thing about these poisonous plants is that they are not found to any extent further west of us in the Gap Country behind the Livingstone Range but seem confined to the foothills. Some years the poison is much worse than others, but any stock that are not kept out of these places in the spring and early summer have a big percentage of their number die.
The grass is there, and we are willing to pay for it; so why deprive the rancher within the reserve and who has leaseholds upon the same of the right to use it? On account of the preceding summer being so dry that no feed would grow, and the very severe winter last year, most of us lost about fifty per cent of our cattle. Why cripple the industry further? It looks to most of us like the proverbial last straw. We run about two hundred horses here, and have spent a lot of time and money in buying pure bred stallions, and otherwise improving the herd. If this regulation goes into effect it is all time and money wasted, as we have no place else to run them, and with the state the horse market is in at present it is impossible to sell them. Another thing; we have invested here in ranch equipment, etc., several thousand dollars, also have spent a lot of money in fencing the boundaries of the reserve and putting up different drift fences to handle the stock better. You will realize that we are in a much different position from the man outside the reserve who has not a cent invested and no interest at all within the reserve.
Do not be under the impression that the rancher runs his cattle out all winter without any feed. We put up all the green feed we can raise and what wild hay is available; as the cattle go down in flesh they are taken in and fed, and as the spring draws close a rancher is feeding everything except horses and big steers. If he had to take his stock in off these grazing areas all at once they would soon eat up his supply of feed, also it would be a useless waste of feed as stock stay in good shape until spring. At the present time we have cattle that are in beef condition running on the range.
The letter in which the above was enclosed was dated January 28, 1921. I have known the writer since he came to Alberta some twenty years ago, and I know that the statements he makes there are correct.
We have heard a great deal from the other side of the House on the question of the Government's mandate. Hon. gentlemen opposite contend that this Government has no mandate from the people to continue in office, and that they should resign and go to the country. In this connection I wish to say that during my campaign there was nothing said about the Government, if returned, remaining in power only for the duration of the war; in fact, the late Secretary of State, the

Rt. Hon. A. L. Sifton, when speaking in behalf of the Government at Macleod and High River, in my constituency, said that if the Government was returned it would, in all probabilty, remain until after redistribution, and that at the next election, instead of the West having, as at present, fifty-five members representing them, they would have seventh or seventy-five. This will show, Mr. Shaker, that it was expected that Parliament would run its full term. These statements of Mr. Sifton's will be found in the Calgary and other papers that quoted his speeches at different points in Alberta.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I have the interests of the farmers of the West just as much at heart as any of the hon. members who belong to the Agrarian party. I have never been asked to resign, nor have I ever heard that it was even intimated that I should resign. But, Mr. Speaker, if I had crossed the floor of the House, I would have expected those of my constituents who voted for me to ask me for my resignation.
In conclusion, I wish to thank the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) for bringing to the attention of the Government and the members of this House the necessity of having an investigation into the grain trade.

Therefore, I purpose after the example set by my hon. colleagues from Nicolet (Mr. Trahan), from Hull (Mr. Fontaine), from Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou) and others, to say in my^maternal tongue, so beautiful, so expressive and so sweet to the ears of whoever can understand and appreciate it, what I think of the present Governement, of its policy in general, and of the amendment proposed by the hon. Before going over the three points I have first mentioned, I protest in the name of the province of Quebec and of the county which I have represented in this House for the last twenty-four years, against the intended and premeditated insult offered us in not having the Address in response to the Speech from the Throne moved or

Mr. Speaker, I conclude by'saying that this Government does not enjoy any more the confidence of the country, because they have usurped power by treading under foot its constitutional liberties; that the time has come for an appeal to the people who are eager to pass judgment upon those who have bungled what we hold most dear: our democratic system.
There is but one way to carry out the designs of the people who are clamouring for a general election; it is to vote for the amendment of my leader-the authorised, avowed and admired leader of the liberal party.
I know beforehand those who will vote against this amendment. First, the whole

Government, because they do not want to get out, then Liberals who disowned their leader and their party and who are not courageous enough to let go such a fat portfolio. Then, again, those who will never be returned to this House and who are over anxious to lay hold of their $4,000 indemnity for a session or two longer; also, those craving for power or sponging upon the government, who are counting on senator- or judgeships and-the last but not the least-the high priests of protection, the pillars of the big interests who well know that, on the day when the Government vanishes, they will no longer be the masters of the new administration.
The Government may have a majority, but it will be neither real nor disinterested and, consequently, it will be impossible for it to last long, for the day is not far distant when Canada will witness in the place of honourable gentlemen opposite a new administration truly liberal and national, and anxious to put an end to the great crisis we are going through at the present time.
