I desire to say just a few words in regard to the amendment to the amendment introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell.) From	what I	could glean,its import	is that	redistribution
his mind, is of such importance that it is the duty of this Government to adjourn the House after supply is voted and certain urgent business is concluded, let the census be taken in the month of June, let the statistics be compiled by the Department of Trade and Commerce, and after the data are ready let us again meet here and pass a redistribution bill and then go to the country and get the verdict of the people as to who should govern this nation at the present time. Well, I do not agree with the amendment, because I do not think that, if we adjourned the House in May or June it would be possible to meet again, as sug-
gested by the hon. member, before December or January; and this would make it absolutely infeasible. Therefore, on that ground I cannot support the amendment to the amendment.
It was not my intention to participate in this debate, but a very important question indeed has been interjected, a question that is agitating the minds of the western farmers, and that is the grain trade. I shall not deal with the various irrelevant arguments that have been put forward in regard to the want of confidence amendment introduced by the leader of the Opposition. I should not like to pass, however, without concurring in the many expressions of congratulation and words of commendation already uttered in reference to the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Mclsaac), who moved the address, and the newly elected Government supporter from Yale in British Columbia (Mr. MacKelvie). Nor can I let this opportunity pass without extending my congratulations to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen). To my mind, a man of his intellect, ability, sagacity and honesty of purpose well merits the high honour which has been bestowed upon him, and I have no doubt if he is given an opportunity he will guide Canada's destinies in safe, sane and successful channels. I do not want to be accused of any lack of courtesy towards the leaders of the dual Opposition, and I will say that they have my very best wishes. They are both very estimable gentlemen, and though, in my opinion, they are mistaken in their firm conviction of what is right and wrong so far as certain policies are concerned, yet I believe they have a duty to perform, and in that duty as leaders of the Opposition they have my best wishes that they may remain in that capacity for years to come.
That is a chestnut

I will not touch the tariff. When the Budget proposals are brought down there will be ample opportunity to deal with matter affecting the tariff. The country has been put to a great expense in connection with tariff revision, a commission having travelled from coast to coast to obtain information regarding the fiscal needs of Canada, and when the Budget proposals of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) are brought down, based upon his findings, there will be ample opportunity for every hon. member to voice his sentiments and record his vote according to his views on the fiscal necessities of the country.

Owing to the great strain and strenuous endeavours occasioned by the war, this is the first opportunity since the cessation of the activities of the late struggle that the Government, or any member of it, has had of putting before the people of Canada its policy. The Prime Minister has been travelling from coast to coast outlining, where ever he has spoken, the policy of the Government, which is uniformly the same. The leader of the Opposition also has been making a tour of Canada, hut we find him most inconsistent. As he travels through territories different from a geographical standpoint, where interests are not identical, we see that he has a policy to suit every individual district. And so far as the leader of the National Progressives, as they style themselves, is concerned, I am sure that hon. members, as they listened to his statement of his policy, could hear the echoes from afar of such men in the past as the late Sir Richard Cartwright and others who shared his views on fiscal matters. However, I do not think that one need have very much mental aptitude to realize, despite the rambling and the vaporizing to the contrary of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), that there is a collusion between those two great leaders.
A collision?

No, a collusion:	an alliance if you prefer; or, if I may put it in other language, a confusion of harmony, the confusion being for the sole purpose of misleading the people. They are out and they want to get in, and if I have an opportunity of discussing in this House the Budget proposals of the Minister of Finance, I hope to be able to deal more thoroughly with what the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) described as the political foot-ball of Canada. Now, I think I have given one reason why the amendment of the leader of the Opposition should not be accepted, and that is the fact that the Tariff Commission is about to revise the artiff, which will mean stability for Canada. That is what we need. If the Government were to take the advice of the leader of the Opposition and resign, and if the Governor General called upon him to form a Government, it would mean possibly a year of unrest and instability so far as fiscal matters are concerned; and that is one good reason for postponing an election until the constitutional period has expired.
Self-preservation.

I believe there is an alliance between the leaders of the dual Opposition for a purpose. You have heard, Mr. Speaker, the well-known expression: "Two minds with but a single thought; two hearts that beat as one". Well, I believe that these words are eminently applicable to these hon. leaders. I have the platform which was adopted by the Organized Farmers of Canada. I see that in one of their planks they advocate the reform of the Federal Senate. I do not know what they propose in the way of reform, but I hope it will not be along the line recommended by a certain Senator from Manitoba. I certainly believe there are ways in which the Senate can be reformed. At the present time the representation in the Senate of various provinces is not on a fair basis according to territory. At the present time the province of Saskatchewan is entitled to six senators. We have four now and there are two vacancies. The present senators are: Hon. Messrs. Ross and Willoughby of Moosejaw, Laird of Regina, and Turriff, who at present, I believe, is domiciled in the city of Ottawa, I would point out that the present senatorial representation is grouped around Regina, within a radius of forty or fifty miles, and all central and northern Saskatchewan is unrepresented in the Senate.
Now I believe that instead of having appointments to the Senate made on the prerogative of the Prime Minister, who nominates whom he sees fit, every province should be divided into senatorial districts and senators should be elected for those districts and be compelled to reside in the district which they represent. Further, I believe that the election to fill any Senate vacancy should be according to the rules which now govern elections to the House of Commons. The right of sitting in the Senate should also be accorded to women. This Government, and I am glad of it, has extended the suffrage to women and they are now entitled to sit in this Chamber as well as in the Provincial Legislatures I see no reason why they should not be enabled to sit in the Upper Chamber of this Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal of talk with respect to matters which may possibly be termed parochial. But the question of freight rates is not a parochial one. In the West we feel that, under the judgments rendered by the Board of Railway Commissioners, we are particularly discriminated against. It was especially hard, Sir, to have an in-

creased rate go into effect about October 1, last year, when we were starting to ship our grain. I believe it to be the duty of this Government-and I give the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) credit for advocating the same thing-to ask for the resignation of the Board of Railway Commissioners if they will not do justice to Western Canada. Now, interlocked with the subject of freight rates is the matter of the operation of the Canadian National Railway which unfortunately has a large deficit every year. In my opinion the Government should plan out a re-organization of the directorate and general management of that system. As long as deficits continue in the operation of the Canadian National System of Railways, there will be a demand for the enforcement of the existing, and possibly higher, freight rates; and therefore this Government should ask for the resignation of the present management in order that a thorough re-organization may be brought about and experts appointed to efficiently operate the system.
I believe, Sir, that Canada, as far as possible, should live on its own resources. In saying that I have reference to the large amount of money that is spent in importing coal from United States. Now in Eastern Canada as well as in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, we have vast coal fields; and I believe it would be a good policy on the part of the Government if they could so arrange railway freight rates, and the rates of our own merchant marine, as to bring western coal at a reasonable price from the head of the Great Lakes to the consumers of the East. I notice that the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) has a resolution on the Order Paper dealing with the matter of the coal supply of Canada, and I am very pleased indeed that the hon. member is bringing this important subject to the attention of the House.
This leads me to the grain situation, a very important matter from my point of view as a Western member. I was very much gratified when the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) brought this matter forward. During the war the grain trade channels were very much disrupted. In i917, owing to price fluctuations, the Government in their wisdom thought it better to fix the price for our wheat. The same course was adopted in 1918. In 1919 there was great uncertainty. The then Minister of Agriculture, now the leader of the National Progressive Party (Mr. 
Crerar), in many communications to me, stated that the Government could not do anything, that owing to the grain trade being in such an unstable condition it was not possible to make any provision from the public treasury. That hon. gentleman later burned his bridges behind him and left the Government. We have heard it stated that there was opposition to the establishment of the Wheat Board. I do not wish to lay myself open to the charge of making unfair accusations, but as a western member I feel that some of us on this side who represent constituencies in Saskatchewan are not being fairly dealt with as far as the Wheat Board is concerned. I am not going to eulogize the work of the Wheat Board because other hon. gentlemen who have already spoken have done so effectively. But there was opposition to the creation of the Wheat Board. The Government organized that Board in the face of direct opposition from the farmers. The member from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), a very estimable gentleman, speaking on May 21st, 1920, as reported at page 2365 of Hansard, expressed himself as follows:
The hon. gentleman who has preceded me touched on one of these (statements) and that is the Wheat Board. We did not ask for the Wheat Board. The inference, if not the statement, is to the effect that the farmers asked for the Wheat Board. One hon. member described it as the pooling of our wheat. While the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) stated that the Government appointed the * Wheat Board I want to go further and say that the Government did it against the strong opposition of the farmers of this country. The farmers did not want it and they did not ask for it.
Now, I think that settles the point beyond all question.

If the hon. member
wishes to be fair, will he please continue and read further from that speech?

I will do so, I do not want to be unfair. It says:
The farmers did not want it, and they did not ask for it. But if the Government stepped in, took possession and broke down the lines which had been built up, financially and otherwise, and if there is pooling in the buying of wheat overseas-
I suppose that is what the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) refers to.
-we have no hesitation in saying that we con>-sider it the proper course for our Government to carry out pooling in the selling of wheat, just so long at least as there was pooling in buying from us.
Nevertheless, there is the plain statement, Sir, that they were in opposition to

the formation of the Wheat Board. However, as I say, I am not going to refer to the workings of the Wheat Board. We all know that it was a success in spite of what the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) said on Friday night, that he was not personally opposed to the formation of the Wheat Board. Yet in his maiden speech in this House he said that he had visited many elevators in North Dakota and they were paying $3.05 a bushel there; that the American farmer was pocketing $1.11 more than the Canadian farmer; that the farmers in his constituency were receiving 70 cents to $1 less a bushel for their wheat; that his participation certificates were in a box at home, and he was quite convinced in his own mind that he would get less for his wheat than was paid to the American farmer. Well, it was very interesting when the report of the Wheat Board was tabled, which showed that the Canadian farmer received about 25 cents a bushel more on the average for his wheat than the American farmer did, owing to the working of the Wheat Board.
Then, Sir, we come to the enabling resolution which would havfe enabled this Government, if they saw fit, to re-establish the Canada Wheat Board. I will give my hon. friend from Maple Creek due credit for very heartily supporting that resolution, merely to show that I do not want to b(e unfair to him. But the member for Assiniboia in speaking on that enabling resolution was not quite so certain about what he wanted as the hon. member for Maple Creek. At page 4112, volume 5, of Hansard, I find the member for Assiniboia is reported as saying:
I do not wish my remarks to be interpreted as indicating that I am diametrically opposed to this legislation or entirely in sympathy with it.
He was climbing the fence.

I do not wish to be unfair to the hon. member for Assiniboia. He said just at the conclusion of his speech:
I propose to vote for the re-establishment of the Wheat Board this year. I pledge myself only for this year.
I think that kind of support was not likely to give this Government very much backbone towards re-establishing the Wheat Board. We know that the leader of the National Progressive party was not in sympathy with it; he was honest in his conviction, but he was opposed to it. He stated in Hansard:
Personally, I am opposed entirely to any permanent policy which means control of the marketing of the grain of this Country.
I suppose there was a reason why he was opposed to such a policy. But when we consider that the Grain Growers' Grain Company and the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company handled about one-third of the total wheat crop of the Prairie Provinces, I believe they should have given the Government a more sympathetic support towards the re-establishment of the Wheat Board.
May I ask what my hon. friend means by the word "they?" He was speaking of two companies and said that they should have given more enthusiastic support.
I mean the directors of both companies and all concerned with their operation, because, Mr. Speaker, they are supposed to be the champions of the farmers of Saskatchewan.

May I ask my hon. friend if he is aware that at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company, about two months after the Wheat Board came into existence, they passed a unanimous resolution asking for a continuance of the national marketing of our grain?

I think I saw that in the press. But what I am getting at is the fact that there was not the enthusiastic support of the organized grain companies in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta that there should have been. The situation is this, that the member for Assiniboia last week delivered a tirade of abuse against the Government, and yet when this enabling resolution was being discussed in the House he did not seem to know his own mind.
Throughout the West there has been an agitation for the formation of a wheat pool. This is a copy of the questionnaire which has been sent out from the Grain Growers' Guide Limited, It says:
Enclose one dollar and answer questions contained hereon.
I do not know whether the Grain Growers' Guide is more concerned about its subscription list, or about the farmers' dilemma in connection with the marketing of their grain. However, I have been ' hoping that the organizations of the farmers would formulate some feasible scheme. I would heartily support a wheat pool or any other scheme which would

enable us to handle our grain in a more efficient manner than we are able to do it under the present system. We see nothing in the press that anything has been formulated. I would certainly urge them to formulate a wheat pool or some other stabilizing agency which will enable us in Western Canada to get rid of many of the grievances with which we are hampered to-day.
I was very glad indeed that the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) urged the Government to appoint a Royal Commission to look into ! the many grievances, major and minor, affecting the grain trade of Canada. I would not like to see this left to the Board of Grain Commissioners; I would rather see an independent Royal Commission appointed, clothed with proper authority to investigate every phase of the grain trade. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Blair) said, "Start at the country elevator and continue to the mills in Europe if necessary." I am going to read a tabulated statement which covers the ground very thoroughly:
That a commission be appointed to investigate: the grading and weighing of grain; the receiving, handling and shipping of grain through country elevators and from country points; the operation of grain exchanges by the members thereof; the work of grain exchanges ; the handling of grain at terminal points; the holding of grain at terminal points; the operation of public and private terminal elevators and eastern public elevators; the operation of the Lake Shippers' Clearance Association ; the operation of the North-west Grain Dealers' Association ; the trimming of grain at the upper and lower lake ports and ocean ports; lake shipments; the shipment of grain to Atlantic and Pacific ports; the operation of Canadian flour and feed mills.
Another thing, Sir, is, I think, of great importance. We have a report from the Quebec Board of Trade which says that in the six years from 1912 to 1918, 1,096 million bushels of grain were shipped from Fort William by water. Of this vast quantity, the:e were sent to Port McNicoll, Port Colborne, Midland and other Georgian Bay ports, for the suuply of all the flour mills in Eastern Canada-some of which was subsequently shipped by rail to New York, Portland, etc., for export, and a small quantity to Montreal and St. John-578 million bushels. To Buffalo-the greater part afterwards sent to New York and other United States seaports for export-there were sent 518 million bushels.
I believe the condition here revealed is a mistake from a Canadian national viewpoint. We have three great transcontinental lines of railway. We have the ports of Montreal,* Quebec, Halifax, St.

John, and I do not see why one bushel of our wheat should reach New York. We have the Transcontinental Railway going into Quebec with a shorter mileage between Quebec and the West than either of the two transcontinental railways. We have an excellent natural harbour at that port, and for the life of me I cannot see why we do not use it. This is another matter which, in my judgment, should be taken into consideration by this Royal Commission-the facilities for marketing our grain and shipping it to Liverpool by Canadian ports only, thus preventing the loss of the identity of our hard wheat through the American practice of mixing it with their soft wheat.
I think there are three main reasons why this Government should carry on at the present time. I cannot see that there has been any really urgent demand for an election from the majority of the people. No matter what Government is in power, there will always be demands from certain quarters for their resignation. As many speakers have reiterated during the course of this debate, not one charge of scandal or graft or corruption can be brought against this Government-a wonderful record. I believe it is the only Government of this country that has been free from taint of graft or corruption, and that consideration should commend itself to the electors. The second reason I referred to a few moments ago-that we want tariff revision and that we want Budget proposals brought down based on the tariff revision with a view to creating that degree of stability in our industries on which the employment of labour depends.
The hon. member for Nelson said that it was very important that we should have redistribution. Why, Sir, we in Western Canada will gain from fifteen to twenty seats after redistribution, and any person in that part of the country who votes for an election before redistribution is not acting in accordance with the wishes of the people out there. Personally I have received more requests that dissolution of this Parliament should not take place until after redistribution than requests to go to the country immediately. In the election campaign of 1917 the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, in his manifesto to the electors, stated that Canada would gain twenty-two seats by redistribution and that there were twenty-four vacancies in the House of Commons. Well, Sir, in war time, when the very existence of our people was at stake, the leader of the Opposition of that day thought it of sufficient importance to

go to the country on account of having possibly twenty-two additional representatives from the West. It is even more advisable that we should now wait until redistribution takes place, after the census in June, before holding an election.
The leader of the National Progressive party seemed to be very much alarmed over what might happen when the redistribution Bill was brought down. He seemed to fear that almost a crime would be committed in the way the country would be gerrymandered. Well, Sir, if we are spared we will be in the House when the redistribution bill is being discussed, and I will stand shoulder to shoulder with the member for Marquette and vote against the Government if they attempt to do anything of that nature. I think, however, that his fears are groundless, because we have an honest Prime Minister, a man who Would not permit the perpetration of such a crime.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) said, with regard to redistribution, that it was a matter of
10 p.m. principle; that hon. gentlemen from the West were capable of looking after the interests of the West- members who will be returned at the next election, and members who are here now. That created a suspicion in my mind, because it is well known that the province from which he comes will probably lose some members when redistribution takes place. I believe that the hon. member was speaking purely from a selfish point of view when he spoke that way.
I have tried during the course of my rambling remarks to make it quite plain that it is my intention to vote against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition. I believe it is my duty, particularly as a western member, to carry on here until we get proper representation for Western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, before touching upon any of the matters which are of interest to the country at this time, I wish to join with those who have preceded me in congratulating the mover (Mr. Mclsaac), and the seconder (Mr. MacKelvie), of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, whose addresses contained very much information of interest to the House and to the country. Coming, as they do, one from each extreme end of Canada, these hon. members have given us information regarding their particular parts of the country which should
be helpful to the members of the House and to the people generally.
I wish also, before going further, to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen), upon his elevation to the position which he now occupies. It is truly an exalted position and one which carries with it very great responsibilities indeed.
I feel sure that the right hon. gentleman, with his ability and his sincerity, will bring to the duties of his office the very best that is in him, and will do all he can to further the interests of the great Dominion and administration of whose affairs has been committed to his charge. I believe that the people of Canada generally are satisfied with the choice. I am sure that when it was announced that the right hon. gentleman was selected to lead the Government of this country a sigh of relief was breathed by the citizens generally upon realizing that such an able man had been selected to look after the destinies of Canada. Of course, our friends across the floor will, perhaps, not agree with what I have to say, but I am satisfied that the great majority of the Canadian people think as I do on the subject of an election. I know throughout the western part of this Dominion, at any rate, and, I believe in the province of Ontario and the other provinces, there is really no great demand for an election at this time; in fact, I am satisfied that the very opposite is the desire of the people, that is, they are quite content that the Prime Minister and the present Government should carry on.
Last session the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) in speaking on the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne, seemed to be very much worried because no hint of policy was contained in that speech. He said that it was empty and barren and dealt more with matters of a foreign nature than with domestic matters. This year, when a definite policy was laid down and a number of very important matters were dealt with in the speech from the Throne, he refused entirely to deal with them. He sidestepped the issue, and ever since this debate opened his supporters, following his example, sidestepped the issue also. It is perhaps policy on their part to do that; but we know and the people know and hon. gentlemen occupying benches across this Chamber know that my hon. friends opposite will not be in a position to do that when they come face to face with the electors of this Dominion; they will then be compelled to face the issue and to deal with the facts. I am satisfied that the great issue that will

be brought before the people at the next general election will be the tariff issue, and my hon. friends opposite will be compelled to deal with that on every platform throughout the Dominion. The leader of the Opposition, instead of meeting the issue fairly and squarely, endeavoured to draw, as it were, a red herring across his trail; he endeavoured to divert the minds of the people and the members to some other issue which is really not an issue at the present time. Through the medium of Parliament he told the people that the great issue at this time was that of a general election, but there is really no such demand. He referred to the Government and its supporters as usurpers of office and office seekers. To my mind, that charge, particularly the one referring to members as office seekers, rebounds like a boomerang on the head of the hon. gentleman, because a charge like that cannot be sustained. We know members occupying the treasury benches are in office at present and are likely to be in office for some time, and consequently, the men who are office seekers at the present moment are hon. gentlemen opposite. I think that is quite clear. Their object in trying to bring about a general election at this time is to get a snap verdict from the people. It has been stated in this House by many speakers-and we know it to be a fact-that the members of the Government during the past three years were so busy with problems arising out of the war and after-war problems, which were many, difficult and knotty, problems such as the statesmen of this Dominion have never before been called upon to wrestle with, that they were not in a position to inform the country as to what had been done and what they intended to do. In the meantime, the Opposition to a man-and I include both branches of that Opposition-were busy throughout the country trying to create a sentiment unfavourable to this Government. To some extent they have succeeded in doing that, and they believe, after they have succeeded in creating a sentiment largely unfavourable to the Government, they may be in a position to win a snap verdict from the people and consequently be returned to office, but I do not think there is much chance of that. If the Prime Minister and his ministers carry on and complete the work that they have been engaged in, the people, after the case has been fully explained to them, will realize that they have had, during the troublesome times through which we have passed, 
a Government that has been capable, honest, and sincere in purpose.
I should like to say a word regarding the matter of our home market, which I consider would be jeopardized if hon. gentlemen who occupy seats at the extreme end of the Chamber on your left, Sir, were returned to power. Of course, they will say that this is a matter which the old political parties, particularly the Conservative party, have held up for years as a bogey before the people of this Dominion, and have succeeded in obtaining their votes in that way. But I am satisfied that if their policy was put into force in this country, it would be a real menace, not only to the manufacturing interests but to the farming interests as well, because they are dependent to some extent on each other. The farming industry alone never made a country great and wealthy; to bring that about manufacturing industries are required as well; in fact, I believe the success of the farming industry of any country lies largely with the manufacturing interests. Their interests are indissolubly bound up together and the one cannot be separated from the other. I have heard it stated on many occasions, and I think I have heard the statement made in the House, that 85 per cent of the products of Canada are consumed and used in the Dominion. I do not know whether that is correct or not, but I am sure, Sir, you will agree with me when I say that if that be the fact, that means a great deal to the farming interests of this Dominion, because it certainly means that the home market is a valuable market to our farmers. Anything that would help to reduce that market or to curtail its purchasing power in any way would certainly not be in the interests of the farmers. I am satisfied that the most valuable market that a country can have is its home market. We have had evidences of that every day, and particularly during the last few years. We know that Great Britain at the present time has an embargo against Canadian cattle. In 1919, I believe it was, we had the spectacle of the United States placing an embargo against Canadian wheat and at present they are raising the duties against Canadian grain and other products of the farm. Consequently, we must look to our own markets to take the produce of our farms, if we wish to be an inde-t pendent people as far as agriculture is concerned. The Fordney Bill, which passed the Senate quite recently, aims at protecting the farmers and producers of the United

States. I think there is a lesson in that lor the Canadian people. If in a countrylike the United States, where they have a better climate than ours for producing certain lines of produce, it has been found necessary to protect their farming interests, surely it is necessary for the Canadian people living adjacent to that great republic to do something to protect our interests along the same line.
I want to join hands with the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) in his request for a commission to investigate the Canadian wheat trade from the time the grain leaves the farmer's wagon till it arrives at its destination, wherever that may be. I am satisfied that many of the elevator companies and others handling the farmer's grain are making immense profits on their handling, through overages, and in many other ways. Some hon. member has already dealt this evening with the difference between the track price and the price on the street. The spread there is, in my opinion, unwarrantable, and I think it is unwarrantable in the opinion of any member who has given any study to this question at all. I strongly support my hon. friend's request for a commission to investigate the grain trade in all its phases and aspects, to ascertain wherein conditions can be bettered in the handling of the grain, and see that the profits shall accrue to the farmer and not to the elevator companies or the men engaged irr the handling of the crop.
The leader of the Opposition, in his great hurry to introduce a motion of want of confidence in this Government, overlooked another very important matter which was mentioned in the speech from the Throne. I refer to old age pensions and unemployment insurance. This did not seem to strike the leader of the Opposition or any of his followers as being worthy of any notice whatever. I do not know what the labour representatives sitting behind the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) thought, when not only the leader of the Opposition overlooked this very important question, but their own leader practically said there was no need of old age pensions or unemployment insurance at this particular time. I believe the labour interests of this country are keenly alive to the necessity of some kind of unemployment insurance, and I should like to quote from a little pamphlet issued by the Labour Congress of Canada, dated February 1921, and entitled "Legislative Programme of the Trades and
Labour Congress of Canada." Dealing with this question of unemployment insurance, they say:'
If any argument were needed as to its necessity it has been fully furnished during the past few months when thousands of good Canadian citizens have suffered through lack of employment and through fear of its consequences. We recommend the enactment of unemployment insurance embodying certain principles.
Then they go on to state what those principles should be. I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Marquette state that unemployment insurance was not necessary at the present time.
I think the matter of unemployment insurance and old age pensions is one of the vital questions confronting the Canadian people at this time, and it is one that will have to be solved by the statesmen of this country in the near future. Unemployment has always existed in this country, and it will always continue to exist, because we are largely an agricultural people, and agriculture employs men for only six or eight months in the year. After that, they have to look elsewhere for employment. Now, if the greatest and basic industry of this Dominion can afford employment to men only for a portion of the year, unemployment will naturally continue to exist in this country, and this question of unemployment is one of the big problems with which we are face to face at the present time. I repeat, I was surprised to hear the leader of the Agra rian party treat this subject of vital importance so lightly. I do not know what the feelings of the labour people of this country will be when they know that both leaders of the two parties aspiring to come into power in this country and take charge of the destinies of Canada did not see fit to devote more than a minute of their time to this question of supreme importance to the labour men of this country. It is a question that will have to be grappled with sooner or later, and personally I would support any system of old age pensions and unemployment insurance that would not throw the burden on the Federal Government or even on the Provincial Governments. I would support a system of old age pensions and unemployment insurance that would compel the men who would get assistance from that fund to contribute something towards it. I feel that is the only reasonable way of bringing into force a system that would be of assistance to the labouring men during periods of unemployment.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has covered a very wide range, and the ground has been pretty well covered, I think, since the opening of the debate two weeks ago. Anything I might add would simply be a re-hash of arguments that have been made before, but in closing I just wish to give this little bit of advice to the Prime Minister. It is this: that he carry on. I believe that the people of this Dominion expect him to carry on.
They are struck with his sincerity and his honesty of purpose in endeavouring to give the country a good Government. They were struck with his sincerity as he went through the country a few months ago laying down the same policy in different parts of the country and not varying his policy to suit the different districts in which he spoke. There was no vaciliation about his policy; there was no trying to shift matters to other shoulders or to get away from the issue in any way. His policy was clear-cut, straight and above board. That is what the people are looking for and I am satisfied that after they have been enlightened as to what the Government has accomplished during the past year, and what their policy is with respect to the future, there will be no danger of this Government's being voted out of office. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the interest and attention which have been accorded me.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to detain the House at any great length, nor is it my purpose to hand out any more bouquets to the Prime Minister or to the mover and seconder of the Address. I think that that phase of the debate has been amply attended to, and with all the best sentiments expressed I am in hearty accord. I simply rise to endorse the request made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders), to have a commission appointed to look into the grain trade. There is no more vital question before the farmers of the West than the handling and transportation of the products of the farm. Years ago our grain came from the machines in a rather clean state and was fit for shipment. Very soon, however, the advent of noxious weeds made it necessary for the elevators to put in cleaners to clean the grain before shipment; but this was soon discarded and at the present time nearly all grain is shipped in a very unclean state, and in this way the farmers do not know what they are getting or how much they will be docked. They have to pay freight charges on the screenings as well as giving it away for nothing 
and I think it would be the very best thing for the farmers to have a commission appointed to investigate the handling of grain from start to finish.
When the hon. member for Macdonald brought this question up, I thought that, as it was a suggestion of a progressive character, the Progressive party opposite would join in the discussion. But strange to say, up to the present time nothing has been said from that quarter on the subject. I suppose time will tell whether the proposal is too progressive or not progressive enough.
I desire to bring another question to the attention of the Government, especially of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. McCurdy) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Ballan-tyne), and that is the drying up of our lakes in the Prairie Provinces. A great many lakes out there have no inlet or outlet and have simply dried up, first turning into hay meadow and then wheat fields. But there are other lakes situated on the river courses and they are drying up with the result that the fish, a great source of food to the farmers, have been practically destroyed. The lakes have become so low in many cases that they have frozen to the bottom that the fish have died and become a great nuisance to the surrounding country in the spring, lying dead along the beach. There has been an improvement made on Killarney and Pelican lakes in the Southwestern portion of the province, which is a credit to the Government; but there is a lake situated entirely in my constituency that has been used considerably as a summer resort. There are a great many cottages built along the beach, and there is a beautiful piece of ground used for a summer school and by picnic parties. But this lake has dried down about three feet and the weeds grow up to the top of the water, which becomes stagnant. I am informed that from three to five thousand dollars would dam the lake up and raise it about three feet. In this way the nuisance would be avoided and we should have a pleasant summer resort.
As to the main question before the House, I must say that I have never had an intimation from my constituency to the effect that I was not doing my duty because I was supporting the present Government. When I was elected there was not a word said about the duration of Parliament, the understanding being that it would run its full term. And I might say that supporters of the hon. leader of the

Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who voted against me and who would support any candidate running in the interests of the hon. gentleman, if he could find one in the constituency, have informed me that it is advisable for us to continue, because the people do not want an election. These people have told me that they expect us to continue until our time has expired. I therefore think that I have a mandate to support the present Government while it exists. If the leader of the Opposition did not get a mandate in 1917, I do not think we are to blame for that. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I beg to say that I shall vote against the amendments submitted and in support of the motion before the House.
On motion of Mr. Michael Clark (Red Deer) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Right Hon. C. J. Doherty the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
Tuesday, March 1, 1921.

Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 17, to define Canadian Nationals. He said:	The purpose of the Bill is to define
what constitutes a Canadian national. The necessity for such a definition results, in a large measure at all events, from the fact that under different measures adopted in connection with the carrying out of the operations of the League of Nations, there
are provisions made defining certain rights and privileges which may be enjoyed by the nationals of the different members of the League. Under those circumstances it is necessary, I think, that we should make a definition by statute so that the world may know who*is, and is recognized as a Canadian national. The Bill contains one section which defines as being Canadian nationals, British subjects, domiciled or ordinarily resident in Canada.

speechtext: Consideration of the Motion of Mr. James Mclsaac for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the Session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, and the proposed amendment to the amendment of.Mr. Campbell, resumed from Monday, February 28.

Mr-Speaker, I was immediately preceded in this debate late last evening by my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Bolton). My friend is of so modest and unostentatious a disposition, that I am quite sure there are a number, of the members of this House even, who are not aware of the tact that he lost three sons in the great war, and has since passed through terrible family afflictions. I want to take the opportunity afforded me, Sir, by following in this debate to say that I observed with the very greatest satisfaction from the manly, firm and modest way in which he voiced his opinions that his sons came by their grit honourably, and that he himself has come through his troubles in the way that a true Canadian man should do. I am sure that the House, in regard to these circumstances, will join with me in at once offering to my friend our sympathy and our congratulations. My hon. friend himself was preceded by another stalwart and manly friend of mine on the other side of the House who, like the member for Lisgar, might well speak more frequently. My friend from Selkirk (Mr. Hay) appears to me, though I have never gone particularly into his political lineage, to have been brought up in the true old Tory school because he was much concerned last night about the "home market". Well, I do not want to refgr in extenso to what he said, but perhaps it may throw light upon argument which I have to offer later

in this debate if I tell him a story which seems to me to illustrate the weakness of the home market if a nation has to depend upon that exclusively. There was a man once who undertook to breed carp and to breed cats. He established his cat ranch on the banks of a lake. In the lake he bred the carp. When the carp had some young he caught some of them and fed them to the cats. The cats eating the carp in their turn propagated their species, and he fed the young eats to the carp. So he went on changing cats for carp and carp for cats. He had a splendid home market but he never got any richer and he never exported anything. We in this part of the House believe in a larger market than that story illustrates.
I am conscious, Sir, of no mental reservation Whatsoever when I join with many of my fellow members in offering to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr Meighen) my most sincere and hearty congratulations, on personal grounds, on his accession at a comparatively early period of life to the Prime Ministership of this great Dominion, a position which his character, his ability, and his record alike make him eminently fitted to occupy.
I want to say that I congratulate also my hon. friends the mover and the seconder of the Address in reply to the speech from His Excellency. The mover's speech was a model for such an occasion, couched in virile and good English, scarcely at all partisan, commendably brief. The speech of my hon. friend the seconder- was an exceedingly able one considering that it was a maiden speech, and I am sure it has engendered in us all friendly anticipation of the times when we shall hear him again. He was not quite so non-partisan as the mover of the Address however, because coming from the county of Yale he could not refrain from reminding us that in that county they raise apples. We had learned that from several speeches of the Prime Minister during the election in that county. My hon. friend's anxiety about apples is a splendid illustration of the real nature of protection. The outlook of protection is always local, always sectional, always narrow, never national. The difference between my hon. friend and myself is this: he is concerned about the comparatively few Canadians who produce apples in Yale; I aim concerned about Canadians all over the country who eat apples. His interest is in making apples dear;

mine is in making them cheap. That is the outlook of protection not only in Yale, but in any part of the country in which the heresy prevails. When a protectionist comes from Nova Scotia-and I am afraid they have protectionists in that province, Sir-he says: You want free wheat in the West? Why, certainly. You want free implements? Why, have them by all means. You want free coal? Ah! that is a different matter. And he turns away sorrowfully, because they produce coal in Nova Scotia. In Peterborough the protectionist says: Peterborough and Progress. Well, I say, Canada and Progress. The outlook is narrow and sectional in the one case; it is really national in the other. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Denis)-I hope he was only an advocate on the occasion- goes before the Tariff Commission and asks for an outrageous duty upon tobacco, because they grow tobacco in Joliette. What do I care about where they grow tobacco? When I want to smoke it I want to get it good, and cheap, and I do not care where it comes from. That is the difference of outlook. So we claim for our views that we have the true national policy, and that the term "National Policy" as applied to protection is a total misnomer.
Let me press the point a little further. There is no duty so urgent upon Canadians of thoughtful and noble mind-and I believe they are all thoughtful and noble, or nearly so-as the duty of paying our national debt, principal and interest. Does this House think that that debt can be discharged, Mr. Speaker, by the export of excess tomatoes, or excess apples, or excess tobacco, or even excess manufactures? Our exports of manufactures are a mere bagatelle. If we are to discharge that debt, principal and interest, we must do it by the tremendous surplus, which, we are well able to produce, of the great unprotected and unprotectable natural products of the country; and we are prepared to do it if you will get off our backs and give us a chance. That is the true national policy: Support the industries that will make your nation great, honourable, and prosperous.
I quite agree with my hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) that the debate on this Address has taken rather a peculiar form. I agree with him that it has been customary, both in our Parliament and in the Mother of Parliaments, in a debate on the Address to discuss the subjects raised in the Address and the past

and present proceedings of the Administration. I shall follow my leader in ^endeavouring to keep up this old tradition.
I am glad to be able to agree with the Administration that in this country we are freer from unrest and external signs of the aftermath of the war than perhaps in any of the other billigerent nations. I agree with the Administration also in what they state in the same paragraph of the Speech from the Throne as to the harvest having been on the whole fairly good. I am sure that Administration would not claim an undue amount of credit for the fairly good harvest; and I think that the credit is only a limited one in regard to that other matter upon which the nation is congratulated. I do not deny them all credit, far from it. This country has on the whole done very well for her returned soldiers, but, Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that we are free from unrest is due, perhaps, in the first place, to the very high character of the men we sent to the front, most of whom have settled down in splendid shape and are bringing to their civil occupations the same grit and the same force of character which put them in the war at the beginning and kept them there until victory crowned our banners. It is due, in the second place, to many efforts which have been made on the part of our employers of labour-I know some of them in this city, Sir Henry Egan and others- who from the middle of the war busied themselves to keep positions open for the returned soldiers, and in this I am glad to say they have been well supported by the Administration. But it is due, in the third place, to this consideration, which we can be all proud of as Canadians, that this country to-day presents perhaps better opportunities than are presented by any other country in the world for a man who wants to live his life in a bracing and delightful climate and by his own endeavours to work out his temporal and material prosperity.
Now, I have just referred to the fact that this bebate has taken a peculiar course. For the first nine days, Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen on the Government side of the House were engaged very largely in taunting my hon. friends of the official Opposition-I do not use the term offensively; it is the only one that occurs to me for the moment-with the fact that they did not refer extensively to the tariff. Well, the Government's supporters are not easy to please, because on Thursday last the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) referred pretty extensively to the
tariff. But the moment he did so what happened on the Government side? They have not up to the present paid any particular attention to what my leader said about the tariff, but member after member has talked about a subject that is not metioned in the Speech from the Throne at all. An investigation is promised in the speech by His Excellency into the questions of Old Age Pensions and Insurance against Unemployment. But, I repeat, a request has come from member after member for an investigation that is not mentioned in the speech, and that request is a very peculiar one. It is a request for a grain commission-a commission to inquire into and investigate the grain business of Canada. Well, at first sight I thought this was an unrehearsed, and therefore unprinted, portion of the speech by His Excellency; but on second thought it occurred to me that it would have been a much more fit theme to place in the motion of my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, calling for censure upon the Government. If the grain business is wrong, who is responsible for it?' This Government, or a government very much like this, has been in power in this country since 1911. During this time we have had grain legislation before the House; the Nestor of the Tory party and of the Administration, my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), is absolutely responsible for the grain laws that prevail in this country at the present time. And they have a Grain Commission; so this proposal that has been adumbrated, that emanated first from the member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) and has been supported all over that side of the House, is that we should have a Government commission to inquire into why another Government commission is not doing its duty. Well, I would like to know if we are going to pyramid commissions upon commissions? If the first Government commission, which [DOT] is the creature of a member of the Administration, the Nestor of the Tory party and the Administration, is not doing its duty, how do we know that the second commission will do its duty? I think we had better prod the commission that we have in the meantime. All that I would like to say about these promised investigations, whether in the speech or out of it, is that I venture a prophecy that they will be pretty much protracted, and as they will be pretty much protracted their well-considered findings will not come before Parliament until the successors of this present

House are doing business here. And when I mention the successors I am afflicted by my friendly feelings for fellow-members and certain anxieties about myself, to such an extent that I think we had better leave the findings and investigations to our successors. The coming House certainly will differ very materially in personnel from that which at present occupies the Chamber.
I heard with very great pleasure the magnificent speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce upon the League of Nations, and as he poured forth those rounded periods containing noble ideals couched in lofty language, as a Canadian I felt proud that we had an "old man eloquent" in Canada whom we need not be afraid to send to Geneva or anywhere else. With regard to the League of Nations, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say this: that the sentiments of the Canadian people from the Atlantic to the Pacific are thoroughly peaceful sentiments as regards our fellow men and that the Administration may be sure that behind any effort they may make to maintain the peace of the world they have the unanimous strength and support of the whole Canadian people. I should just like to say further in regard to the League that I think if there is a danger attaching to its operations it is to be found in a tendency too greatly to multiply its machinery and to increase too much its international obligations. There are a great many obligations that are in their very nature national, and to endeavour to get a Parliament of the World at the present stage of human development is, perhaps, to anticipate the millennium a little too rapidly. While I say that, I feel certain that the League is a tremendous step in the direction of making it sure that in the future history of this world, if any nation should venture to break international law flagrantly as Germany did, and confess their doing it while they do it, there is almost a certainty that the civilized peoples of the world will rise and say: You are the [DOT] common enemy of the race, and you must be prepared for being handled by the rest of mankind.
While touching on this topic may I say that I am sincerely pained from time to time to hear the jibes that are sometimes thrown across the border at our friends in the United States. I am equally pained by the jibes that come from certain sections of the population-a very small part of it,
I am glad to think-of the United States towards Canada. Mr. Speaker, I can conceive of no greater destiny in th 3 im-

mediate future, of no higher duty, of no more sacred privilege for Canada, than to stand the nearest of the dominions to the Old Land, between that Old Land and the other portions of the Empire, and close, on the other hand, to the great American people; and to bend her influence, as she is well able to do, from her geographical position and from the sentiments of her people, to the production of a perfect understanding between all those who speak the British tongue and value British institutions, whether they be in the Republic or in the Empire. If we could have such a perfect understanding between these peoples, we should indeed have taken the first and the greatest step towards a most effective League of Nations.
Now, I think I have touched upon all the subsidiary portions of the speech of His Excellency. The Government recognize, as any responsible government must at this time, that the main considerations of Government and Parliament for some time must gather around questions of finance, questions of trade, questions of the national financial obligations-and questions of tariff, if you like. So the Government have frankly and very honestly and courageously told us their views upon tariff, and that the tariff will be the main business of the session. I have no sympathy with the contention that there is any limit to the rights of this Parliament to deal with tariff questions in this session or in any other session so long as Parliament lasts. Why, Mr. Speaker, the tariff is and has been during all the time we have been a nation one of our methods of taxation, and to talk about any question of taxation being out of the purview of Parliament for a single moment is to talk what I conceive to be parliamentary nonsense. Neither, as I shall show when I come to deal, with the amendment, have I any sympathy with many other views that .have been expressed from this side of the House. I shall be glad if anything that falls from my lips this afternoon shall be of assistance to the Government in their investigations of tariff questions and in arriving at right conclusions before we reach the Budget, if we ever do reach it.
In entering upon this subject, I thought I could not do better than devote a little attention to a speech delivered in this Parliament by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) during the last Budget debate. I do so because that speech is of importance, having regard to the source from

which it came, and also because it enables me to refer to some of the matters raised in the Governor General's speech. Indeed, the speech derived a fictitious importance! from the source from which it came, be-f cause it was delivered by a minister of the Crown who has since become Prime Minister of Canada. It was so important in the view of the party managers of my hon. friends opposite that, I understand, they printed 40,000 copies of it and sent it broadcast throughout Canada. The first part of it consisted of an almost impassioned defence of certain taxes which, I think, when the Budget was before us, were called "excise taxes." Like a good many other things, or people anyhow, that want to disappear, they adopted an alias and became "luxury taxes." The fate of those taxes is really the only comment that is necessary, the only answer that needs to be made to my right hon. friend as to his defence of those taxes at the time. A consideration of the fate of those taxes reminds me that this Government is very prone to political infanticide. I think, in the last two speeches from the Throne, the farmers from the West and producers generally throughout Canada were specially admonished to great efforts of production. In any case, I know members of the Government and many other hon. gentlemen opposite, before the war terminated and until last summer, took the opportunity, from platform and even from pulpit on Sunday evenings, and in Parliament, to urge upon the people efforts at increased production. I had, on principle, no objection to those efforts, but I said always that they needed to be supplemented by efforts on the part of the Administration to make arrangements whereby you could sell your product. The only way you will ever increase production is to make a ready sale for what is produced, and that was always my comment. But, referring to this matter of political infanticide, I notice that the question of production has disappeared from the speech from the Throne; it has disappeared from the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, and they are now concerned about sales. During the war there was almost no need to urge production, because we had the necessary inducement to produce; we had the inducement of the greatest markets we ever enjoyed, opened to us by the exigencies of the war, and our customers were foreign peoples and foreign governments. But perhaps the principal offender, or the principal worker as regards preaching this 26

principle of production, was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) , who previously to last summer missed no opportunity, for at least two and a half years of preaching this doctrine, when suddenly the bottom fell out of prices, and he turned on his heel and he said: The trouble with this country is that the farmers have produced more than they can sell, and then he hopped off to Geneva. That was a nice thing for men in the West who, in obedience to the Government's injunction, had hired men at $6 a day and had lying on their hands stuff in abundance which they could not sell.
Another offspring of the Government that we do not hear much of in Parliament these days is called daylight saving. The Minister of Trade and Commerce dandled that interesting nursling on his knee for two sickly seasons, and then he handed it over to the chief nurse, the Prime Minister, who, at the bidding of forces, I do not know where, suffocated the infant with a pillow behind the Speaker's chair late one Friday evening.
I do not know what is the precise condition in which the Board of Commerce is now. It had a mixed parentage; it was not entirely the child of this Administration. I am afraid that with diabolical ingenuity the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) had something to do with leading the Government on to thin ice in that matter. I know, when they constituted the Board of Commerce, he said: We have been asking for this all the time. Well, he got it. But what is its precise condition now, I do not know. If it is alive, it is not functioning; we do not hear anything about it, and indeed, the only thing that we have seen of it lately has been the incursion of its late chairman into a by-election down in West Peterborough.
The Prime Minister, with numbers of others in the Government, came into power in this House with a pledge against free wheat. I took part, as my right hon. friend did, in the debates which preceded the election of 1911, and we were told that if ever free wheat was given, the keystone of the protectionist arch was gone. Well, it is gone, and it was taken away by the gentlemen who came in promising that they would never take it away.
The Prime Minister, when he came into power, was rather an enthusiastic advocate of indirect taxation. I am not at all sure if he did not make a speech doubting if the Federal Government had power-that

was in his green and salad days-to put on an income tax. He shakes his head. Well, I have known lawyers to do that about things that were very doubtful. I remember the speech; but not being a lawyer and being a modest man, I am quite willing to admit that I may have misinterpreted it-especially a speech by my right hon friend. But for three years of the war he sat behind a Minister of Finance who said that an income tax was a bad tax for the country; that it could not be thought of. I am glad the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who, by the way, is free from all those doings, states that this year he expects to collect $40,000,000 by income tax, and if he gets $80,000,000 next year, I shall not blame him; I am quite willing to have mine doubled. But the point is, the views of the Government on both these things went by the board. Now I was quite prepared when the Budget came down, for the luxury taxes to meet the same fate that so many of the infants of the Government had already met, but I must confess that I scarcely expected that we should see in this country or in any other British country a Budget introduced by Order in Council, because that is what happened. My hon. friend, for a good-natured man, nearly got angry with me when I told him he ought to think out his taxation proposals and bring them down in the Budget, and stand upon them for a year. I have been looking up in the recess some authorities on this question, although I did not need to, because I happened to know what I was talking about; but I looked up a speech of Mr. Gladstone's in which he laid down in Midlothian at seventy years of age certain elementary principles of finance. The principles which he claimed in that particular speech were also and equally subscribed to, by Mr. Goulbourn and Sir Robert Peel, on opposite sides of politics in the early days of Mr. Gladstone's political career. The first principle was one that this Government might very well practise:	"Never be afraid of
economy in detail." In that very speech the great Gladstone held up his hands in horror at the thought that somewhere in the Empire something of a (job) had been perpetrated by the creation of an office carrying with it the modest sum of £2,000, or $10,000, a year. If he had lived in our present day he would have seen almost any one of our provincial administrations, of whatever stripe, equal to creating one of these jobs over-night. Economy in detail; I pass that by, and come to his second great 
principle of finance, which was:	"You
ought to have one financial statement, and only one financial statement in the year." The reasons are obvious. My. hon. friend knows them now. He has had them brought under his notice by the people dealing in automobiles, and other of the manufacturers and traders of this country. When a Budget statement is brought down, a Government is prepared to stand or fall upon it, and must be, because while it is kept secret until actually brought down, immediately it is brought down tradesmen and dealers must be prepared to deal upon that Budget with the reasonably certain knowledge that the arrangements made in it will prevail until the next Budget statement. I do not want to spend too much of the time of the House in whipping a dead horse. The taxes are gone; but I take the liberty of inculcating this lesson in regard to them. It is melancholy to reflect, in regard to this question of political infanticide, that this House was kept up until seven in the morning to pass those taxes. We passed that Budget at seven o'clock in the morning, and in two minutes thi Minister of Finance destroyed the whole thing by an Order in Council. Then they talk about constitutionalism and the proper treatment of Parliament. Why, Sir, it is the most horrible treatment that ever was handed out to Parliament.
There is another lesson I would like to draw from these taxes. I called them at the time an internal tariff, and I told the minister exactly what he has since found out. I told him-indeed, I was too moderate-* that he would find these taxes difficult to collect. Well, it was far worse than that; they were impossible to collect. What happened was that the honest man paid the taxes and gathered them from his customers, and was troubled with all kinds of red tape because he did not send in proper statements, but men not so particular told the Government to go to the bow-wows, and did not collect the taxes at all. My hon. friend knows that happened all over the country. He knows now that the taxes are bad, and if he had only listened to me he would have known they were bad when they were brought down in the Budget. Well, the Prime Minister with his usual courage, which frequently amounts to daring, when asked in Peterborough about these taxes was ready with his answer,- he is always ready with his answer when anybody interrupts. He said:	The taxes
were right when the Government put them

on, and the Government is right in taking them off.
Hear, hear.

And my hon.
friends opposite applaud. What can you do with reasoners of that description? The most slippery eel that ever slid through the waters was easily caught compared with men who will applaud a statement like that. My right hon. friend, as I said, gave rather an impassioned defence of the taxes in their original form. He sat behind the Minister, and voted for them in their altered form, and he sits there to-day just as docilely now that the Minister has passed them into the condition of the world before creation, that is, the condition of being without form and void.
I should like to ask the Administration at this point, do they really think they are justified in asking this House for a vote of confidence? I do not want to go into the details that have been offered so profusely from this side of the House, but it is true, however, that probably no Administration ever ruled as they have done during the last two-and-a-half years and had to apologize for so many discarded policies-and with each discarded policy they have parted with a piece of their personnel. Then they come to this House with all the assurance in the world and say: We are the men to govern you, we want a vote of confidence. I should like to know if they really think they are deserving of it. If they do, then I must proceed to other reasons why I do not think so.
I noticed this in the second part of my right hon. friend's speech last summer. That second part of his speech was a performance in which he showed much more than his usual courage, but much less than his usual discretion. Mr. Morley-Lord Morley, as he is now-said on a somewhat famous occasion that the economist who is not a politician gets into very serious scrapes; but, he said, they are nothing to the scrapes which the politician gets into who is not an economist. I could not help thinking of those words as I heard and read, as I have done several times, the speech in question of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). There was abundant internal evidence, if I am a judge, of the speech having been prepared from a brief; and if my diagnosis is a correct one, there never was able barrister so befooled by ill-informed solicitors. I know from the Prime Minister himself that it was prepared from a brief because he practically told us in the
speech that he had not studied these questions. That may be a surprise to him, but I am going to demonstrate that he practically told us he had not studied these questions. Fluency sometimes degenerates into flippancy, and I think it did so on this occasion. My hon. friend and leader (Mr. Crerar), had produced some figures in the House proving what I thought was admitted by all and deplored, in Canada, that there was a great deal of rural depopulation in Ontario. Those figures have been supplemented in very careful examinations by Mr. J. J. Morrison, the Secretary of the United Farmers of Ontario.
Oh, oh.

I do not ask
hon. gentlemen opposite to have the least respect for Mr. Morrison; but if he were the least respectable man in the world, if his figures are according to Cocker, my friends have got to respect him for that. I thought we all knew there was rural depopulation. Well, what does my right hon. friend say on this subject? He says:
1 never saw a farm abandoned that appeared, at all events from the road, to be fit for anybody to farm.
My hon. friend studied the values of farms from the road, possibly when driving past in an automobile. His language admits it. Well now, my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is on the whole a very faithful supporter of my right hon. friend; so is the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best). They both know something about farming, and they know that no man in his senses will try to study whether or not a farm is really worth anything merely from a survey from the road. He will want to go on the land and look at it. But we are blessed with a Prime Minister who can tell you all about these things from the road; that is where he studied his political economy. Have not I gone far to prove that he had not looked into these matters as closely as he should have done? He has been far too busy hunting Bolsheviks. But he went further. He said: The figures are all against my hon. friend anyhow, because the prices of agricultural land are going up. Well, that is very much the same as if absolute ocular demonstration were brought to him that a certain tenant had left a certain house and he were to reply: But he cannot have left the house because the rent has been raised! Why, the raising of the rent might be the cause of his leaving.
Oh.

You will notice, Mr. Speaker, I waited for the laughter of my right hon. friend and his supporters. A great deal of the rise in value of agricultural land is not due to the fact that the land is used; it is because of speculation in land. But what amount of rise in prices * will prove or disprove facts that are gathered by an examination into the population of the various areas of locality? -every such examination proving to the hilt that people are leaving the country districts and that many country districts in Ontario now have fewer people than before? But my right hon. friend could not ascertain these things from the road; he would need to go into the figures carefully and to study these matters zealously. Well, ill-prepared as he evidently was according to his own statement for dealing with this project, he nevertheless undertakes to show that the fiscal policy of Great Britain for seventy years has been a failure. His first step in the progression of fallacies by which he attempted to prove that contention was to state that since the year 1850 Great Britain had had what he calls an adverse balance of trade. Now,
I want to tell my right hon. friend-and on this point I am not going to reason with him; I am going to tell him what is so- that he is absolutely wrong in assuming, at the beginning of his thinking upon this subject, that an excess of imports over exports is necessarily an "adverse" balance of trade. It is not so. Adam Smith, the father of political economy, in his great book which is still the highest authority on political economy that ever was published, characterizes my right hon. friend's views as absurd,-too strong language, possibly, for Parliament, but not too strong for the old Scotch economist and philosopher, who goes on to say-and here he is not giving an opinion but history-that almost every nation in Europe had had its ruin prophesied because of this so-called adverse balance of trade, but that they had gone on to prosper. That is history, Sir; not opinion. Let me give two simple illustrations of the way in which the so-called adverse balance of trade of Britain was constituted, of what her excess of imports consisted. Suppose I go to a bank, Mr. Speaker, and borrow $1,000 at 8 per cent. At the end of twelve months I have to pay into the bank $1,080. Now, the bank takes in $1,080 where it only paid out $1,000; its
(Mr. M. Clark.]
imports exceed its exports. My right hon. friend says that that is an adverse balance of trade. Well, the bank never thought so, so far as its own interests were concerned; and certainly the borrower does not.- But that is exactly how half of Britain's excess of imports before the war was constituted. She accumulated so much wealth by her free trade that she had investments all over the world drawing interest, and the interest on these investments went into Britain in the shape of imports bought by individuals within the nation out of their -wealth, but constituting an excess of imports in the nation's trade balance. And just at this point, may I say to my right hon. friend, if he had studied these questions, if he had thought out these points, he would have known that people do not go on buying profusely year after year for seventy years out of poverty but out of prosperity. Let any hon. gentleman in this House try to conduct the business of buying, without the wherewithal to pay, in any store in Ottawa, and see if he can keep it up for seventy days, never mind seventy years. Now, I want to illustrate in another way another portion of what constituted Britain's excess of imports. Suppose I traded a yearling steer for 20 bushels of wheat with a neighbouring farmer. That would have been about a fair exchange a year and a half ago; a yearling steer, at prices then prevailing, would have been worth somewhere in the neighbourhood of twenty bushels of wheat. And suppose I arranged with my neighbour that I would take my steer over in my wagon and bring back the wheat. Clearly, so far as the carrying part of the business was concerned, that would not be a fair deal, and I would naturally, if I were a Canadian anyhow, say to my farmer neighbour; now, I want a couple of bushels extra for carrying both the steer and the wheat. And if the other man were at all reasonable he would give me twenty-two bushels of wheat instead of the twenty that bought the steer; that is to say, I should earn two bushels by doing the carrying both ways. My right hon. friend would call that an adverse balance of trade. Well, I would not; I would call it favourable to me to the extent of two bushels. And that is exactly what constituted the other half of the adverse balance of Britain's trade. Why, at the present moment she is building fifty-one per cent of the entire ships constructed in the world. Before the war she did the carrying trade of the world; and she earned by her carrying trade the other half of her excess imports. But that

was not adverse to Britain. The merest tyro in political economy knows that it provided her with that wealth which saved the fortunes of the world when she had to go to war and was able to realize on that wealth.
