But I do not wonder that hon. members on the other side seem to get somewhat tired at my referring to Britain. I did not do so in the debate in which my right hon. friend spoke, and I do not wish to restrict my considerations to Britain now. This argument was introduced by himself in a way he felt to be rather peculiar at the time, because he admitted that the hon. member for Red Deer preceding him had not said quite so much about Britain as in former speeches. I shall show my hon. friend from the history of our own country that excess of imports is not necessarily an adverse balance of trade. We had what my hon. friend would call a favourable balance of trade in the year 1895. A Tory Government had been in power for seventeen years and they produced a "favourable" balance of trade, all right. We had a total trade of $202,000,000; we exported $102,000,000 and imported $100,000,000. Was the country prosperous then? If it was, why did they part with the Administration which had been running the National Policy for seventeen years? There is the fact. The total trade was a bagatelle; the nation was stagnant; at least I have always heard so, if I am not rightly informed upon the subject my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) and my hon. friend from Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) can repeat some of the speeches which were heard in such profusion about the lack of prosperity before 1896. And when I first came into this House-nobody pretended to tell me that the nation was prosperous at that time. What happened afterwards? Immediately after 1896 this country became prosperous. I do not want to argue this from the party point of view, but for some reason or other the people were prosperous. As the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to say, some of his opponents proved the prosperity of the country from books, but, said he, "I do not do it in that way, I do not need to. Everyone in my audience knows the country is prosperous because you have the evidence of it in your pockets." It was growing time of Canada. What was our balance of trade at that time? Why we imported hundreds of millions of dollars worth more every year than'we exported; it was the expanding time in Canada's history as a great nation. Now
these are the facts and I am exceedingly anxious to convince my right hon. friend.
I trust he will be a big figure in the public life of Canada long after this tongue is silent and these eyes are closed, and I take with a grain of salt his statement when he goes down to the eastern provinces saying that he has nailed the protectionist flag to the mast for life. A right hon. gentleman who can take three different views on the luxury taxes in six months is quite equal to changing his views on the tariff.
My right hon. friend said that Canada began to catch up in its business, by the way, in 1916. Now he is such a good friend of mine that I do not like to prefer a charge of want of generosity even against his arguments, but I do think that was an ungenerous argument. Why, does not everybody know that the nations of Europe were glad to import anything we could send to them in the way of food, and in the way of munitions, while the war was on? It was no trick, as we say on this side of the Atlantic, to do business in war time. They had to have the food, they had to have the munitions. The twenty millions of men fighting had to be fed and the food and the munitions were imported, of course, and we exported them from this side. But if we began to "catch up" in 1916 all I have got to say is we began to "catch down" very soon after my right hon. friend became Prime Minster, because the exports of Canada are not nearly as favourable now as they were at the time he spoke only last June-there has been a change in the scene since then. It is a remarkable fact, however, if it be a fact, [DOT] that in 1850 Britain began to have what he calls an adverse balance of trade, and in 1896 Canada began to have what he calls an adverse balance of trade, and at the moment they had it they began to prosper and to increase their total volume of trade and to become rich and a considerable people. That is how I read history on this question of balance of trade.
Now I am going to tell my right hon. friend when an excess of imports may become adverse. It is not so when it represents interest on capital invested abroad. It is not so when it represent the payment for carrying services done for all the nations of the globe. But it easily be-oomes so when it represents borrowings if those borrowings are carried too far. At the present moment we hear a great deal about the excess of our imports from the United States. Well, I do not think there is any mystery about those. I remember

when the ex-Minister of Finance raised a seventy million loan in the States during the war. I said I did not object to the loan, we had to get money somehow to carry on the war, but I told him year after year that a better way to get it would be by direct taxation. I said: Let the House understand what you are doing; when you are borrowing all this money you are employing the factories and workmen of the country from which you borrow, because your borrowings come in here in goods; and while a young country may go a certain distance in borrowing capital for its development it is very easy to go too far. I want to say here and now, Mr. Speaker, that with the magnificent asset of property which we have in our great territory, with its varied riches, what we want in this country is not so much capital as people. Bring people in of the right kind who will work up our resources. The wealth is there if you will enable them to work it up and produce by taking obstacles out of the way of the sale of the product. I do not think there is any doubt that Sir Edmund Walker was absolutely right in the last sentence he uttered in his recent statement to his shareholders, when he said: This country is all right but we need to go cautiously, for the outstanding sin of our people is extravagance and a readiness to contract debts. If that is true of the people, it is vastly more true not only of our Federal Government but of our municipal and our various provincial governments. We have got to work more for [DOT] our country and borrow less. Why, Sir, municipal and provincial bonds were issued in this country last year to the tune of $324,000,000; debts contracted upon our territory, that is what they were. Two hundred and twenty-three millions of this $324,000,000 are held in the United States and, as I say, the example was set to these municipal and provincial governments by the Federal Government, at least during the war. We have got, as my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) has said again and again, to borrow less. We have got to economize more. We have got to work harder and we have got to trade more freely. Well, I have laboured that point at considerable length; I could not avoid it. I have gone far to prove to the House that an excess of imports is not necessarily an adverse balance of trade. I have laboured the argument fully because if you grant the first point, of 
course the second is easy. My right hon. friend's next position in his progression of fallacies was that Britain having followed for seventy years a wrong method of trading, her people were poor in large sections and they were poor because of free trade. He says it must be so, Ban-nerman said so. Now it is true that Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman made a statement in a certain speech that there were twelve millions of British people near the poverty line. But what was he talking about when he made that statement? He was talking about the iniquitous land laws of Great Britain, and he was attributing the poverty to a wrong handling of the land of Britain and the need of different methods of taxation. But of all the men in the world, Sir Henry Bannerman was the last man to attribute any of the poverty of Britain to free trade; he was one of the greatest free trade supporters England ever had. But my right hon. friend comes along and says: Sir Henry Bannerman makes the statement. I do not know whether my right hon. friend knew where he made it, or what he was talking about. If he did know, then he said in effect: " The statement is true but Sir Henry's conclusion is all wrong; it is not the land laws of Britain that are wrong but the fiscal policy of Britain. Sir Henry did not know what he was talking about! He was only a member for thirty-nine years for one constituency and he had not had time to study this question." Then Mr. Rowntree said that Britain was poor. Well, Mr. Rowntree attributed a large amount of the poverty of Britain to intemperance, to the drinking of strong drink, and I think that the commonsense of every hon. gentleman will force him to admit that if a man works hard enough on Scotch whiskey with a limited income he will become poor whether' he is living under free trade or under protection. That was Mr. Rowntree's view.- But the Prime Minister says: " No, Mr. Rowntree does not know anything about it. It is free trade that makes the people poor."
Well, there is a method of testing this, apart from Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman's opinions or Mr. Rowntree's opinions or the opinions of my right hon. friend. If he will read Macaulay's History of England he will find in the third chapter that in the time of Charles II, when there were only a few million people in Britain, there were 250 paupers in the thousand.

He mentions his authorities-statisticians, not the politicians whom my right hon. friend quotes. At the time when Macaulay wrote the third chapter of his History there were 80 paupers in the thousand; in 1872 there were only 40 paupers in the thousand-that was after free trade had been in operation a little over twenty years; and in 1907, a few years before the war broke out, pauperism had been reduced to 25 in the thousand. And from the time of free trade Britain's population had nearly doubled. That is the condition of poverty as far as it can be learned from the Board of Trade figures of the British Government. So that the second contention of my right hon. friend is just as baseless as the first. If it had been true that they had been following a wrong system of trading, of course it might have led to the poverty that there is in Britain and that there is in every big country- and that there has been for two thousand years, anyhow, because we were told then by an undisputed authority, that the poor we have always with us. If it had been true that Britain traded wrong, then it might be true that povery was the result of that wrong method of trading. But neither statement has one particle of support in the solid facts of the case.
The next step in my right hon friend's progress of fallacy is that he made a favourable comparison as regards United States labour in contrast with British labour. I had not had time to go fully into the conditions of labour in the United States, but I had quoted-and I think my right hon. friend was referring to that quotation-an article which appeared in a paper of the highest repute in the Old Country, written by Ernest Hodder Williams, a publicist in Britain of high standing, who had visited the United States almost every year. But he found his article upon the investigations of a journalist of the highest standing who is well known to the statesmen who attended the Peace Conference; his name is R. Stannard Baker. I am going to quote a single paragraph from that article, for the double reason that I think it is wise that we should know something at any rate about conditions of labour in the United States before we compare them unfavourably with conditions of labour in Britain; and if my right hon. friend is really an admirer of labour conditions in the United States, then the labour men of Canada should know it, because I think in that way they would avoid the policy which has produced this
condition. Mr. Williams, gathering his information from Mr. Baker, wrote:
One of the causes of the recent steel strike in America was the fact that the twelve-hour day and the seven-day week were so common in industry. Many men in the steel works lived at least four miles from the mill. They got up at four-thirty in the morning, at six o'clock they began work, going steadily until five in the afternoon, with no regular stop for luncheon hour, though during waiting periods they had time for something to eat; home at six o'clock, then after supper bed. They made big money, but they did not live-they existed, worked and slept. According to Judge Gary's own testimony, there are over 69,000 men in the United States Steel Corporation working twelve hours a day.
I defy my right hon. friend or any other man in this world to go into Britain to-day and find conditions of labour that will for one moment compare with what is brought out in that paragraph as prevailing in the great Steel Corporation, which is one of the glories of protection according to my right hon. friend.
The next step in the fallacy is perfectly natural. "Ireland has participated in the general ruin." I always thought that my right hon. friend's friends attributed the difficulties and troubles of Ireland to a very different cause. But it is all free trade, it appears, because my right hon. friend tells us, in almost his first incursion into economics, that free trade dwarfed the nascent industries of Ireland. Four million people inhabit Ireland. Its agriculture is one of the finest in the world. Before the war Ireland was producing the largest number of bushels of wheat to the acre of any country in Europe. That is an important industry. Who said it was dwarfed? They supply every year a large amount of Britain's need of store cattle. Has my right hon. friend ever heard of the tobacco industry of Ireland?-one of the greatest in Europe. He has heard of Irish linen? -the finest that is made anywhere. He has heard of Irish lace? If he has not, and his boat calls at Queenstown, he will see some of it in going over to England next May or June, for the Irish Women come on board ship to sell their lace -beautiful stuff. Has he heard of Ireland's shipbuilding? I venture the prophesy that in the next twelve months the Irish people who live in Belfast will build more ships than will be built in all Canada with the Canadian Government behind our shipbuilding industry. But my right hon. friend says in his review of history, that free trade has dwarfed the nascent industries of Ireland. Well, naturally where people

have been following the wrong system of trade they get poor, they have horrible conditions of labour, and they have been fleeing the country as they would a pest house. They must have been doing it for this reason-because my right hon. friend says so. He says that free trade has filled the emigrant ships with fugitives from their native land. Well, that is of all the causes of emigration from the British Isles the most recent cause that I have heard or read expounded. Why, Sir, in the early fifties of the last century a thousand people were leaving the British Isles every day, and then they were wondering whether those old lands would stand the drain on their blood and the strain of time and circumstance. The Old Land was struggling then up towards thirty million of people, and she sent out her thousand a day, and she has kept on sending them out all over the world. To-day in spite of that steady stream of emigration, she has neared the fifty million mark in population, and last year- good luck to her and God bless her?-she had the largest number of births in her history. Yet free trade has 'filled the British emigrant ships with fugitives from their native land!" Well, in Britain, they take a different view of this subject, as my hon. friend himself will in time. They say there, with pride:
We sailed wherever ship could sail;
We founded many a mighty state;
Heaven grant our greatness may not fail
Through craven fear of being great.
"Fugitives from their native land!" Why, my right hon. friend must be something of a "fugitive" himself. Where did his ancestors come from? His policies are a little medieval, but I never took him for an aboriginal. My right hon. friend has the reputation of being a fighter, and he deserves it. It is true, in a sense, that free trade was the cause of this expansion, and I submit to my right hon. friend the reason; you cannot travel abroad unless you have the price. They had ta stay in Britain under protection because they had not enough money to enable them to get out, but the moment they got free trade they expanded. It is true in a glorious sense, and if free trade has built the British Empire I want to say that that is the greatest of free trade's glories. My right hon. friend carries his fighting propensities too far when he fights with Providence for having built the British Empire; he must really restrain his terrible animosities a little. It is a fact that people do emigrate most when they are most prosper-

ous. As I say, they have the price and they also have the ambition, having done so well, to get out and try to do a little better. Of course, having had the "unfavourable balance of trade" and being "impoverished," and having had her industries "ruined" and having been obliged to "flee their native land," the people of Britain, my right hon. friend is persuaded, are about to desert a wrong policy, and he bases himself on the reports of certain committees. Well, I will concede this: that there are selfish men in Britain as well as in protectionist countries, and if they could persuade the government to change a fiscal policy by reports of committees so as to put illegal gains into their pockets, I am sorry to confess, there are Britishers who would take the gains. So they report that their trade would be helped-their particular trade- by the abandonment of free trade. My right hon. friend mentioned-and I take only one of his cases as an illustration-the matter of the iron and steel trade in Great Britain. He read the report of a committee asking for duties on iron and steel. But my hon. friend from Maisoneuve (Mr. Lemieux), punctured his argument on that point by putting one simple question: "Have the Government acted upon this report?" My right hon. friend was bound to answer that they had not, and I venture to prophesy that they will never dream of acting on it. I will tell my hon. friend why: iron and steel are the basic or building materials of the very greatest of Britain's industries. If Britain were to put a duty on iron and steel and make those things dearer, what would become of the cutlery trade of Sheffield; and what would become-which is vastly more important-of the shipbuilding of Great Britain, which is the glory of the country and of the Empire and which won the war? That is my answer to my right hon. friend upon this question: they will not tax iron and steel; do not let my right hon. friend, in trying to form an opinion about what is going to happen in Britain, attach too much importance to what the journeymen in politics say; I advise him to keep his eye upon the big figures in British public life, and that he listen to what they say. What are the Cecils saying about free trade? The moment there is a question of an antidumping law to keep out a few chemicals and a few tungsten burners, which bulk to a tremendous extent, I need not say, in the trade of Britain, the Cecils get restive and show an inclination to leave the Unionist Coalition over there, because they know

this question and they know that Britain's commercial greatness has depended upon her fiscal policy. Lord Derby is in the same boat-a man of enormous wealth and enormous responsibility and of great connections in Lancashire-he shows restiveness and an inclination to leave the Government. And what did Mr. Lloyd George himself say only a week ago? I draw particular attention to this, because Mr. Lloyd George is the head of the administration in Britain:
If international trade fails, I do not care what you do, you will have nothing hut starvation and ruin.
That being the opinion of the Prime Minister of Britain he is a very sanguine protectionist who would base the policy of this country upon any expectation that Britain is going to change her fiscal policy.
What about America in this connection? My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) the other night asked us how we would feel if the Fordney Bill passed. Who is Fordney? I never heard of him until this Bill was brought in. He is a politician, of course, trying to implement his pledges to the farmers in the last election. That is not the place to go for American opinion. If you want to form an intelligent forecast of what America is likely to do on trade, go to her captains of industry; go to her great financiers; go to the New York journals, most of them. There are two supreme needs of America at the present moment; one is imports and one is exports-strange as that may appear. The financial magnates and the really instructed men who know about America's position in the world of trade and commerce know this; she must have imports, in the first place, because at Washington there are treasury bills variously estimated at from ten to fifteen billion dollars representing the debts of various foreign nations to America contracted during the war. These debts can only be discharged if America imports goods to pay for them, so that she must arrange her fiscal policy so as to go on importing. But these men that I speak of are equally clear in the view that America must develop a great export trade. They say, in so many words: she must follow the example of Britain in seeking outlets for the capital she accumulated during the war by helping foreign development through her investments abroad. They are under no misapprehension as to how Britain's so-called adverse balance of trade was caused; they want to send out their capital, and they say they must do it.
Now, it is a dangerous thing for one who has occupied the time of the House longer than he intended to inflict a quotation upon hon. members, but I have in my hand the Wall Street Journal of Friday last, containing a review of topics of taxation, the tariff, and America's foreign trade relations, by Thomas W. Lamont, one of the leading members of Pierpont Morgan and Company, and one of the greatest financiers and authorities on finance in the States. I do not apologize for reading this, because the opinions of such a man about what is likely to happen in the immediate future in connection with America's trade relations must have enormous weight with every thoughtful Canadian and must have an effect, if we are wise, on the steps we take in developing our own policy. I quote from this article:
I do not for a moment mean to suggest that this country should forthwith go to a free-trade basis. Anything approaching such a complete, change is impossible. But the tendency toward, freer trade is bound to become more marked. Our position before the war as a debtor nation was a far different one from what it is to-day. When in those days we sold food and raw materials for export we were able to find our pay for them in a number of different ways. The peoples abroad sold us services in the way of ocean transportation, they sold us insurance. Lastly, on a large scale, they loaned us capital, -which is only another way of saying that they provided credits with which we paid our own, imports.
Now the position is reversed. Prom being a nation in debt to the peoples abroad, to the extent of say $5,000,000,000, as we were in, 1914, we have become, on net balance, a creditor to the peoples abroad to the extent of $12,000,000,000, perhaps even $15,000,000,000, Therefore, whether we will it or not, from this time forward we must act the part of a creditor nation; we must be governed by the economic and commercial laws that govern creditor nations. We must begin to realize, if we do not already realize it, that we cannot continue to pile up these credits indefinitely without disarranging our own and the world's markets. In other words, we shall find our operations working against the old mercantile theory of trade, that same ancient theory that England, as a great creditor and commercial nation, found herself compelled to abandon a hundred and fifty years ago. We shall find ourselves ardently desiring to buy as well as to sell. If such shall prove to be the case-and I see no escape from it-we shall automatically tend toward freer trade. We shall inevitably grow to realize that the ideal status for the world is for our country to produce those things which it can product cheapest and best, and to exchange those things for the products of other countries which those countries are able to, produce better and more cheaply than we.
I shall not be surprised if the new Congress, realizing our country's enormously changed situation, will find the difficulties of thoroughgoing tariff revision so great that they may-abandon any immediate attempt at it.

This quotation will go on Hansard, and I trust my hon. friends opposite will peruse it carefully and find out what the really big men of the United States are saying and thinking about these things.
Such is the fairy tale that the Prime Minister of this Dominion told the House and the country in his speech on the last Budget. It is exactly contrary to the historic facts of the case. If my right hon. friend will acquaint himself, not with the views of economists, but with the writings of standard authors, he will know that Britain, at the end of her protective period, was steeped in poverty as regards the masses of her people. Read Carlyle's "Past and Present"; read the best works of fiction relating to that period; read Macaulay; read the speech which Emerson delivered at Manchester in 1847. The year after free trade was passed, but two years before it came into operation, Mr. Emerson, speaking at Manchester, referred to conditions prevailing at the end of the protective period as conditions of "gloom and commercial crises, affliction and beggary". That is the language, not of a Britisher, but of one of the most distinguished sons of New England in the United States. Since that time, Britain, by her fiscal policy, has increased enormously in wealth, in prosperity, in the comfort of her people and in the greatness of her world-wide destiny. That is the true history of the case.
I should like to have referred to some of the other arguments which my right hon. friend has used in the country in support of the policy to which he gives his honest and open adherence. He says: "We believe in protection"-and the address repeats the fallacy-"because it keeps the workmen at home and it keeps industries in Canada." It did not do that during the first years of the protective or so-called National Policy in this country. A million French-Canadians went to find their homes in the United States, and the population of Canada, at the end of the period, was practically stationary. It was when there was some slight departure, all too slight,
I admit, from that policy, that we in this country began to expand, and we would have expanded to a far greater degree if the departure had been greater. It begs the whole question.
Another argument used both by the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is the argument of antiquity. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said, I think, down in Elgin, "Why,

we have had this policy in the United States for 141 years and in Canada for 42 years." My right hon. friend, showing how well he is adapted for being a leader by following his follower, took the figures from the latter and repeated them in the Eastern Townships of Quebec. Well, 141 years in the United States and 42 years in Canada-that is a very brief period in the history of a nation. It was only in 1776 that Adam Smith's work was published, and he knew so much of the difficulty of penetrating the human cranium with new ideas that he had very little expectation that his views would make much progress in his life-time. But if m>
right hon. friend wants to argue from antiquity, he should go further back. There was a king, who lived long ago; he was a very rich king, and he was a very wise king, wiser than my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), wiser even than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is related of him: " And the king made silver and gold at Jerusalem as plenteous as stones, and cedar trees made he as the sycamore trees that are in the vale for abundance. And Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt and linen yarn; and the king's merchants received the linen yarn at a price." So that the wisest man that ever lived was not afraid of imports; he was a free trader; he would trade in Egypt or anywhere else where he could get good horses and linen, if the other people at Jerusalem would take the stuff those other countries produced and pay for it. My right hon. friend says-and in this he has also copied the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce

"England"-I prefer the term "Britain", myself, but we use the word "England" in that way-"England is the only nation that ever has gone in for free trade." Well, that may be so, though Holland, one of the brightest little countries in Europe, has gone pretty near it. But may I say to my right hon. friend that Britain is the only country that could have cleared the seven seas of every German ship in four months, and that is what my right hon. friend called "muddling through the war?" Britain is the only country that could have won the battle of Jutland, and she won it. Britain is the only country that established constitutional government hundreds of years ago, at a time when every other nation in Europe was a tyranny and North America was a wild. Was she wrong in blazing the trail in

that case? Was it to her disadvantage to have constitutional government? Was it rather not to the disadvantage of the laggards of human progress, for whom my right hon. friend becomes the apologist? I do not think the example of blazing the trail-the expression is a Canadian one-is one that we should be warned against by our leading statesmen in this fair young country. I think I have said enough to make my right hon. friend and my hon. friends opposite a little thoughtful about what Britain is likely to do, about what her free trade policy has done for her, and about what America is likely to do. They will become more thoughtful as the days go by. I gather, though, that a lot of the people of Canada are thinking a little differently now on this question from the way they used to think.
It is time I remembered that there is an amendment on the subject before the House-though I claim that every word that I have uttered is thoroughly germane to the subject and in line with the best traditions of debate. It cannot be said that I have in any way funked the main question in the Address, and I apologize for the time I have spent over it. Now, there is an amendment to the amendment. Well, that amendment to the amendment has no attractions for me, for two reasons. In the first place, when I heard it put forward, I reflected that in human life it frequently happens that people who try to sit between two stools presently find themselves occupying a more lowly posture. I do not care for the amendment from that practical point of view. But this amendment being before us, I think it is a fair thing to say that there are three possible views to be taken of it. We may vote complete confidence in the AdministratiiJh; we may vote partial confidence in the Administration; or we may vote no confidence in the Administration. One of these courses we may take in the first instance, and we may follow the other afterwards. Well, as I look at things, it would be impossible to vote partial confidence in the Administration first, and then vote no confidence in it afterwards. That would not be a logical course of procedure, so as far as I am concerned I shall vote as I feel, which on the grounds I have elaborated at great length is want of confidence in the Government. Not that the amendment is free from fault. One objection to the amendment to my mind, is that it states as a fact what
is not a fact. I do not think for one moment that the Prime Minister and his colleagues are guilty of usurpation. "Usurpation" is a word with a well-defined meaning. Usurpation is the seizure of Government by force against the constitution and against the law. I have not looked at the dictionary, but I have ventured on that definition myself. That being so, I think my hon. friend who proposed the amendment gave away his case when he admitted the Government were in office according to law and according to the constitution. The second objection is that it professes to wish to get a proper representation of the people. But if it were carried and an immediate election took place, that is just what it would not get. On this point I differ very, very acutely from my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), when he says there is no need for redistribution to precede the election.
I think, in ordinary times, and under ordinary conditions, redistribution ought to precede the election, immediately if possible, or as nearly as possible; and if my hon. friend had been here I should have asked him what is the object of redistribution? It has only one object in the world- to get a proper representation of the people at the ensuing election. So, if the object of the amendment be to get a proper representation of the people, if it prevented redistribution it would fail in attaining that object.
There is another point in regard to representation which I would like to mention, and if the Government live long, enough to deal with the subject, I hope they will give serious consideration to it also. If the elections are going to take place in this country under conditions such as have prevailed recently we are going to he face to face with conditions under which constituencies will be very generally represented by minority members. In Elgin we had an hon. gentleman elected, whom I am very proud to have as a colleague-he could not help the circumstances, he had to run under the conditions that prevailed, hut he was voted for only by three-eighths of the constituents. In Peterborough only 4,000, in round numbers, voted for the successful candidate, out of 13,000 votes cast. If we are to have numerous candidates in single-member constituencies, I do not think it will make for stable conditions and the maintenance of the best kind of representation in the House, to have men elected to represent minorities, and I would ask the

minister seriously to consider when they come to the question of redistribution, if they ever do, the possibility of having the single transferable vote in single-member ridings and trying out proportional representation in given areas of the country. That is a matter deserving very serious consideration. We are living in times when changes are very rapid, and may easily become too rapid, and one of the great advantages of proportional representation is that it would give you some guarantee of having in each succeeding Parliament a fair proportion of men who, like my right hon. friend, have attained their political knowledge and political position by constant service, year after year, in the House of Commons. I would seriously impress that view on my right hon. friend. Let me put it plainly in other words. I think it is desirable that men of a certain size in our public life, so far as they are willing should be retained for the public service whether they call themselves Liberals, Tories, or Progressives. Politics is the science of Government, and like any other science, it can only be learned by application, and by the practice of it. In Great Britain a politician of a certain size is never lost to the public service until he is lost through death. If he loses his seat in one part of the country, he finds a seat in some other part, and under proportional representation I think that men of a certain size would be sure of getting elected to the House-not by any gerrymandering process, but by the process of giving proper representation to minorities. May I be very personal in the application of my argument? Let me suppose a case. My right hon. friend sits for Portage La Prairie. Now it might be-on personal grounds I hope it won't be-on personal grounds, I said-that Portage La Prairie will turn its back on my right hon. friend.
Oh, no.
It is a possibility.
Oh, no.

Well, of
course, people who are very sanguine before elections are liable to have their eyes opened when the elections take place. There may be strange things happen in Toronto. I am only begging for a possibility. I say, that might happen. Now I venture to think this: If you had a system of proportional representation in the city of Winnipeg, and my right hon. friend were one of the candidates his size would ensure that if there were five members,

he would come pretty near the head of the poll, because he would get the votes of men of size all over that great city. That is just a little illustration of how proportional representation might work out. It is a matter which the Government will have to consider very seriously if it wants to secure real representation in this House, if we are to have various groups running candidates in various parts of the country.

How would you re-elect
newly appointed ministers?

I always
thought that was an absurdity, an anachronism, better got rid of. There are many people in Great Britain, and more in Canada, who think that sending ministers back for re-election is really a thing of the past and ought to be abolished. I do not think there is much in that practice.
I have another objection to the amendment. It is contrary as far as I know, to the invariable practice of the Old Land in regard to amendments to the Address.
They nearly always hinge upon some question of principle, and I think it is well that that should be so. In this connection may I say that I think it is unfortunate that the official opposition in this House are apparently not in a position to take direct issue with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister upon the tariff question. I wish to be quite frank in this matter. My hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King), vith very great courtesy, has extended an invitation to Progressives all over Canada to fight under his banner. Well, there are reasons why consideration of that proposal is impossible, and I want to give them with perfect candour. In the first place, I believe it is impossible for a great party successfully to face the electorate speaking with two voices upon what is the main issue of the day. Now, I submit that in all kiifdness to my hon. friend. The Prime Minister, within his perfect rights, has agreed with the Progressive party and with my hon. friend himself that the tariff is a great issue to-day. The Prime Minister says it is the greatest issue. We agree with him and join issue with him on the question. We are opposed to the principle of protection; he is in favour of it. I submit to my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) that he should tell his friends that it is really impossible, in the serious condition of the minds of our people, to speak with two voices upon what is the great issue of the day. I hope my hon. friends opposite will applaud the next thing I say. It is impossible for a party

truly liberal to have any success linked to the medieval superstition or imposture of protection, and I may say that I borrow both these epithets from William Ewart Gladstone; he got light upon the tariff question when he was just about the age of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and he came in his old age to look upon protection as a superstition and an imposture. I put it to my hon. friends in all seriousness that it is impossible for them to turn a friendly face to a superstition and an imposture. In this connection, may I remind the House that last year I quoted from a distinguished man who for so many years represented Quebec East? That constituency is still fortunate in having a distinguished man (Mr. Lapointe) for its representative and he gave a definition of Liberalism a couple of years ago which was very simple and easy to remember, and which I believe to be absolutely correct. He said that Liberalism *is freedom. Well, I hope he had in his mind besides freedom in religion and freedom in civil rights, freedom in trade also. If it is freedom it means ultimately some time freedom in trade as well as in other respects. And I want to say very seriously to my hon. friends from Quebec-I hope I shall not be charged with carrying on a courtship in that quarter, as so many of our public men have been, for if I court ' the people of Quebec, it is not for their votes or anything I want from them-I want to say to them that I should greatly value their intellectual and moral adhesion to my views. Let me say that in my opinion my hon. friend from Quebec East was right in his definition; Liberalism, historically as well as etymologically, means freedom. But let me carry his thought a little further. In fighting for freedom, how are the forces ranged? In fighting for freedom, from the time the word was used in 1828 and 1829 when Catholic Emancipation was carried and the Tests and Corporation Acts were repealed, and all down through the fights of Liberalism in Britain. I will tell my hon. friend how the forces were ranged. Liberalism was always fighting for the rights of the masses against the usurpation of the classes-using that word in a greatly different sense from the way it is used in the amendment. Well, how does protection stand in regard to the classes and the masses? Protection perpetuates the injustice of taxing the many for the sake of the few; it is an accentuated form of special privilege, and against special privilege,
whether in Canada or in Britain, all true Liberalism has always fought. On these grounds I appeal to the people of the province of Quebec to study these questions. There may be capitalists, there are capitalists, in the city of Montreal, who are protectionists, but Jean-Baptiste est libre-echangiste-pas mon ami, le "Jean-Bap-tiste'' de cette Chambre, mais le vrai Jean-Baptiste-; il est en faveur du libre-echange. Protection, standing as it does for special privilege, is typical Toryism. If you have any doubt look opposite and see who support it.
And that impels me to state that there is no course for us in this corner of the Chamber but to vote for the amendment in each division that will be called. In the first place, we canot vote a confidence which we do not feel, and in the next place, whether we will it or not, the Prime Minister, though he made an appeal to me-a compliment which I want to say sincerely I felt intensely-has made it impossible for me to vote for the Address. There are advantages accruing to the nailing of one's colours to the mast. My right hon. friend is being commended by his supporters because he has nailed his colours to the mast. He comes to me and says: "Nail your colours there too." But the mast is on a sinking ship from my point of view; I do not mean the ship of administration, but that battered medieval ship of protection. Now, my right hon. friend, in that speech on the last Budget which has got so much of my attention, gave me absolution beforehand for voting for the amendment. He said in that speech, when we were dealing with this same question on which the right hon. gentleman has nailed his colours to the mast:
I can understand a man whose feet are based on free trade voting against this budget; I cannot understand those who believe in the principle of protection voting against it.
So if my hon. friend'wants support from this House, according to his own showing, for this Address, which puts the principle of protection in its very heart and centre, if he can find any protectionists opposite he may fittingly make his appeal to them for help. But he cannot fittingly appeal to us. He is for protection; we do not believe in it. Having no confidence in the Administration, and having less if possible in its policy of protection, we shall vote, as I understand it, for the amendment.
My right hon. friend, in my opinion, was skating on very thin ice when he said: If you get your election by this bald amend-

ment-and I admit the hairless condition of the amendment-what will you be fighting on them? What will you have to go to the country on? Surely my right hon. friend knows that the moment a Government takes office in this country it is on its trial. It is composed of marked men. It can be tried any time properly by vote of censure in this House, and is always tried sooner or later before a higher and a final tribunal. It is the Government and its policy that we shall vote on if we go to the country. Besides my right hon. friend must know-I do not want to refer to recent elections at too great length, I am not greatly impressed by what Mr. Gladstone once called the science of political meteorology; if we in this corner of the Chamber had got as much excited as some people seem to do every time they win an election we should all have been in hopeless hysterics long ago; we have got so used to winning by-elections that they are like water on a duck's back with us, and do not excite us at all; passing events-my right hon. friend I say, must know by even a casual glance at recent by-elections that the choice at the present moment is not purely a choice between Grit and Tory. There are third choices and the people know it.
Something has been said qbout the issue being confused. My hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders) said my leader was not clear in his enunciation of policy. Well, he stands upon a policy that was drawn up by my hon. friend the member for Macdonald, absolutely.
Hear, hear.

My leader applauds me.
He has not departed from a single plank that my hon. friend put under him, he stands on it still. If my hon. friend is on it still, he is mighty near the edge waiting to jump off. There is no doubt about where we arS in this matter. My hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Argue) very properly and very fairly asked us on the cross-bench portion of the Chamber what mandate we had to be here. Well, I can only speak for myself on that subject. One afternoon in the House, after the war was over, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) brought in some question regarding shipbuilding. I took the liberty, which I have frequently taken in this House, to try and show him in very moderate language that he would promote shipbuilding if he would promote foreign trade-a thing

which appears tolerably evident to anybody who thinks out the subject-and the consequence was that within a few hours, two of the strongest protectionist speeches were delivered that I have ever heard in this House during the time I have sat in it; and I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that the fumes that arose around me, to my trained nostrils were the fumes of Toryism and not Unionism. I was smoked out. I went to the cross-benches next day, I escaped for my life. Because I have breathed the air of freedom of opinion all the time I have lived, and freedom of trade as well. That is where I got my mandate. I told the people who elected me that I believed the same thing that I believed when they first elected me. When I was elected for Red Deer I was elected as a free trader. I believe in freedom. When I supported my right hon. friend in the war I believed that the greatest fight that was ever waged for freedom was being waged on the battle fields of Europe. I believed in freedom then, I believe in freedom now-freedom first and last for me. There has been no inconsistency about my position. If Liberalism means freedom then I am as good a Liberal to-day as ever I was. But for the time being we are " Progressives " because I have given reasons why I am a little doubtful about certain brands of Liberalism. Liberalism to me must be real Liberalism.
Do not let my right hon. friend have any trouble about what will go before the country. It is the Government that is always on its trial. It is on trial in this House, and the people have a second choice. Where, I think, those who want to return hon. gentlemen opposite, who want to return to the old methods of political thought, fail, is in not having a thorough appreciation of the psychology of the people at this time. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, the people of this country, and of every other country, are thinking in a way they have never thought before. There is a consciousness-which may in some cases be only a sub-consciousness-that having participated in common sacrifices, having escaped a common danger, having won a common and glorious victory, they ought to participate, to the full in the things for which the battle was fought and for which the victory was won. There is a democratic sentiment in this country, arising in all quarters of it, which cares little for old party names and less for old party shibboleths. I myself care very little for

detailed programmes. Tell me the spirit and the principle of a man or a party, and I will tell you whether that man is a Tory or whether he is a Progressive. It is the spirit that counts. We read in our newspapers and we said in our speeches during the war that the world would not be the same after the war, and it is not the same. It is not the same because everywhere there is a grim determination that democratic principles shall prevail among the peoples of the earth and that special privilege shall die. There is a determination that life and meaning shall be put into that old phrase which has been used from time immemorial on this side of the Atlantic: "Special privileges to none, equal rights and opportunities for all." There never was a time when the rank and file of the people, not only in Canada hut in all nations of the earth-and this is the issue that will be fought in the next election-were praying more earnestly, if not in the words in the thought of the old Corn Law rhymer, Ebenezer Elliott. During that supposed time of prosperity in Britain when protection prevailed, Ebenezer Elliott voiced the sentiments of the people themselves in regard to this matter -and he is voicing the sentiments of democratic people everywhere to-day-when he wrote:
When wilt Thou save the people, O God of , Mercy, When ?
The people, Lord, the people-not Crowns and Thrones, hut men.
God save the people, Thine they are,
Thy children, as Thy angels fair.
From guilt, oppression, and despair,
God save the people.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House will agree that it has just had one of those very able, very learned, and very eloquent appeals to which the hon. member for Red Deer sometimes gives us an opportunity to listen. If we cannot on all occasions agree with the opinions or ideas advanced in this House by the hon. member for Red Deer, we can still join in paying this tribute to him, that he speaks with a vast amount of sincerity and a vast amount of boldness, because I believe he is one of the members of this House who is not afraid to state his actual opinion upon any occasion or upon any question.
I reg et, as we on this side of the House will regret, that upon this important occasion he considers it his duty to vote for the first amendment moved, namely, the want-of-confidence motion in the Administration. He has given to the House during the course of his two and a quarter hours' address reasons which, I am satisfied, appeal to him and convince him what is the right course for him to take. But they certainly are far wide of the reasons which have been advanced by the official leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) for voting want of confidence in this Government. There is no resemblance between the reasons advanced to-day by my hon. friend from Red Deer and the reasons advanced upon the opening day of the session by the official leader of the Opposition.
While I admit that my hon. friend from Red Deer was quite within his rights to take the stand which he has taken this afternoon, and to submit as his chief reason for voting in favour of this amendment the fact that he does not approve the fiscal policy of the Government, I realize, as I am sure the House will realize, that that has been the attitude of the hon. gentleman ever since the general election of 1917. He was not a supporter of the fiscal policy of the Government then, he is not a supporter of it now. If he has no confidence to-day in this Government on account of its fiscal policy, it is no new thing whatever, it is merely the repetition of an old idea or old attitude on his part.
I confess that we on this side of the House were pleased with the somewhat genuine and generous tribute of congratulation which he sounded at the opening of his speech towards the Government and those of us who support it. He spoke of the business properity and the contentment which has been pretty general in this country since the war, as we all know, and he attributed a limited amount of credit to the Government for this satisfactory condition, although I am prepared to say he gave the chief credit to Providence. He congratulated us also on the fact that there was a certain amount of prosperity now throughout the length and breadth of Canada. We are glad of his good opinion in this respect; and we are glad that he has been manly enough and bold enough to declare that in his estimation the charge of usurpation of office which was launched against this Government by the official leader of the Opposition on the opening day of the session is entirely unfounded and unjustified.
There was this to be said in regard to the argument of my hon. friend from Red Deer upon the fiscal question. After he had enumerated what, I imagine, were in his view the shortcomings of the Administration; after he had touched on the pro-

posal emanating from hon. members on this side of the House for the appointment of a Grain Commission; after he had made some very humorous comments upon that subject which is known in this House as Daylight Saving; after he had enlarged more or less upon the luxury taxes and declared, what he had always declared for three sessions, must eventually prevail, then he turned round and said, "For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall vote no confidence in the Government; hut I can find other and stronger reasons for such a vote when I refer to the speech delivered in this House eight or ten months ago upon the tariff question by the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Government."
I am afraid that that speech of the right hon. leader of the Government made a deep impression upon the hon. member for Red Deer. I believe that last session he was not satisfied with himself in respect of that speech. I think he tried very hard to obtain an opportunity to deliver a second speech upon the subject of the Budget by way of reply to the speech of my right hon. friend, and it seems to me that for eight or ten months back my hon. friend from Red Deer has been nursing this sore question in his heart, he has been pondering over that speech, and this afternoon he has given the House his deliverance upon the question.
My hon. friend will forgive me if I do not attempt to follow him into what I think I might fairly describe as an academic discussion of the fiscal and economic policy of Great Britain. For over one hour to-day he elaborated that fiscal system and his own particular views thereon. Now, I am not greatly concerned, neither is this House, with what is the precise fiscal policy today in Great Britain. We are concerned, and vitally concerned, as to what is the fiscal policy to-day and for the future in the Dominion of Canada. And if I do not further allude to my hon. friend's very able and very learned discussion of the British trade policy, he must not think that I have not been thoroughly impressed by his knowledge of the whole vast subject, and that I am not fully aware that he, of all men perhaps in this House, is best able to discuss the British fiscal system; but I do not think that the time of the House is as well occupied in a discussion of that subject as it would be in a discussion of our own fiscal system.
However, my hon. friend did take huge satisfaction to himself by demonstrating to a conclusion, in his opinion, that an adverse balance of trade was a real benefit
[Mr. Guthrie.!
to a country, and that irrespective of whether that country were Great Britain or Canada. Now, to my mind the two cases are not parallel at all. There is a tremendous lack of similarity between them; the conditions are wide apart. My. hon. friend from Red Deer justified his statement that prosperity reigned in Great Britain when there was an excess of imports over exports by reason of two facts -the immense British investments overseas from which handsome revenues were returned; and Great Britain's control of the world's shipping from which also tremendous revenues were returned. These were the two facts which justified his statement to-day that Britain prospered under what we call an "adverse balance of trade." When he turns to the Dominion of Canada, let me point out to him, both these conditions are absent. Canada, we are forced regretfully to admit, has no foreign investments to speak of. Canada does not er*joy the world's foreign carrying trade. These two sources of revenue, which offset the effect of an adverse balance, are absent in the Dominion of Canada, and if your adverse balance piles up the day will come sooner or later when the balance must be met, and must be met in the only currency the world recognizes-that is, gold. My hon. friend says that in 1895, although our imports were valued at $100,000,000 and our exports at $102,000,000, prosperity did not reign within, the Dominion of Canada. Then, he said, as our adverse trade balance began to climb up, our prosperity seemed to return. Yes, it is true our prosperity did seem to return; as our balance kept piling up it seemed that there was greater prosperity in Canada. But I think we were a little short-sighted. We do not feel the effects of the adverse balance of trade the first year, or the second year, or, perhaps, the fifth or the tenth year; but we are feeling it to-day and we shall feel it for many a year to come-until the situation in this country is righted. Let me point out this to my hon. friend: just at this moment- and I am speaking only in approximate figures-I understand that we are buying annually a billion dollars worth of goods from the United States, and we are selling to them about half that amount. We might carry that on for a few years, but the day of settlement is bound to come, and how are we going to settle? The day of settlement is at hand now, unfortunately, and we are settling by going out in the market and buying American currency, and by doing that we are depreciating our own dollar or

appreciating the American dollar-and you have the exchange situation. If you continue to purchase from the United States annually and in vast amounts more than you sell to them; if you keep piling ujd that adverse balance, your exchange is going to get lower and lower. There are two ways that I know of, and only two, of correcting that. You can correct it by selling the United States more goods, or you can correct it by ceasing to buy so much goods from the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that in touching on this question of purchasing from the United States I am touching directly upon one of the questions which is very near and dear to the heart of the Agrarian party, or to that portion of it which belongs to the United Grain Growers.
I know that it has almost become a principle with that organization to deal as far as possible with the people in the United States, disregardful of whether or not injury results to the traders of Canada. I mention this matter particularly at this time on account of a statement which was made in the House last Friday night by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. J. F. Reid). Fortunately or unfortunately for me, about a month ago I had occasion to make a speech in the riding of South York, represented by my hon. friend who sits next to me (Mr. W. F. Maclean). During the course of my remarks on that occasion I was dealing with the question of the tariff policy of the party known as the United Farmers' party. I was dealing with that plank which demanded free trade in agricultural implements, and I pointed out to my audience on that occasion that it would suit the purposes of the United Grain Growers and the Farmers' party generally if they could obtain free trade in implements, and that, strange as it may seem, that organization has for a long period of years past been dealing in agricultural implements in the western part of this country almost exclusively with firms and manufacturing establishments in the United States. A report of that meeting seems to have got into the newspapers-not an accurate report, but I do not know that I have very much complaint to make with regard to it. It seems to have been published pretty generally; it was one of those telegraphic reports that do get into the papers. It was referred to and put on Hansard the other day by the hon. member for Mackenzie. The part to which I wish to draw attention at this time is reported 27
in Hansard, unrevised edition, at page 353. It says, among other things:
The ploughs listed in the catalogue, Mr. Guthrie said, were made in Wisconsin; harrows, cultivators, mowers, etc., in Illinois; portable engines and washing machines in Pontiac, 111. ; cream separators in Buffalo, N.Y.; and wagons in Iowa.
Then the report purports to give my exact words, because what follows is in inverted commas:
"In the lines of goods which I have mentioned, which are called 'U. G. G. goods'," Mr. Guthrie said, "there is not a Canadian article catalogued."
I take no exception to that report of my speech save in one particular-I did not mention wagon. I mentioned the other things but made no reference to wagons. Now, that statement of mine was contradicted by Mr. Rice-Jones, general manager and vice president of the United Grain Growers. He gave a report to the press, and it is in regard to that statement that I wish to place some information before the House-particularly in view of the fact that I am in the presence of the president of the United Grain Growers, if I judge aright from the catalogue of that organization, which I have before me. Mr. Rice-Jones, in his statement, which is reported at page 353 of Hansard, says:
The Hon. Hugh Guthrie's statement as reported in a despatch is incorrect. He states there is not a Canadian article in the machinery listed in our catalogue as United Grain Growers.
Now, I did not state that, but it is pretty nearly the truth, as I am going to prove. The statement goes on:
Even the list of machinery which is specifically mentioned as being manufactured in the United States is incorrect.
I am subject to correction. Then he goes on:
Mowers and rakes and wagons, for instance, are all purchased in Canada.
When I saw that contradiction published in the papers, I thought that in justice to myself I had better look the matter up again, and the first place I looked was in the sworn testimony of Mr. Rice-Jones given before the Tariff Commission. I obtained an extract from it, and I am going to read it to the House so that it will go on Hansard. Mr. Rice-Jones appeared before the Tariff Commission at Winnipeg, and after having made a statement of how much more cheaply he could sell his goods out there if there was no tariff, the chairman of the commission



began to ask him some questions. Now, this is from the record; I will give the evidence:
Sir Henry Drayton: Where do you get this machinery from? From whom do you buy your plow?
Mr." Rice-Jones: It is the Lacrosse plow.
Sir Henry Drayton: From whom do you buy your cultivator ?
Mr. Rice-Jones: From the Light Draft Harrow Company.
Sir Henry Drayton: Where do you get it?
Mr. Rice-Jones: It comes from Ohio.
Sir Henry Drayton: What is the name of the firm?
Mr. Rice-Jones:	The Light Draft Harrow
Company.
Sir Henry Drayton: What is the name of their home town?
Mr. Rice-Jones:	I cannot recall the name
just now; I can get it for you.
Sir Henry Drayton: It cannot be a very well known name.
Mr. Rice-Jones: It is just a small company.
Sir Henry Drayton:	Is that concern just
manufacturing for you?
Mr. Rice-Jones: No.
Sir Henry Drayton:	Is it a concern with
which you have made a special contract?
Mr. Rice-Jones: No.
Sir Henry Drayton: The next is "seed-drill 20 single disc." Where do you get that?
Mr. Rice-Jones : At Lacrosse.
Sir Henry Drayton: That is Lacrosse, Wisconsin?
Mr. Rice-Jones: Yes.
Sir Henry Drayton: Where do you get the washing-machine ?
Mr. Rice-Jones: From the Meadows people.
Sir Henry Drayton: Where are they?
Mr. Rice-Jones: I cannot tell you offhand where their plant is.

Mr. Rice-Jones: Ohio.

grinders come from?
Mr. Rice-Jones: The Letz Company.

from?	.

Wisconsin.

Mr. Rice-Jones: Yes. I can get you that information.

where these places were and you do not appear to know anything about them. Where do you get the small gas engines?
Mr. Rice-Jones: From the Hercules Gas Engine Company of Evansville, Indiana.

Machine Company of Dayton, Ohio.
