I am going to emphasize that because of Mr. Rice-Jones' statement that mowers and rakes and wagons, for instance, are

all purchased in Canada, and yet he swore before the Tariff Commission that he bought his mowers at Dayton, Ohio.
What was the date of the hearing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think the date of the Tariff Commission would be about September, October, or November of last year. I do not think I said anything about wagons at South York but I began to look through the catalogue on the subject of wagons, and if I did say anything about wagons, I do not know that I made such a terrible blunder. Mr. Rice-Jones says in regard to wagons: "In fact, we have not purchased a wagon in the United States for three years." I turn to their catalogue -this is not the most recent one, it is the one for 1919-and I read in it about a wagon called the "Abingdon" wagon. This is what the catalogue says at page 74:
The "Abingdon" is known throughout Western Canada as one of the highest grade imported farm wagons in Canadian service. For some time the importation of the finest American-made wagons has been practically impossible, but our extensive purchases, made at an early date, enable us to continue to offer them.
That is the denial of the statement of Mr. Rice-Jones, so that I do not think I was so far astray in what I said. The point I was trying to make was this-and I will make it briefly now-that in almost the whole list of farm implements and farm machinery, scarcely a single article sold by the United Grain Growers and advertised in their catalogue is of Canadian manufacture; almost exclusively this farm machinery is of American manufacture.
I am now going over the list a little more carefully. I do not find that the United Grain Growers Association sell what we call threshing machines; I do not find them advertising threshing machines or binders; but I do find them advertising the following farm machinery, and I say that according to their catalogue and the sworn statement of Mr. Rice-Jones the great bulk of it is American manufacture:	Ploughs, disc
harrows, common harrows, seed drills, cultivators, "Forkner" cultivators, haying machinery, including mowers, rakes, bunchers, sweep rakes, stackers, tedders, grain grinders, potato planters, sprayers, and diggers, portable elevators, gas engines, cream separators, washing machines, road machinery, manure spreaders, "Abingdon" wagons.
I can not find in that long list a single

article made in Canada unless it be a steel rake. I can go further; I can even identify most of the articles from the plates upon them. I can tell precisely the factories in which most of these goods were turned out, because I have made it my business to get that information, and while my hon. friend is in the humour and in his place, I should like to ask him one question that he can probably answer. If he does not want to do so, it does not matter. In this catalogue a large motor truck is advertised and greatly commended. I have been told that the Smith Form-a-truck is of American manufacture. I have not been able to verify that, but perhaps my hon. friend, who is president of the company, can bell me whether that is the case or not.
I regret I cannot give my hon. friend the information.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It is about the only thing that could be called a farm implement that might possibly be of Canadian manufacture, except also a little grinder manufactured in Quebec, and I will give my hon. friend and his company full credit for that. But what is this organization doing? What is the party supported by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) doing to-day? Look at the millions upon millions of dollars that are going out of this country every year to buy American machinery and pile up an adverse balance of trade. Is it any wonder that one of the foremost planks in the tariff policy of the Farmers' party is the plank calling for free farm implements? They are paying now only from twelve and one-half to fifteen, indeed, I think in some cases as high as twenty per cent, in duty, but in spite of that tariff, they are successfully bringing into this country and selling to a tremendous number of people in the West, American farm machinery against the competition of Canadian manufacturers. If they can do this with a duty of twelve or fifteen or twenty per cent against them, what will they do should they come into power and wipe out that little bit of protection and give free trade in implements? If the free implement plank were adopted in Canada, they would increase their purchases with the United States enormously, because there would be no barrier at all to prevent them; it would be a matter of only a few weeks, or at most a few months, until they would be in a position to close up practically all the industries in this country engaged to-day in the production of that class of material.
But there is another point of view in regard to this matter. It is said that we in Canada are to-day suffering, to some extent at least, from unemployment. Is it a patriotic thing, or a sound thing economically, to take the money of the people of Canada at this critical period, to send it across to the United States to give employment in the factories there, to pay wages and keep employed citizdns of the United States, while so many good Canadians during the past few months have been looking for jobs in this country? Would it not, in the first place, be a more patriotic thing, and in the second place, a sounder thing economically, if the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), and his friends of the United Grain Growers, would look about them in this country to the scores, yes, even hundreds, of Canadian manufacturers who can supply the goods they require, and try to make terms with them, spend their money in this country and thus give employment to unemployed Canadians.
It will be-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend can follow me, but I do not wish to be interrupted. I am going to give my hon. friend a few details in regard to the manufacture of these articles, and he can take the matter up with his people when he goes home. I will deal with the question of gas engines, which alone forms a big item. Does the House know that to-day gas engines are manufactured in 65 Canadian factories, and the only kerosene or gasoline engine that the Grain Growers advertise is the "Hercules" machine made in the United States, every variety and style of it is here advertised and not a single one the product of the 65 factories scattered throughout the provinces of the Dominion. I will supply a list of these manufacturers to my hon. friend if he will make use of it. I come now to the question of cultivators. He will not for one minute say he cannot buy just as good a cultivator in Canada as he can in the United States.

They will not sell them
to us.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Fourteen	factories
in this country to-day, employing Canadian labour, are turning out cultivators just as good as can be bought anywhere in the United States, but not a single Canadian cultivator does this company sell or advertise in their catalogue.
I come next to grain grinders. Mr. Rice-Tones says that they adopt the Letz-

which is made in the United States. Now there are no less than eighteen firms in Canada making grain grinders, and from all I can gather there are better grain grinders made in Canada than in the United States. There again they give the American manufacturers the preference by advertising exclusively American-made machines, and excluding all the eighteen manufacturers of grain grinders in this country.
I come now to power washing machines. Many of the machines I have mentioned are made in the riding I have the honour to represent, and I feel keenly interested in the matter. Cultivators are made in South Wellington, gas engines are made in South Wellington, power washing machines are made in South Wellington. I would like to see the factories in the riding I have the honour to represent receive some of these orders, and thereby give employment to men in the province of Ontario. Fifteen factories in the Dominion of Canada are making these power washing machines, employing Canadian labour, but with not one of them does the United Grain Growers deal. Not a single Canadian washing machine do they advertise in their catalogue. In every instance they advertise the American machine.
So it is with the cream separator. I am told they are making cream separators at Renfrew, and very good ones too. I know they are making good ones at Peterborough, I know they are making good ones at Hamilton, but in spite of this fact this patriotic organization of traders in the great West deliberately decides to advertise and sell the King separator, made in Buffalo, New York. It will not sell a single Canadian-made separator. It is all very well for the president of that company to occupy a seat in this House and try to interrupt; but I bring this matter forward in order to give the public the facts, to put the facts on Hansard, and then let the Grain Growers' Guide publish these facts broadcast if it will. My attention has been drawn very forcibly within the last month to the fact they are publishing things about me and at the same time are misquoting what I said. Now I will give them a chance to quote from Hansard what I actually do say, and see if they will publish it.
There is one statement in the press despatch reporting an alleged speech I made in South York which is certainly not correct. It is reported in that despatch that I said the Grain Growers or the

Farmers' party was " a menace to Canada." I never used that word, nor anything that sounded like it, nor any word that bore its meaning. I did say this, in the course of my remarks, that the most serious opposition in this country to the present Government was to be found in the Farmers' party. I said it was a party that had its origin in the far West among a population which was not entirely British, where the farming population, I believed, of the western provinces was said to be about 60 per cent foreign-born and about 40 per cent British-born. I said I had information that the movement had its genesis among the American farmers in the great West, that they were of a class of people who desired to trade with the people back home, and evidently from this catalogue, they were determined to carry out their desires. I said the movement had started in the West, but had swept eastward. It had taken a strong hold in Ontario and had now got down to the Maritime Provinces and I paid them the compliment of saying they were the most formidable opposition which the Government had politically in Canada to-day. I made no statement that they were a menace to Canada, as I am quoted in the press despatch as saying, and to which statement such severe exceptions was taken by my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) the other night.
I think I can also pay them this further compliment-that so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, we know pretty well where the Farmers' party stands in respect to the tariff. There is no question in the world where the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), stands on the tariff. He is a free-trader out-and-out, first, last and all the time. He proclaimed to-day as forcibly as any man could proclaim that while the hon. member for Yale (Mr. MacKelvie), desired protection on apples, he, the member for Red Deer, desired free trade in apples, that while the member for Yale desired to make apples dear, he, as a free trader, desired to make apples cheap. Now will he be consistent and apply that same argument to wheat? If his desire is to cheapen everything in this country, I can tell him that a cheap country is not the best country to live in for anybody. It never was, and I think it never will be. But I will say this for my hon. friend from Red Deer: he is outspoken, you know where he stands.
I can also pay that tribute to the leader of the Farmers' party in the province of Ontario; I assume that Mr. Drury is the

leader of the Farmers' party in Ontario.
I do not know whether he owes allegiance to, or is a follower of, my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), but he is at all events the recognized leader of the Farmers' party in Ontario. I have never yet heard a fair, candid statement from my hon. friend from Marquette as to his tariff policy. I have heard him talking in the language of free trade one minute, and not of free trade the next. I have heard him say he would not be a free trader "in one fell swoop," and I read in a speech he made somewhere in the West that he was a free trader "by easy stages." I do not know exactly what he would do if he came into power in this country, but it is not so with the Prime Minister of Ontario. He gave us a sworn statement on this question, so we cannot question his stand. He was sworn before the committee of this House on the High Cost of Living, in 1919, and in looking over the evidence I find that at page 194, he says: "I want free trade on the manufactured goods."
That is short, concise, and direct. We know where Mr. Drury stands, and the point I desire to make is that we insist upon knowing where the rest of this House stands on the question of the tariff. There is so much pussy-footing, so much camouflage, so much soft-pedalling in the East, and so much loud pedalling on the free trade doctrine in the West, that it is pretty hard to know just where the official Opposition stands to-day, with the exception of my good friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster). He is outspoken enough, I think, to satisfy most of the people of this country. To my mind, he is a very outspoken free-trader. Having said so much, I cannot say anything about the remainder of the official Liberal party in this House, and I believe it is time the House knew, and time likewise the country knew, just where they stand. I think one of the most important matters at this particular moment is that someone devise some means of having at the earliest possible moment a clear-cut declaration, by a vote, to establish where each and every member of this House stands on the tariff policies that have from time to time been proclaimed in Canada. A delicious sidelight was thrown on the situation by our good friend the member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier), when in his speech in the House the other day he described in his own clear and graphic manner how the Liberal fiscal policy was framed at the Liberal convention in Ottawa in the year 1919.
He evidently was a member of the committee which was charged with the preparation of the plank in regard to the fiscal policy. He described to us how they met in their committee room, and how the presiding officer on that occasion, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), true to his-
Will the hon. member pardon me? He is mistaken; I was not the presiding officer.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Well, a prominent
member of the committee I should say. However, the hon. member certainly pictured to us how eloquently the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) had pointed out, in the presence of the members of that committee, his view of the matter at all events, which was that the Liberal party was the historic free trade party in this country, that it was the real free trade party in Canada, but that he was completely brushed aside by his friend, the member for Shelburne and Queen's, who interjected: "In theory, we are a free trade party, but only in theory."
At six o'clock the House took recess.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with a brief discussion of the platform of the various parties in regard to the fiscal question, I Wish to say that I omitted before the adjournment to make reference to one statement made by my hon. friend from Red Deer during the course of his remarks this afternoon. It was in reference to his argument upon the question of the balance of trade. Among other things, he mentioned that the municipalities and the provinces of this country were rapidly piling up debt in the United States. This fact, he said, had an influence upon the question of the balance of trade as between Canada and the United States, and, in some way, he seemed to charge this Government with responsibility in respect of these municipal and provincial loans.
Now, as a matter of fact, the indebtedness of this Government to the United States at the present time is in a very satisfactory position. We know that we have a net indebtedness in Canada of about two and a quarter billions, but it is a gratifying thing to know that a very large proportion of this net debt is owed within our own

borders and to our own people. I suppose it goes without saying that debt cannot be considered as a good thing under any circumstances, but I think a national indebtedness is least objectionable when it is owed to your own people. Approximately, our debt as a nation in the United States today is about one hundred and seventy-five millions. We owe Great Britain, I think, about double that amount, but apart from these two items the whole indebtedness of this country is practically confined within our own borders. This Government has nothing to do with provincial or municipal borrowing. Provincial and municipal borrowing is not a new thing. It has been going on, I think, ever since the days of Confederation, and in pre-Confederation times also, but there is this difference today in regard to provincial and municipal loans. Formerly those loans were negotiated in London. To-day they are negotiated in New York, and if these loans add to the burden, or the adverse balance, of this country in respect of trade between Canada and the United States, the rebuke of my hon. friend from Red Deer should have been directed against the provinces and the municipalities of this country.
It is argued from time to time that the adverse trade balance as between Canada and the United States has no influence upon the present discount on Canadian money in the United States. It has been argued in my hearing that year after year when, as between the two countries, there was an adverse balance of trade, our money was never at a discount, our money was always at par. Consequently, it is said that an adverse balance of trade has nothing to do with the matter. But, Mr. Speaker, this must also be remembered: In those pre-war years this country, the corporations in this country, the provinces and the municipalities, were all heavy borrowers and in those days our borrowings were in Europe. Our borrowings were in London, in Holland, and in France, and by far the greatest portion of them were financed through New York, and this foreign borrowing, coming through American exchanges to a large extent, rectified the balance of trade and assisted in keeping our exchange level. But we have no foreign borrowings nowadays. We cannot raise money to-day in the London money markets. We cannot raise money to-day in European countries, we cannot avail ourselves of that source of relief in regard to the exchange. As I intimated before six o'clock, so far as I am 
aware there are only two ways of rectifying the adverse exchange-the one by seeing more goods, and the other by ceasing our overpurchases in the United States.
I was proceeding to examine what one might call the official Opposition platform in regard to the fiscal policy in this country. I think that I had remarked that my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) had given the House a most graphic description of the manner in which that policy was formed and adopted by the Liberal Convention which assembled in the city of Ottawa in the summer of 1919. After the policy had been thought out, considered, and formally adopted, it was sent broadcast throughout the Dominion of Canada. Official copies were issued in modest pamphlets such as the one I hold in my hand, and more elaborate publications appeared, with portraits of the leading spirits in the Convention, and were sold in the bookstores at a rate as high as a dollar a piece. Naturally the resolution upon the tariff is one of the important pronouncements of the Liberal Convention. It is not a long pronouncement and it will not hurt if I place it on Hansard in connection with my remarks. It is called simply "Resolution on the Tariff" and reads as follows:
That the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing: of two purposes of the highest importance: First: diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second: reducing the cost of the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress and prosperity of our country.
That, to these ends, wheat, wheat flour, and all products of wheat; the principal articles of food; farm implements and machinery; farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery and repair parts thereof; rough and partly dressed lumber; gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils ; nets, net-twines, and fishermen's equipments: cement and fertilizers should be free from customs duties, as well as the raw material entering into the same.
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to fifty per cent of the general tariff.
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
Some hon. GENTLEMEN: Hear, hear. Mr. GUTHRIE: V,Tell, Mr. Speaker, the applause from the Opposition was. not

very general. I noticed that in some quarters there was no applause at all; and that is my chief objection to the manner in which this tariff plank of the Liberal policy is being dealt with by the official Opposition throughout the length and breadth of Canada to-day. It only seems to apply in spots either in the country or in this House. But it will be noticed that there are four pronouncements involved in their tariff plank: the first is a general demand for substantial reductions in the customs tariff; the second is a fairly long free list; the third is another demand for substantial reductions in wearing apparel and footwear and articles of general consumption; and the fourth pronouncement is in favour of an increase in the British preference to fifty per cent.
Now, the question which, I think, is most interesting to the members of this House and to the people of this country is simply this: Do the official Opposition intend to stand upon that platform, or is it one of those platforms which are sometimes made for the purpose of subterfuge of camouflage or the like? I remember well in the old days, twenty or twenty-one years ago a favourite story which my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was fond of telling the House. It related to a coloured porter who wanted to put the passengers off the platform at the end of his sleeping car. He told them that they must not stand there. "Why not?" they demanded. "Oh," he replied, "a platform is not to stand on; a platform is to get in on." And if my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's were in the House now, I would remind him that the tariff plank of the Liberal party formulated in 1919 is entirely different from any tariff policy carried out by the Liberal party during the fifteen years they were in power. From 1900 to 1917 I was a member of that party, and for eleven years I was a supporter of the Government then in power, and I think that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's will agree with me when I say that there was no free trade talk in the Liberal party in those days-there was no such tariff plank in the policy of the Liberal party as I have read to the House to-night. The tariff policy of the Liberal party in those days was a continuance of the old fiscal policy which came into force in 1878. And what I maintain now is, that forty-two years ago Canada adopted a fiscal policy which has continued in force until the present time.
I am quite well aware that prior to 1896 it was not an uncommon thing for leaders of the Liberal party to pronounce in favour of free trade. I often heard declarations from Liberal leaders in those days to the effect that the Liberal party was in favour of free trade as they have it in England;
I heard declarations by Liberal leaders that they would not be content until protection had disappeared "root and branch" from our fiscal system. I heard those declarations prior to 1896, but I think the House will agree with me that when the change took place and the Liberal party came into power no one in any quarter of the country ever heard such declarations from Liberal leaders. The Liberal Government adopted the settled fiscal policy of the country with slight alteration and they maintained it in force during their whole term of office. I call to the attention of my hon. friend from Red Deer that when he entered the House of Commons in 1908 his complaint in Parliament and out of Parliament was that he was the only free trader in the House. And it was so. He was the only one who had the courage to state a case in favour of free trade. He used to .take us by the buttonhole and lead us into the corridors to instruct us in the intricacies of the doctrine of free trade. He did not find very many apt pupils, I agree, but still he was then, as he now is, an arden free trader. But his complaint in those days was that the Government was a protectionist government, not a free trade government.
The principle of protection was maintained during the whole regime of the Liberal party from 1896 to 1911, and only at this late date, during the summer of 1919, do we have a pronouncement from that party which, if not an out-and-out free trade pronouncement, is a pronouncement which involves such a mutilation of our fiscal system as to render it absolutely innocuous and worthless if put into force, but at the same time is a pronouncement behind which, I believe, the official Opposition does not stand as a body to-day. Had my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition during the recent by-election in Peterborough read to the electors of that riding the tariff pronouncement, as I have read it to-night, had my hop. friend from Shelburne and Queen's done the same thing, and had the present hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon) said to the electors, "I stand upon the Liberal tariff policy of 1919," I think I can safely predict that the hon. gentleman would not

now be the representative of that constituency.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was not the issue.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Do you wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the people have some curiosity to know just where the parties and members of this House stand in regard to this fiscal question? I hope that within a measurable time matters will be so adjusted in this House that we will have the acid test applied and that each hon. member will be asked to declare, by his vote, just where he stands in regard to the fiscal policy of this Dominion. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition says that the tariff was not the issue in West Peterborough. I agree that he has done everything in his power to avoid that issue both in the by-elections and in this House. I agree that in the amendment which he has moved to the Address he has up to the present moment	rather	successfully
avoided that issue. It is apparent that he has framed his amendment for the express purpose of avoiding the issue, simply because he knows that he cannot command the united support of his own party behind him upon the tariff issue.
And now just a word in regard to the first amendment.	You will note, Mr. Speaker, that in his somewhat animated address in moving his amendment my hon. friend made no charge against the Government of malfeasance, of misfeasance or of non-feasance. He did not suggest that anything in the legislative record of the Government in the past was in any respect improper or lacking, nor did he offer the slightest suggestion to the House that the published platform of the present Administration which was issued last summer contained anything which did not meet his approval. In a word, he made no charge whatever against the Government from a legislative or an administrative point of view.
He contented himself solely with a highly excited and exaggerated denunciation of the Government as usurpers, as buccaneers,
I think also; as a Government that would prostitute parliamentary authority, as autocrats, and I do not know what else. But his great difficulty was to find substance, to find a foundation, upon which to rest such a charge, and the more he delved into history for precedent, the more he found himself refuted in the position which he himself took. What strikes the candid observer, what strikes the diligent listener
TMr. Guthrie.]
to this debate, is that every single precedent that has been brought forward has proved to be a precedent which establishes the constitutional position of the Government and refutes the statement of the amendment that the Government has nc authority to continue in office.
My hon. friend dipped deeply into British parliamentary history, from, I think, the year 1865. He occupied the time of the House in telling us just how long each Parliament had lasted in Great Britain. He reviewed the Triennial Act, the Septennial Act and the Quinquennial Act, and he did the same thing in connection with the history of this country from Confederation down to the present time-for what purpose I know not, because he established nothing as a result of it. Had he desired to examine the parliamentary history and the parliamentary records of Great Britain and of Canada he would have found those records full of instances which fit the present case. I ask him to examine any period in the last forty or fifty years in the parliamentary history of Great Britain or of Canada; if he does, he will find absolute justification of the position which the Government has taken at this time and the strongest refutation of the position which he himself has assumed.
My. hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power), also indulged in some parliamentary history and cited one or two instances, which, he thought, afforded something like constitutional precedent. I propose as we pass along to mention these two precedents, because I think that they most clearly establish the Government's right to continue in office to the close of the parliamentary term and completely refute the charge made in the amendment offered by the leader of the Opposition.
We have in the first place the precedents of Great Britain. The one best known is that of 1892 to 1894. It is well known that the Liberal party under the late Mr. Gladstone carried the elections of 1892 in Great Britain. They were established in power but the majority was not satisfactory. The combined vote of the Irish Nationalists and the Conservatives might upset them at any time. In 1894 Mr. Gladstone, becoming a very old man and being in ill-health, determined to retire. He tendered his resignation to Her Majesty the Queen, and she sent for Lord Rosebery, who formed a new government. The Gladstone Government had then been in office only two years but there were loud cries from the Conservatives of England for a dissolution. The

charge was made by Mr. Balfour that there was no mandate; that the new Government should dissolve and appeal to the people. But all Liberal authority at that time supported Lord Rosebery, among them Lord Morley, Sir William Vernon Harcourt and others, and Lord Rosebery determined to carry on and refused to dissolve the House. In taking this course he maintained that he was following constitutional precedent, and I submit that he was. But his predicament was a very odd one. He met Parliament; he brought down the speech from the Throne, and on the first day of the sitting he was met by a motion from Mr. Henry Labouchere to amend the address and the motion carried in the House of Commons by a majority of two against the Government. I read from volume 2 of Herbert Paul, page 260:
Although the majority for this irregular proposal was only two, it put the Government in a most humiliating plight, and they were compelled, with the contemptuous assistance of the Conservatives, to negative their own Address as the only feasible plan for getting rid of the amendment.
But even in this serious situation Lord Rosebery did not think of resignation; he persevered, as was his constitutional right. During that session Sir William Harcourt was only able to carry his budget by a majority of twelve. A month or two later Mr. Speaker Peel resigned, and the Government only succeeded in carrying the Speakership and elected Mr. Gully by a majority of eleven. However, in the summer of 1895, the Opposition were strong enough to carry a vote for reduction of a vote in a Finance Bill-it was carried by a majority of seven, and only then was it that the Rosebery Administration resigned. Were they right or were they wrong? They were elected in 1892. The Gladstone Government ceased ' to exist in 1894 for the same reason that the Borden Ministry ceased in this country in 1920. A new Government came into existence in England under Lord Rosebery. The demand was made in England by the Conservatives of those days for a dissolution. The Liberals said: No, and continued until they were defeated in the House and had to dissolve.
That Government was not a war Government.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Well, we will come to a war government, later on because there was one in 1890. In 1895 the Salisbury administration took power. They dissolved the House, carried the election and continued in office until 1900 when the "kharki election" took place in England.
An old Tory trick.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
It was charged, of
course, by the Liberals that the Conservative party in bringing on an election had taken advantage of the Boer War. Peace was not concluded, I think, for a year and a half afterwards, and it was alleged by Liberals that the Conservatives had taken a most unfair advantage and had held a war election. The Conservative party were returned to power on that occasion by a very substantial majority. Lord Salisbury was Prime Minister. In July, 1902, ill health and old age being given as the reasons, he retired, and Mr. Balfour was called upon to form a new administration. Then the boot was on the other foot. There are quotations from the speech of Mr. Asquith, Lord Morley and Sir William Harcourt on record in which it was urged that as a new administration had been formed which had no mandate from the people that the government should dissolve parliament. The charge was made by Mr. Asquith that this was a war government; that the party which had attained power had taken advantage of war time to secure an election for themselves which in normal times they could not have secured. But in spite of such criticism the government determined what its constitutional right was. It did not heed the taunts or the criticism of Mr. Asquith and the Liberal party but continued in office until January, 1896. Then dissolution took place and the Liberal administration went into power.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Well, I am going to give you a Liberal precedent now. The Liberal administration went into power under Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman. Unfortunately, the duties of office weighed upon him, and after a period of only two years, his health became so poor that he was obliged to resign, and on the advice of his physician, on the 6th of April, 1906, he proceeded to the Continent where his Majesty then was, and tendered his resignation. His resignation was accepted and Mr. Asquith was sent for. He went to Europe and was there asked to form a new ministry. He returned to London on the 10th of April and announced that he would do so. Once more the clamour was made against the new administration, this time by the Conservatives-it looks to me Mr. Speaker, as it depended a great deal in Great Britain, and perhaps, in Canada as well, on the question of " whose ox is gored." The charge was that as Mr. Asquith had no

mandate that he should dissolve parliament, but Mr. Asquith continued to carry on, and did carry on, until the expiration of the parliamentary term. Now, these are all the precedents I have been able to find in Eritish history throughout the last twenty-five years, back to 1892 and I challenge my hon. friends opposite to find a solitary instance in which a contrary proceeding was adopted in Great Britain.
I am quite willing to accept the challenge and I will quote proceedings to-morrow.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Now, I am going to turn to the Dominion of Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Of course, Canadian precedents, unfortunately neet with laughter on the other side of the House.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Unfortunately, they are all against my hon. friends opposite. I will go back to 1891-I started with 1892 in Great Britain and I think I covered the whole ground. Again I will issue the challenge: in every single instance in this country from 1891 down to the present time the precedents which exist establish the right of the government and refute the contentions of the Opposition.
In 1891, on the death of Sir John Macdonald, a new administration had to be formed. The House knows as well as I do that when a prime minister dies or resigns his administration comes to an end. The ministers do not need to resign; the resignation of the prime minister operates as the resignation of the whole government, and a new administration comes into being. Then came Sir John Abbot. He did not dissolve the House; he went right on. Unfortunately his health failed, and his Government came to an end by reason of resignation-a case on all fours with the present instance. Then Sir John Thompson was called on to form and did form an administration. He did not dissolve the House; he carried on. Unfortunately, in the course of a short time, he died and Sir Mackenzie Bowell was called upon to form a government. Sir Mackenzie Bowell did not dissolve Parliament; he formed a new government and carried on.
I do not think that in the Dominion Parliament from 1891 until last July there was a single instance where the precedent established both in Great Britain and Can-

ada was not precisely followed in the case of every new administration; Time after time in the various provinces of Canada the same situation has arisen. In 1896, in three provinces, three distinct administrations came to an end by reason of the fact that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who had attained power, called to his Councils three provincial premiers. In Ontario the government of Sir Oliver Mowat was in power. He resigned:	his government came to an
end; he came to Ottawa, and a new government was formed. This is pure Liberal doctrine. Mr. Hardy formed a new administration, but he did not dissolve the legislature. Subsequently Mr. Hardy resigned, and the late Sir George Ross came in and formed a new government, but he if I remember correctly did not dissolve the legislature. In Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was prime minister. He was called to Ottawa in 1896, while still premier of that province. He was succeeded in Nova Scotia by a new premier, Mr. Murray, who formed a new government; but there was no dissolution, no mandate from the people; the government simply carried on in accordance with constitutional practice. So in New Brunswick where Mr. Blair was prime minister, Mr. Blair came to Ottawa, a new premier came in; a new government was formed in New Brunswick but there was no dissolution. So, also, as recently as 1917, the same thing happened out in the western provinces when Mr. Sifton came to Ottawa, and, so also when through the resignation of Mr. Scott in Saskatchewan, when Mr. Martin took office, I do not think there was a dissolution, but I am not sure of that. More recently than all, within the last few months, in the province of Quebec, a Liberal premier resigned, a new government was formed in Quebec, but there was no dissolution, simply a carrying on to the end of the parliamentary term. What I maintain is this: We have a plain direction in the law of this country, section 50 of the British North America Act, which was quoted to this House by the leader of the Opposition, and which says that Parliament shall extend for a term of five years. We in this Government have followed both the letter and the spirit of that law, and our action has been in entire accord with the best parliamentary procedure. I do not know just what body of the people is clamouring for an election at this time.
Everybody.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I know the leader of
the Opposition imagines that there is in this country some tremendous demand that; he should be the rescuer of Canada during the present crisis; but I have been travelling throughout Canada lately, and I have not noticed any loud or prolonged or widespread cry for assistance, guidance or direction from the hands of my hon. friend. It is said by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) that he does not agree with the constitutional doctrine propounded of the leader of the Opposition in his amendment but he thinks that on account of the by-elections, this Government should resign. In all fairness, I am going to put the case to the hon. member for Marquette. This Government came into being last July, since which date there have been five appeals to the "people in four provinces of Canada. In three of those appeals in three separate provinces, the people have in the most decided tone commended the Government and sent us a supporter. In two instances in Ontario, the Government has not been sustained, in one constituency a supporter being sent to the leader of the Agrarian movement and in one constituency a supporter being sent to the official leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: -and this Government is prepared to stand on its record before the people and to be judged by the people on that record. Sometimes I think the official leader of the Opposition assumes unto himself, in respect of his position, a good deal of authority which he does not actually possess amongst the electors of the Dominion of Canada.
That is to be proved.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Exception was taken on Friday last by the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair), to a statement made on this side of the House to the effect that the official leader of the Opposition represented merely a remnant of the Liberal party. I do not see why my hon. friend should take such grave exception to a statement of this kind. I can tell my hon. friend exactly what he knows to be the fact, namely, that in eight provinces out of the nine in this country, he represents only a remnant of the old Liberal party. My hon. friend has only to cast his eye about this Chamber to satisfy himself upon this point.
In two of those provinces my hon. friend does not represent a single elector if one may judge by his following in this House. So when my hon. friend talks of the great Liberal convention and the great Liberal party in the Dominion of Canada let me tell him-and I am only telling him what he knows already-that the old historic Liberal party in this country, save in one single province, has ceased to exist. Let me point out to him the figures. In the Maritime Provinces there are 31 representatives sitting in this Parliament, and my hon. friend can muster only 11; and one on the cross-benches will give him 12.
Just try an election.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I thought a few real facts would waken some of them up. Let me tell my hon. friends opposite that in the great province of Ontario there are just as many old line Liberals supporting my right hon. friend and his Government in this House as are supporting the leader of the official Opposition.
No.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Somebody dissents
from that. It will not take very long to count them. I was fond of making the statement before the West Peterborough election that the Government had one more than the Opposition, but now I think we stand just ten-ten; that is, the Government has just as many of the old Liberal party from Ontario supporting it as has my hon. friend opposite. Then let me tell my hon. friend that from lake Superior to the Pacific ocean he as only two supporters of the old Liberal party, in a total of about fifty-seven constituencies.
All my friends around me must well remember the days when we looked to British Columbia and the Yukon, with 14 seats, as a great Liberal stronghold. But glance at it to-day in this House. How many followers does my hon. friend muster behind him of old line Liberals from British Columbia and the Yukon? Does he lead a remnant? No, not even a remnant, not a single supporter. From the old Liberal province of Alberta, one single member supports my hon. friend. From the old Liberal province of Saskatchewan with 16 seats in this House, there is not a single representative of the old Liberal party sitting behind my hon. friend. Take Manitoba. One single representative from that great province. Am I not right then, Mr. Speaker, when I say that my hon. friend the leader of the official Opposition, when he assumes in this House or in this country to speak for the old Liberal party of this Dominion, is assuming a good deal more than he is entitled to? He has only to look across the House. He has only to recognize the members of the old Liberal guard, sitting on this side of the House.
It is hard to recognize them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No longer Liberals, I admit-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
-because when the
testing time came we found that the line of cleavage was so deep, so well defined-
So many loaves and fishes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
-we found the issue which had to be determined was perhaps the greatest issue which any of us would have to determine in our public lives, and when we took the decisive step, we took it deliberately, knowing what it involved.

And now we are proud to be members supporting the present Administration, supporting a party which we ourselves helped to form in the first instance, on a platform which we ourselves helped to prepare, and in support of a Prime Minister who was the man of our own selection. That is the real situation which exists in this House to-day. There is no use trying to camouflage the facts. Those are the plain facts as they exist to-day. While it is charged in various quarters that the former supporters of this Administration are flocking back to my hon. friend's support, I can discover only two of them. I see a great many who have crossed the floor and joined the Agrarian party, but I have seen only two in all who have become out-and-out members of the official Opposition. I do not even like to call them the old Liberal party because, as I said before, they represent merely a small remnant of that old party.
Now just a word as to the sub-amendment. To my mind it raises a question of considerable difficulty and importance in the House. I do not know but what under certain circumstances the sub-amendment might have been considered well-timed and appropriate, but I think there would be great difficulty in the way of any government accepting such an amendment under present circumstances. I see great difficulties in the way of the Government accepting a sub-amendment to the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne, which itself is a pronouncement of Government policy put into the hands of His Excellency the Governor General, to be presented to the House. I can, however, see force and reason in the sub-amendment, while I do not see either force, reason or propriety in the amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the official Opposition.
There are a number of important considerations which must be dealt with. There is one practical consideration which is quite outstanding. It is a stock-in-trade charge of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that this Government is non-representative, is mis-representative is unrepresentative, and so forth, but let me tell him that if Parliament were dissolved and an appeal made to the people of this country with the constituencies arranged as they are to-day, we would have a Government just as mis-representative, just as unrepresentative, of the people of Canada as one could well imagine. You would have absolute non-representation in 25 or 30

seats in the West, but that is not the difficulty with which I am for the moment concerned. I heard a fiery denouncement in this House by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) a few nights ago. He thought some monstrous iniquity would be perpetrated upon the people of this country if the census were taken in June, and a redistribution of seats were to take place soon thereafter. Why, it is the natural and proper thing according to our law. The situation in Canada to-day, particularly in regard to the industrial centres, demands that there shall be no delay in regard to a redistribution of seats. The thing has become so anomalous as to be almost a public scandal. Think of it-and surely these facts will appeal to hon. members of the House-or in the city of Toronto, a riding like Parkdale sends one member to the House of Commons-
One too many.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: -while the adjoining rural constituencies of Peel, Halton, Duf-ferin, South Perth and East Elgin, all put together, have not the population of Park-dale, yet they send five members to the House. I am told the situation is just as scandalous in the province of Quebec. I heard in the city of Montreal a few days ago that ten rural ridings in the province of Quebec, returning ten members to this House, did not have the population of two certain ridings in the city of Montreal.
Was one of them Brome?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Yes, Brome was one of them. Now, Mr. Speaker, is not that a situation that demands a speedy remedy? Why should it take three, four or even five industrial workers in the city of Toronto to cast a vote equal only to a single vote cast in the townships adjoining the city? I have heard it said at a public meeting in the city of Toronto that the inequality is so great in Ontario that during the provincial elections of 1919 in Ontario the Conservative candidates in the city of Toronto polled more votes than the combined vote of the party now in power in Ontario under Mr. Drury.
Is it not a most glaringly unfair situation? Whatever government is in power in this country, such an unequal situation calls for a speedy remedy. You cannot impose such a disqualification, such an inequality, upon industrial workers resident in the city nor should it be allowed to continue. All men and all women are supposed to be free and equal
under our law, and the theory of our constitution is that they shall have equal treatment and opportunity. We pride ourselves upon our democracy; yet we suffer to be continued in this country a system which allows four or five members to represent a rural district with a population only equal to one constituency in the city of Toronto. I do not say that any particular political party is to blame for this situation, which has simply been allowed to grow up in this country.
I have read debates in this House in the early days, long years before I became a member, when this question was under discussion. An argument was advanced that the city of Toronto should not have equal representation with the rural districts, because, as a rule, there were three or four members for other constituencies living within the city boundaries. I read another argument on the question, in which it was contended that it would be unfair to the candidate to impose upon him a large territory and a large population in the country because he would not have time to get around during elections. These are surely considerations of a most minor character. The theory of our law is equality, and the sooner we come to equality of voting and representation in this country the better.
There is opportunity to remedy this situation in the near future. I would not hesitate to say that cities like Montreal and Toronto and other cities in Quebec and Ontario, as well as the great cities in the West, are entitled to greater and more equal representation than they now have and must get it at an early date. The time is not far distant when they can be given it. Under our law the census will be taken in June. If dissolution took place now and an appeal were made to the country, the residents of these industrial centres would to a large extent be disqualified at the next election; they would not be entitled to proper representation. The greatest inequality would exist. That, Mr. Speaker, is to my mind one most substantial reason why the Government should continue to carry on, and why we should take the census.
On the contrary, there is only one possible reason which can suggest itself to any one why we should not carry on, and that reason will be definitely evidenced when the vote on the question now before the House is recorded. That question is

simply this: Have we or have we not, the confidence of the House of Commons? That is the test, and the question will be settled when this vote is taken. The duty of this Government, if it is decided that it has the confidence of the Commons, is to go ahead and do its work, take the census and bring down to the House a fair redistribution Bill applicable to every part of the country.

Sir, that I have conclusively established that the majority in this House does not represent the majority of the people. But to corroborate my statement, let me call the unquestioned testimony of the most ardent supporters of the Union Government. I refer you, Sir, to the statements of the Hon. Mr. Carvell, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) and the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie), made here when they opposed the War Times' Election Act as an iniquitous measure. Forsooth, this Act was so vicious in principle that it had to be removed from our Statutes which it disgraced. It broke faith with citizens established in this country for more than ten years. It gave the franchise to foreigners who had never had any interest in our land. It unsettled our whole electoral economy and subverted the very foundation of our citizenship which we had afterwards to re-establish. This Government is not supported by the representatives of the majority of the people. Said the Prime Minister:
In point of character, of aim and of purposes',, we are the same Government. In addition to the prosecution of the war we had thirteen other specific duties.
Let us consider these two statements together. On both of them the right hon. gentleman is contradicted by his ex-leader, by his colleagues, and by his own speeches. At Milton on November 29th, 1917, the right hon. member for King's, N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), said:
There is only one issue in this campaign, whether we shall keep our pledge or bond given to those men, or whether we shall abandon them when they need our help most.
This declaration the right hon. gentleman repeated a hundred times in different parts of the country. And his (Mr. Meighen's) colleagues-what did they understand? Let us listen to the hon member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar):
That is not to say that I do not feel strongly on the tariff, but I feel the present issue is not the tariff but the winning of the war.
Listen to the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) :
When the Government was formed in 1917 there was a tacit understanding that until the war was over, our soldiers home, and demobilization completed, we should carry on, and that is the view I take now.
And, again, the same gentleman said:
The present Government, as originally constituted was not created for the purpose of making a general revision of the tariff. This Government was for a war purpose and to carry out a war policy.
	,
And he continued:
The members comprising the Government held strongly divergent views on the tariff question. We recognized at that time that those differences existed, and we decided to lay aside our differences for the time being.
What is true of members of the Government is equally true of members of the House on both sides: the members of this House were not elected because of their tariff leanings. Hear now, Sir, the right hon. Prime Minister himself:
There was never a clearer issue before the people than to-day. It is simply an issue of Union Government and the vigorous prosecution of the war, or Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Canada's virtual withdrawal from the war.
It is simply an issue of Union Government and vigorous prosecution of the war. Can he now verily state, as he does, that in point of character, of aim and of purpose his Government stands where it stood in 1917? Can he contend that, in addition to the prosecution of the war, thirteen points had been put before the people? The right hon. gentleman would lead one to believe that he is a distant rival of the father of the fourteen points; but he is surely not a lover of the truth.
On the question of the tariff, to which I now come, the right hon. gentleman is armed with a double-barreled gun, one barrel loaded against the Liberal Opposition, the other against the Progressive party. Against the Liberals he shoots the idea that we are not serious in our endeavours to reduce the tariff; that we are high protectionists, as he is himself; that we avoid the issue; and he suggests to the Farmers that they had better support him because they know where he stands. Against the Farmers he fires the opinion that they are radicals allied to the worst and most subversive elements-men preaching dangerous doctrines. The inuendo is an invitation to Quebec to form an alliance with him. These rhetorical methods are typical of the right hon. gentleman. They have been described in the press as follows:
The tactical methods upon which Mr. Meiglien relies to achieve his ends upon the public platform were fully illustrated in the public addresses which he delivered during his recent western trip. It is Mr. Meighen's method to state at the outset of his speech the case as between himself and his opponents. He states it with care and deliberation and with a great appearance of fairness. After doing this he proceeds to the destruction of the Opposition by direct and vigorously delivered assault. Unreflecting observers are likelv to attribute the resulting victory to the strength of Mr. Meighen's case; but more sophisticated unlookers are apt to remark that it is chiefly due to the weakness of the Opposition's case as set

forth by Mr. Meighen. The Opposition's case in reality some times differs somewhat from its case as set forth by Mr. Meighen in preparation for his tilt at it; and there are times when Mr. Meighen's platform triumphs are victories, not over real opponents but over "men of straw,"
Speaking in this House, the Prime Minister did not renew his attack on those radical communists who, he suggested, formed part of, or at least are allied with, the Farmers' party. Was his ammunition expended? Let not our Farmer friends believe it. For the time being both barrels of his firearm were busy discharging the ammunition compounded of his subtle sophistries against those "miserable Grits" who in their platform had dared to touch the , most holy arch of tariff protection, and against their leader, who, in the judgment of the right hon. member, was intensely anxious to see that no clear issue got before the electors at all. Standing in front of the temple, ad instar the Pharisee of old, the Prime Minister says:	"Oh farmer, praise the Lord with
me that I am not like my contemptible opponent, non-committal and deceitful. In the speech from the Throne I have written a paragraph that defines clearly and definitely where the Government stands; a paragraph that states the principle in words that no man can fail to comprehend." Let us see whether my right hon. friend can get out of this more justified than his exemplar.
The paragraph to which he refers is as follows:
It is the opinion of my advisers that in such revision regard must be had to the necessities of revenue and as well that the principle of protection to Canadian labour and legitimate Canadian industries, including agriculture, which has prevailed for more than forty years in this country, must be consistently maintained.
Will my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) lend me an expression for the purpose of defining correctly this plank of the Government's platform? Yes, Sir, I find it in his recent speech in the House. It was not intended to apply to this paragraph of the speech from the Throne, but it fits in very nicely as a description of it

"A new policy, wonderfully vague in its definitions." I say "a new policy" advisedly, because the protection of industries, including agriculture, as suggested by the speech from the Throne, is a radical departure from the well-known policy of the Tory party, which has always been the protection of industries at the expense of agriculture. But is it not
also gloriously indefinite? Because I never heard of any details being given out by the Government to show how they reconcile high tariff with the interests of the agriculturalists. On the contrary, notwithstanding this paragraph in the speech from the Throne, the right hon. gentleman tells us, as reported in Hansard, page 40:
We are not proposing any departure from the historic policy of this country pursued under this Government, under the late Government, under the Government of which the leader of the Opposition was himself a member.
"We are not proposing any departure," he says, but in the same breath he says also:
In the speech from the Throne there Is a paragraph that defines clearly and definitely where the Government stands, a paragraph that states the principle in words that no man can fail to comprehend.
"My advisers are convinced of the necessity for the revision of the customs tariff," says the speech from the Throne. "We are not proposing any departure; if we were we would ijot have the support of the Minister of Immigration," says the right hon. gentleman, and he concludes with a frantic appeal to the member for Red Deer to support this party whose position he knows to be consistently maintained. Let us dig a little deeper, Sir, perhaps we shall find in the Prime Minister's declaration some particle of truth. Speaking of my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration, he says:
The one man who has been consistent on this tariff issue. He is standing where he stood when the Liberal party were in power on the tariff issue.
Speaking at Winnipeg on the 13th of November, 1920, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Calder) said:
Three years ago I did not understand the tariff question as well as I do at the present time. I was more or less a parrot, just as other people are parrots. I got up in the Legislature and advocated free fertilizers when I did not know the first thing about it.
Listen again to the Prime Minister's later declaration:
The Minister of Immigration ... is standing where he stood when the Liberal party were in power on the tariff issue.
Oh, truth, beautiful truth, the right hon. gentleman is no lover of thee! It is part of the political tactics of our friends opposite on the question of the tariff to throw into the eyes of the electorate the dust of two sophisms. To the big interests they say: Beware of the farmers and of their radical ally; if they attain to power they



will subvert the whole economic structure. To the farmers they say: Do not trust the Liberals; they are protectionists in fact if not in principle. Neither of these statements is true, Sir. All over the world the stabler element in each country is the farming element. The farmer owns the land, he tills the soil, he has taken root. He is not transient in character, and he is not radical in principle. Is he a communist? Why should he be ready to share a hardly gained heritage with any prodigal spendthrift? Here let me borrow an expression from the Prime Minister himself:	The absurdity of
the argument is simply pathetic. In respect to the Liberals, could there be a more impudent statement than that the present Government stands where the Liberal party stood when it was in power? Did we not lose power on the question of reciprocity, so savagely fought by our opponents with their delusive bogey, "no truck or trade with the Yankees." The Liberal party can stand on its record. In 1893 they passed resolutions advocating tariff reduction and reciprocity. During their fifteen years on the Treasury Benches they removed the tariff on many articles; they reduced it at least twenty-five per cent, and afterwards to the extent of thirty-three per cent by the British preference, and they fell on the battlefield of freer trade espousing the cause of reciprocity.
In 1919, they reaffirmed their faith in the policy of freer trade and reciprocity, and that policy they will, if returned to power, carry out in the full measure that circumstances will permit. That they have not all at once embodied in the laws their advocated principles is not to be wondered at, it is to their credit and it is certain they will not fall into radicalism in the future. They are the doctors; the country is their patient, and a patient very sick after forty years of protection. It would be criminal to administer to him too suddenly a full ration of the healthier food of freer trade, hut under their good care the patient will recover, and will gradually come to it. The farmer of today is like a man starting upon a journey and in search of a companion. Two offer themselves, both fully armed with the same weapons. One is armed to hold him up, en route, for his purse or his life. This is the protectionist, using the tariff for the enrichment of the few at the expense of the many. The other is armed to defend the farmer in case of need. This is the Liberal aiming to protect

legitimate industry and to prevent dumping, but caring not for the sap-sucker, mushroom industry. His choice between the two is not doubtful. Let us hear his leader:
I would describe our position thus,
Says the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in his Winnipeg speech:
Our eyes are set on the goal of the elimination of protection as a principle in our fiscal policy. We propose to get to that goal by stages that will make it as easy as possible for our industries to readjust themselves to it. During this period revenues will, of course, come from the tariff, and there is no reason why customs duties cannot continue as in Great Britain to afford a very considerable portion of our revenue, and if need be the principle of a countervailing excise tax can be applied, in this way compelling the home manufacturer who enjoys the protection to contribute his share to the national treasury. Furthermore, there is no reason why a form of assistance cannot be given to industry without the pernicious privileges that obtain under the operation of a protective tariff. Energy to turn the wheels of our factories is one of the main essentials in the development of industry. We have that power in Canada in abundance in the unharnessed energy of our magnificent rivers. It is quite a proper function for governments to develop this, as indeed it has been developed in Winnipeg, and place it at the disposal of the manufacturer at cost.
The Liberals can stand on their record, and our farmer friends know where we stand. The Minister (Mr. Guthrie) accuses the farmers of not encouraging Canadian industries, and in the full swing of his oration, he did not allow proper explanations to come forth. I thought at the moment it was not very generous and not befitting the greatness of a minister of the Crown, but it is only human on the part of the hon. gentleman, not to allow the desired effect of his address to be spoiled. I am not the guardian of my farmer friends; they are quite capable of looking out for themselves; but it did not suit the purpose of the minister to be told that if the farmers could purchase cheaper in Canada, they would be good enough business men to find their requirements in their own country. It also did not suit the minister to be told that if the farmers did not purchase in Canada, the reason was because, owing to the co-operative character of the farmers' organisation, the big industries of Canada would not sell to them. It did not suit the minister either to be told that if the Canadian manufacturer does not come up to the mark with his American competitor, the reason is that he lacks the incentive of competition, which is the life of trade

and which gives to the latter this superiority over the Canadian manufacturer, who, fed with the milk of protection, is not in that healthy condition which ensures the survival of the fittest.
As to the difference between England and Canada he would have been told, had he permitted the interjection, that by a striking departure from what was done in England, our capital, energy and manpower were in Canada diverted by protection from our basic industries and the development of our natural resources that await the hand of that sturdy canadianism which stands courageously upon its own feet and regards as contemptible the tutorship of the protective tariff. But I am sorry for the Minister of Immigration and Colonization. I have a liking for the hon. gentleman, and I regret to see that he is absent from his seat to-night. " A Liberal I was, a Liberal I am, and nobddy can make me anything else,"-does he say? Alas, in his duel with the Prime Minister, he was vanquished. Vae victis-to the victor the spoils. Here he stands, hands, feet and soul tied to the chariot of a Tory leader who drags him in his triumphant course to the capitol. " I was a parrot," groans the poor victim. Indeed, it is somewhat unfortunate for the Prime Minister himself. Geese once saved the capitol; parrots never did, and the capitol itself was never nearer to the Tarpeian P.ock than it is to-day. Horrified at the treatment she had received at the hands of the Prime Minister, the Truth fled to London, Paris and Geneva, running after our three diplomat ministers for refuge. Suffocated by the flight, she found them at- the Peace Conference, busying themselves in that nursery of their newly-born child, " Canadian Nationhood." Poor new Susanna, what vain attempts had you not to suffer from these three wicked elders!
For three years, Sir, these hon. gentlemen have assumed the mission of convincing the Canadian people that a complete evolution has taken place in our national status; that we are no longer a colony governed by Downing street, not even a self-governing dominion, but an independent nation in the sub-league of the British commonwealth.
I shall not quote all the interesting statements we have heard in this House on that subject. Let us summarize them in these words of my right hon. friend, the Minister of Justice:
28i
We stand to-day by common acknowledgment of the statements not only of the other dominions, hut of the United Kingdom itself, nations each equal in status with every other.
There is a dazzling light that shines upon this country, and shows her forth to the world as a nation standing on a footing of equality amongst the nations.
Then, using the favourite method of his leader, he proceeded to put up his man of straw. Referring to hon. gentlemen on your left, Mr. Speaker, he said:
They have not seen this developing work of time in which their late leader had so implicit faith. They do not seem to have the aspirations that he had. They want to see their Canada always in her swaddling clothes-clamouring to be kept in the nursery. In the Egyptian darkness of their colonial condition the light appears to be too much for their unaccustomed eyes.
That stale old saw so often used, and more often abused, is completely worn out. It contains two fallacies, and was broken into pieces in 1919, by two graphic words of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). When speaking on the ratification of the treaty of peace, he said:
I reaffirm my admiration for the theories enunciated by the members of this Government. I wish they were right, but I am afraid they are wrong.
Is it not childish, Sir, to try this make-believe on the Canadian people: "Canada stands to-day in the world on a footing of equality amongst the nations?"
Why, what other independent nation, even the most humble, is presided over by a Governor General? What other sends her law cases to the tribunal of British Islanders, in appeals of last resort? What other nation has to pass under the jurisdiction of British diplomats in her official or business relations abroad?
What other nation would allow British newspapers to discuss openly who should be the representative of His Majesty the King in this country, all booming their respective candidates? If we are a nation, Sir, let the right hon. gentleman take a step further and introduce legislation enabling this Parliament to determine who shall preside over our destinies.
Last April, when in Paris, it came to my notice that a high Canadian official was desirous of obtaining an audience from the President of France. Our provincial agent could not arrange it; Canada's High Commissioner could not arrange it. The British Ambassador alone was accredited to the French Government. But a citizen of Monte Carlo could apply to the representative of his own country.

Sir, I wish we were a nation, but we shall not allow the right hon. gentleman to pay us with words. We have lost none of the aspirations of our late beloved leader, but we want the real thing, not its shadow. His statement therefore is doubly untrue.
Mr. Speaker, there is an element of real nationhood which is sadly lacking in this country. It is the binding spirit of national unity. They have it in France. They have it in England. They have it in the United States. When a Frenchman speaks of his France, his sweet France, he has spoken his last word.
