speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I desire to
say a few words before the question is put. I have followed with considerable interest the speeches of both my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Mclsaac), 
and the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Mac-Kelvie), and to both gentlemen I tender my hearty congratulations. I do not quite understand the language of the roaring waves of the Atlantic Ocean, nor am I inspired by the atmosphere of the deep valleys where the apple blossoms seem to delight every citizen of that part of the country. But after having heard such a description from representatives of the extreme East as well as the extreme West, I feel like asking my hon. friends this question, whether, after all, Ottawa, within sound of the Chaudiere falls, is not the proper place for the capital of the Dominion? But the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty), and the ex-President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell), went to Geneva with a message from this Government. What was that message? They went to represent Canada as a nation and not to undertake responsibility for all wars that may take place in the future in Europe or anywhere else. Who, in South America or even North America during the last war, made a sacrifice equal proportionately to Canada's either in life or in money? The duties of our delegates at Geneva were properly discharged when they opposed strongly section 10 of the Treaty. If we are no longer colonials we have to decide for ourselves what attitude this young country shall adopt in future in any European wars. For my part I regard this country as a democracy, and responsibility for the expenditure on our part of money or the contributing of arms and men should, I think, be entirely within the discretion of this nation.
At the great Conference, we have heard, many problems were solved}, and many great questions settled. But to my mind there is one great subject which should have been thoroughly discussed and not have been left over for future consideration. In the name of humanity, in the name of the suffering orphans, in the name of small nations, Canada with great courage responded to the call and sent her bravest sons to do battle during four years of war. Canada has lost over 50,000 of her best men. Noble act on the part of this country! Our soldiers were equal to the soldiers of that "contemptible little army" that kept the Germans in check for so many days in the northern part of France; they were equal to the French soldiers who took charge of 450 miles of front during the war. Our sacrifice shall

remain fruitless if the millions of orphans and thousands upon thousands of widows are not provided for with food and clothing and given ample support and maintenance.
It is true that Austria has received some help; and it is also true that during last winter very many of our people suffered greatly, being in dire need. Let the nations who profited by the war be called upon to help the survivors of these unfortunate sufferers who were driven to take part in the great struggle at the behest of their respective Kings, Emperors or Presidents. What did the nations in South America do during the war? How many of these nations, many of whom have joined the League of Nations, are ready to do something in return to relieve the widows and orphans of those who made the supreme sacrifice for the salvation of the world? What have Norway, Sweden, and Denmark done? I am informed that these countries have requested the privilege of joining the League of Nations. If this is so I would ask our delegates to get into communication with the proper authorities with a view to making these nations, which are to join the League, contribute to some extent to the debts which Canada contracted during the war.
Last session during one of my speeches I alluded to immigration into this country, and I suggested that immigrants from rural districts in foreign countries should he encouraged to come to Canada. Events which have transpired since that time have caused me to change my mind more or less. I am now convinced that for the present our effors at immigration should be directed towards the repatriation of our own people who have crossed the boundary line into the country to the south within the last few years in the hope of making a better living. I invite those former fellow citizens of ours to come back to Canada. They are the ones who at present, and at all times, should be encouraged to once more make their homes in the Dominion, because they understand the Canadian Constitution well and know how best to fulfil their duties as Canadians. I would therefore advise the Government to confine their efforts along the line of immigration to inducing former Canadians to return, and seeing that they are the only immigrants for the present admitted to Canada.
The speech from the Throne contains the statement:
My advisers are convinced of the necessity for revision of the Customs Tariff.
What revision does the Prime Minister expect to make? The Minister of Finance went through the Dominion endeavouring to discover what public sentiment was on the question of the tariff. Well, while everybody was endeavouring to arrive at the best solution, the Prime Minister away down in Eastern Canada was preaching high protection. The right hon. gentleman did not have the courage to even wait until a complete report could be obtained from the Minister of Finance before giving expression to his views. Later on in the session I shall avail myself of the opportunity of stating my opinion on the tariff.
I will merely say now that from what can be gathered from the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite there appears to be only one class of people in Canada who are greately interested in the tariff question, and that is the manufacturers and their representatives in this House. Mr. Speaker,
I am in favour of an early appeal to the' Canadian electors for many reasons which have already been discussed by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me. I believe that the sooner an election takes place the better it will be for the welfare of all classes of the country. I have faith in the Canadian people, I have faith in my party, and I have faith in my leader. I believe that the amendment is a wise one and I shall gladly support it.

Question.

(Last Mountain) : Mr. Speaker before the question is put, I desire to offer a few observations. Preliminary to doing so I wish to extend to the mover and seconder of the Address my hearty congratulations upon the excellent manner in which they acquitted themselves of the task entrusted to them. I also wish to offer my congratulations to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meig-hen) on his attainment to the high office that he now fills. When the right hon. gentleman was promoted to his present office I was asked by many of my constituents what kind of a man the new Prime Minister was. I invariably replied, Sir, that in my opinion he was one of the brainiest men in the House-a man of very keen intellect and a sharp tongue. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the keenness of the Prime Minister's intellect may remain with him for many years, but I could also hope, for his own good and I believe for

the comfort of his opponents, that his tongue might lose some of its sharpness.
I wanted to take part in this debate for more than one reason, but mainly because one.is sometimes misunderstood and one's motives misinterpreted if he casts a silent vote. I have reference to the interpretation that was placed upon my own actions, and that of some other members of the group with which I am associated, in connection with the resolution introduced last session by the Right Hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) pertaining to the re-appointment of the Canada Wheat Board for the purpose of handling our 1920 crop. I had believed, Mr. Speaker, that it was pretty generally understood by hon. members on both sides that those of us on the cross-benches from the province of Saskatchewan were in favour of that resolution and in favour of the Canada Wheat Board being re-appointed to handle the wheat crop of 1920. What was my surprise to learn from a paper published in the province of Saskatchewan, known as the Regina Leader, that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, in speaking to the deputation representing the farmers of that province intimated that he had not understood our position to be as I have outlined. In order not to lay myself open to the accusation of misquoting the minister I will give you his own words as reported in the Regina Leader of October 8th, last. I will not read the whole report as it is a lengthy one. I will simply invite your attention to that part of his remarks which makes reference to those of us who occupy places in the Progressive group. The Minister said:
This year the question of the continuation of control necessary came up for consideration. The matter was thrown into Parliament for discussion, and was debated at length. The Farmers' organizations of the West were represented by Mr. Crerar, Mr. Maharg, Mr. J. F. Reid, Mr. Johnston, Mr. Gould, Dr. Clark and others. The hon. Mr. Calder asked the deputations to read their speeches. So far as he could recall, none of these gentlemen insisted on wheat control, they would take no decided stand. As usual, they were prepared to let the Government take Its own course, and if things did not turn out right they would have an opportunity to attack and criticize, and so on.
So far as he could recall, none of these gentlemen insisted on wheat control, they would take no decided stand. As usual, they were prepared to let the Government take its own course, and if things did not turn out right they would have an opportunity to attack and criticize, and so on.
(Mr. Johnston.]
As I said a few moments ago, I thought when this legislation was before the House, and I still think, it was pretty generally understood that those of us from the province of Saskatchewan occupying these cross benches were in favour of that legislation. It is true that not all of us spoke upon the matter when it was before the House. I admit, Sir, that I am a new member and do not pretend to be thoroughly familiar with parliamentary procedure, but if it is necessary that every hon. member should voice his opinion upon all matters of legislation that come before the House, I have learned something that I did not know before. But what are the facts in connection with this matter? As will be noticed from the quotation I have just read, the hon. gentleman directed the attention of this deputation to the speeches of hon. members of this group, and he named six of us. The other evening when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) was speaking or.e would think that some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House believed they had him cornered, so to speak, in respect to his attitude on the reappointing of the Wheat Board. But I would direct their attention and that of the House to a paragraph of the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia as it may be found on page 4113 of Vol. 5 of last year's Hansard. These are his words:
In conclusion, let me state that I propose to vote for the re-establishment of the Wheat Board this year. I pledge myself only for this year.
It will be noticed that in the interview with the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization which I have quoted, his memory was so faulty that he could not recall any of us on these cross benches having spoken on the subject. I would also refer to the words of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), the leader of this group, to be found on page 4119 of the same volume. He stated:
Everyone who knows anything of the European situation must realize that conditions there are very unstable, and in these circumstances, perhaps, there is justification for the Government assuming the power which they are asking for under this legislation.
That was the resolution which had been introduced by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). And, further, I will quote from the speech delivered by the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg), and in doing so I

apologize to him, as he has not yet spoken in this debate, but I want to get these quotations together. In referring to the action taken by the Farmers' organization in Western Canada, he said:
At their convention they went further; they asked not only enabling legislation,-
I might say that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce when introducing this resolution termed it, I think "enabling legislation." The hon. member for Maple Creek continued:
-but that the Government continue the Wheat Board for another year. The Canadian Council of Agriculture passed a similar resolution, and recently, through their executive, they have again stated that so long as there is governmental control of buying in the European markets, we must have governmental control in Canada in regard to disposing of our wheat.
The hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization-and I am glad to see him in his seat- in speaking to the deputation of farmers in Regina last fall directed their attention to the speeches of the hon. members of this group, and said that they would not take any definite stand. I have just quoted from the speeches of three of the six hon. members that he mentioned at that time to show that they did take a very definite stand. And one would think that if a member of the Government or the Government itself were looking for advice, as the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization said they were in looking to this group, they would have turned to members on their own side of the House. It is easy to perceive that the hon. minister was trying to build up a case against those of us in this group who happen to come from the province of Saskatchewan.
Now I would direct the attention of the House to some of the remarks of hon. members of his own side of the House, and at page 2596, volume 3, of last year's Hansard, will be found a speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), during the course of which he said:
My hon. friends opposite, everyone of them practically, have stood four square for the control of the sale and handling of wheat in this country. They have insisted on the control exercised by the Canada Wheat Board.
To me that seems to be something that the hon. minister could not have taken into consideration. And again I would ask the attention of the House to the words of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) when introducing this legislation. He said:
So that the Bill differs from one which is to come into force immediately-
Speaking to the resolution he had introduced.
It may not go into force at all. I hope it will not be necessary to put it into force.
The point I wish to make is, that the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization in meeting that deputation of farmers in the province of Saskatchewan-and I think it is only a fair interpretation to put upon his remarks at that time-was trying to place some of the blame for the Canada Wheat Board not being reappointed to handle the 1920 crop upon some of us from that province who sit on these cross benches.
I believe the quotations that I have laid before the House will prove that we were in favour of that legislation and had nothing whatever to do with the Wheat Board not being reappointed.
In connection with this wheat control, Mr. Speaker, we have heard it said very often in this House that the farmers of Western Canada are opposed to the Wheat Board. That was in a measure correct, but when the circumstances leading up to control being assumed by the Government of handling our wheat is taken into consideration, I think there was some reason why the farmers of the western provinces were opposed to that control. As is well known, control was first taken for handling the 1917 crop, and I have in my hand a copy of the report of the operations of the Board of Grain Supervisors for Canada. This Board, as is well known, handled the crop of 1917 and 1918, and the balance of the crop of 1916 that was still in the country when they were appointed by Order in Council on the 11th of June, 1917. I wish to read from this report in order to show just how this board was appointed. It says:
The Government created the board because the accumulating effects of the war upon international trading in general, and trading in wheat in particular, made some such step necessary. The financing of the war by the various countries involved had led to a vast extension of credit and currency in those countries, and this tended toward a general increase in price levels. This was accentuated as regards wheat by several powerful contributory causes. The wheat surpluses of Russia, Australia, India and the Argentine were either inaccessible altogether, or difficult to secure by reason of the increasing shortage of tonnage. Not only the Allied peoples in Great Britain, France, Belgium and Italy, but also the neutral countries in Northern Europe, were dependent upon North America for their necessary wheat supplies. And the methods by which the governments of those countries bought their wheat

in North America in 1915 and 1916 added to the difficulty. Their agents bought wheat, for example, at Winnipeg in competition with each other, and with Canadian and American millers, and in some cases the same government had different buyers for Canadian wheat and flour. The primary object of these buyers for the European governments was to secure quantities of milling wheat; the price was a secondary consideration. And as the grain exchanges in North America were still open and unrestricted, these government buyers soon became the dominating operators.
The effect of all this was not only an increase in the price of wheat, with occasional violent fluctuations, but was in a word the disintegration of the grain exchanges both in Canada and in the United States.
This disintegration appeared dramatically in Winnipeg in the spring of 1917. During the previous winter months the agents of the AJlied Governments had bought wheat freely to be delivered in May and July. They bought this wheat mainly, if not altogether, from the operators of country elevators, who as they bought wheat from the farmers from day to day sold it for May and July delivery. Neither the buyers for the Allied Governments nor the elevator operators who sold the wheat were gambling in futures. The buyers were providing to the best of their judgment for the future needs of the countries they represented, and the sellers were securing their loans from the banks by hedging their purchases in the only way known to commercial men of providing against risk. These future contracts called for grades 1, 2 and 3 Northern. It turned out that much of the wheat thus sold or hedged did not measure up to these contract grades. As a rule, and under normal conditions, this presents no great difficulty, because the buyers are willing to accept lower grades on the contracts at fair discounts. This, indeed, is a well-established commercial practice. In the spring of 1917, however, the British representatives intimated that they were unwilling or unable to accept lower grades at discounts, and that they would require the contract grades. This forced the sellers to try to buy the higher grades on the open market, with the result that the prices of these grades went skyrocketing. As prices soared the sellers were called for increasing sums of money, and the limit of their credits was soon reached. In effect the market was cornered and a disaster upon a large scale was impending.
To avert this, the Winnipeg Grain Exchange-
I wish that noted, Mr. Speaker-not the producers of Western Canada at all, but the Winnipeg Grain Exchange.
-investigated the conditions, found them as above, closed the market for futures, and by the aid of the Dominion Government, secured the consent of the British authorities to a settlement along commercial lines. As a result, the British accepted the lower grades of wheat on the contracts at fair discounts, the discounts were speedily fixed and the situation cleared up.
While, however, the situation iwithin the Grain Exchange was cleared up for the time, there remained the possibility that a similar crisis might develop at any time so long as

the British and European governments continued their methods of buying in an open market at Winnipeg, and this possibility alarmed the grain trade. In the meantime, the increasing cost of living was alarming consumers in North America generally, and the United States had established its food control system. The dependence of Great Britain and her Allies and of European neutral countries upon North America for wheat meant that there was no limit to the price to which wheat might go, except ability to pay. Under these circumstances, a delegation from the Winnipeg Grain Exchange waited on the Dominion Government, and asked for government control of the grain markets during the war.
At that time Mr. Balfour was in the United States on his mission, and the vice-chairman of the British Cereal Commission, Mr. Anderson, was one of his party. Mr. Anderson came to Ottawa, bringing with him Messrs. Robson and Stewart of the Wheat Export Company, the agency of the British Royal Commission, and a series of conferences took place between the Canadian Government, the British representatives and the delegates from the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. These conferences resulted in the creation of the Board of Grain Supervisors.
I have read that long report so that it might be known that in the first instance the control of the grain and wheat market in Canada did not come about as a result of the request of, or for the benefit of, the producer, but rather at the direct request of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and those connected with it.
Again, it is claimed that the farmers objected to the Canada Wheat Board which was formed to take over the handling of the grain in 1919. That was true in some quarters; but what were the circumstances leading up to that objection? All will remember that the market was opened early in the grain season of that fall. It remained open for a few days and during that short period wheat advanced very rapidly; then the Government stepped in and appointed the Canada Wheat Board. It was only reasonable that the producers of grain in the Canadian Northwest, seeing these conditions, with the market open and advancing rapidly and the Government stepping in and taking control, should come to the conclusion that the Government did not want the producers to get all that their product would bring them. That was the reason why there was opposition to the Canada Wheat Board. But after the Wheat Board had handled the crop so successfully, the grain producers of Western Canada, who know a good thing when they see it, were perfectly satisfied; accordingly they wanted the Canada Wheat Board appointed last year to handle the 1920 crop. Speaking for myself, I was absolutely in favour of the resolution as introduced last

year by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I take strong exception to the words of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization when he met that deputation in the city of Regina.
The market conditions in the part of Saskatchewan in which I live and in the constituency that I have the honour to represent in this House were very bad during this last fall. I happen to live on the old Canadian Northern branch line running from Regina to Saskatoon and on to Prince Albert. Now, the condition there was simply this: early in the grain season we were not able to get cars. As everybody in Western Canada knows, the market was not open very long when the price started to go down, and before cars were available the price had gone down to such an extent that the farmers did not feel like disposing of their wheat; the consequence was that they held on. Many of them, having taken advances against their wheat in store, were squeezed out on that advance. The peculiar feature of it was that a few days after scores of these men had been squeezed out of their wheat, lots of cars were available. We were told that the cars were needed for the coal trade and that that was why we could not have them for the purpose of moving oitr grain. I happen to know that in many of the towns along that line there were large numbers of orders for coal, but the coal was not being delivered. If these cars were in the coal trade, why were they not delivering the coal? If cars were not available while the wheat was still in the producers' hands, how did it happen that the moment the wheat was out of the producers' hands, and in the hands of the dealers, plenty of cars were available? That was the case and on top of that came the increase in freight rates, and I am not overdrawing the situation when I say that the inability to procure cars and the increase in freight rates have driven many of the farmers of that part of the country into insolvency. There is no doubt about that, and consequently they are not feeling very kindly disposed towards the powers that be. The other day I noticed that the chairman of the Railway Commission is reported to have made this statement in the city of Montreal:
As long as he was chairman of the board, freight and other rates would be fixed so as to enable the railways to pay all operating expenses and allow for a reasonable profit on their investment. Mr. Carvell went a little further. Eastern Canada, he said, took the reasonable view of such matters that he did, but he "had nothing to say about the rest of the country." The people there, he said, "seem to
have sentiments differing from the rest of Canada."
If the railways of this country are going to be able to charge such rates that dividends can be paid whether or not the users of those railways are put out of business, it is high time that the Government took a hand in the matter.
I wish to refer very briefly to the request made by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Henders) for a commission or committee to investigate the grain business of this country. I noticed that some newspapers a day or two ago drew attention to the fact that no members of the Progressive group had backed the hon. member in his request. Mr. Speaker, every member of this group wants an investigation if there is anything to investigate. But, as pointed out by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) this afternoon, we already have a Grain Commission appointed by this Government, and if that Commission is not doing its work, it is the business of the Government to see that it does its work properly. If we are to have this business investigated, let it be a thorough investigation, and let the work of the Grain Commission be investigated as well.
. I am reminded about another board appointed by the late Government to do service for the Canadian people. I refer to the Board of Commerce, which, if I understand the matter correctly, was appointed to enquire into and, if possible, to assist in lowering the high cost of living in Canada, and to run to ground any profiteers. What was the outcome, and what did that board accomplish? A very few weeks or months after its appointment, the chairman resigned; a little later on the vice-chairman also resigned, and after struggling along for a few weeks, the third and last commissioner, Mr. Murdock, resigned, and coupled with his resignation were certain charges. Briefly, the charges were there that when the board, in its endeavours to carry out the work that it was appointed to do, got into the position to do something effective, the protecting hand of one or more members of the Government of the day was outstretched, and the work of the board was set at naught. The leader of the official Opposition, (Mr. Mackenzie King) asked that a commission be appointed to enquire into the Murdock charges; but, so far as I know, nothing has been done in that regard, and the Canadian people will have very little confidence in any commission that

this Government may appoint to investigate the grain business, or any other line of activity in this country, unless they are given to know what was in or behind the Murdock charges in connection with the workings of the Board of Commerce.
In the fall of last year, after the original members of the Board of Commerce had all resigned, and certain members of the Civil Service were appointed in their place, we had the spectacle of the sugar barons of this country, when they found themselves in a position to lose money, coming to Ottawa and appealing to the so-called Board of Commerce, which in turn placed an embargo upon the importation of sugar into Canada. Public opinion ran so high that the Government eventually had to intervene and rescind that order of the Board. The question that the people of Canada are asking themselves to-day, and that they have been asking since that time is this: Is the action, as we have it, of the sugar men of last fall similar to some things that happened and that are contained in the Murdock charges? And the people are waiting for the information.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. *J F. Reid), in speaking the other evening, had something to say about the work of a Mr. Murray who is attempting to muzzle the press of Canada, and I thought it well to add something to what that hon. member had to say at that time. I shall give to the House a full introduction to Mr. Murray, so that there may be no mistake as to his identity. I am taking this from the Morning Leader, published in Saskatchewan, under date of February 19, 1921:
Gilbert Mackintosh Murray, B.A., former editor of "Industrial Canada," for many years secretary of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and who evolved the brilliant scheme of forcing the press of Canada to support Protection and a Protectionist Government through the distribution of advertising patronage, is needless to say, persona grata with Hon. Jas. Calder, Hon. Dr. Reid, and other influential cogs in the governmental machine at Ottawa.
Prior to resigning the secretaryship of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Murray resided for the first six months of 1919 at Ottawa. During this period his services were supposed to be "loaned" to the Government; his salary, however, was paid by the C. M. A., the Government giving him at the same time a per diem living allowance of $10.
It was right following upon this Ottawa sojourn of Murray's with all the inspiration of close contact with ministers of the Crown fresh upon him, that Murray, in the role of chief propagandist for the Meighen-Protection-ists, launched his great scheme for making the press of Canada solidly Protectionist by getting the manufacturers to withhold their advertising from such papers as the Toronto Globe, The Morning Leader, the Saskatoon Phoenix, etc., etc.

At a meeting of manufacturers held in Toronto, which was attended by Murray, he himself laid before them his plans as chief propagandist of the protectionist forces, including his ready-print schemes and other little ideas for spreading Protectionist propaganda and thus, as he says, "educating the voters of Canada." A special committee was appointed to look after certain phases of the propaganda campaign and a fairly substantial initial sum was raised to help the project off to a good start. Among the chief contributors to the initial campaign fund was a well known implement firm and one of the largest textile firms of Eastern Canada.
In fairness to a large number of Canadian manufacturers, it is only right to admit that they, together with at least one prominent official of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, strongly opposed the Murray plan of campaign on the ground that the C. M. A. and the cause of Protection would lose immeasurably more than they would gain should the Canadian people ever get wise to the fact that a cold-blooded plan was in operation to force public opinion to a favourable consideration of Protection by the chloroforming of editorial opinion and tampering with the Canadian press news services.
The whole-hoggers, however, were in control ; Murray received orders to go ahead and accordingly the boycott against the lower tariff newspapers was started and the other branches of the propaganda campaign were put through their initial stages preparatory to the final "big drive" in the great task of "educating the voters of Canada" to say "Hurrah for Protection !"
I have two other clippings here from the same paper with reference to this matter. First, there is an explanatory note in reference to these ready-prints, which reads as follows:
"Ready-prints" or "patent insides" are partly printed newspapers supplied by certain publishing houses to the publishers of weekly newspapers, who complete the work of publication by printing the local news and advertising, etc., before issuing the finished papers to their subscribers.
Then it goes on to say:
G. M. Murray the would-be chloroformer and poisoner of the Canadian press, on December 6, 1920, issued "Confidential" circular "M-251", dealing with "Ready-prints and Patent Insides". Murray starts Circular M.-251 with the following statement:-"The situation as regards ready-print services in Canada has undergone considerable change within the last year."
The statement is absolutely true, inasmuch as during that period Gilbert Macintosh Murray became actively interested in the ready-print business-doubtless, as in the case of his proposal for tampering with the Canadian Press news service, for the purpose of "educating the voters of Canada" by getting certain propaganda published in as many Canadian weekly newspapers as possible.
Largely as the result of the activities of Murray and those identified with him in seeking to "educate the voters of Canada," two new ready-print concerns were started, one for the purpose of supplying ready prints to weekly publishers in the prairie provinces and the other for the purpose of supplying eastern publishers.

That statement is significant, Mr. Speaker, because we have heard a lot in this House about certain gentlemen having one policy for the East and one for the West, while the Government had but one policy. But here we see that Mr. Murray, their chief propagandist, with his ready-made prints, has one output for Western Canada and another for Eastern Canada. The article goes on:
At the outset, the proposition was outlined to Murray's political friends at Ottawa, including members of the present Government, and duly approved as satisfactory, following which the necessary capital was raised by some of Murray's monied business friends, the initial sum of approximately $40,000 being subscribed to start the scheme, among the largest subscribers being a well-known Brantford firm and firms in St. Catharines and Montreal.
A close conecting link between the two Murray ready-print concerns was supplied in the person of W. Nelson Wilkinson, who was placed on the boards of both companies.
Mr. Winkinson was formerly connected with the Toronto World, was subsequently engaged in the Publicity Department of the Government at Ottawa, and has for years been on close friendly terms with Murray.
Starting with a ready-print more or less colourless, it is Murray's intention at the proper time, a few months prior to an election, to endeavour to "educate the voters of Canada."
I want to point out in that connection that we have heard something in this House about a menace. To my mind, this is a real menace. This man Murray has started this ready-print business and he contracts with country newspapers all over the country to supply them with these "patent insides". They enter into that contract, believing they are going to get news as newspapers generally carry it, but a few weeks prior to an election, having tied themselves up with this contract, and not being able to get paper from any other source, they will be forced to publish papers, in all probability, at least so far as Western Canada is concerned, carrying a line of political doctrine to which they are absolutely opposed. The article goes on:
The following "confidential" circular sent out by Murray December 29, 1920, to the Canadian manufacturers to further enlist their support in his nefarious campaign to undermine the freedom of the press shows the extremes that he and his Ottawa friends are prepared to go to in their desperate attempt to maintain the Meighen-Calder Government in power.
This confidential circular is rather lengthy, so I shall read only enough to give the House an idea of the kind of propaganda that Mr. Murray has undertaken.

The ostrich is said to bury its head in the sand at the approach of danger. Don't be an ostrich! Look your danger squarely in the face and prepare as best you know how to meet it.
To-day the free trade storm signals are set as a warning to the navigators upon the sea of business. Make no mistake about it. They are there to be seen, clear as the sun in the sky, by all except those who keep their heads in the sand. The organized farmers, under the leadership of fanatical theorists, have been worked up into a veritable frenzy of resentment against a fiscal policy that they have come to look upon as a special privilege. They are out to effect changes by a process of destruction,-a process that once initiated may go to untold lengths before it can be checked. If those who would thus be destroyed don't speedily organize for their own defence, and marshall all their resources in money and brains to meet the attack, they will almost certainly find themselves powerless to ward off a blow for which the Grain Grower arm is already bared, nerved with the last ounce of strength and determination.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I thought it well to bring this matter to the attention of the House and to place some of it on Hansard so that the people might know to what lengths those in this country who derive benefit from protection will go to retain that benefit. Mr. Murray has very able assistants in hon. members of this Government in decrying the Western Grain Growers and trying to make the people of the eastern provinces believe that many citizens of Canada out there are Bolshevik in our tendencies, have ideas of secession, and are out to wreck the nation, and I do not know what else. I would ask the people of this country, however, to size the matter up for themselves. The few of us here on the cross benches in this Parliament, endeavour to the best of our abilities to represent the views of the organized farmers in Western Canada, and possibly we may not be a fair sample of the Western Grain Growers; but it would not matter if we were displaced by others, for there are many out there who are quite competent to take our places, and I am sure that they are in no sense nation-wreckers.
Regarding the resolution before the House and the amendment thereto, I have given some consideration to this matter, and this thought has occurred to my mind: It has been said that the present Government have usurped power. This may not be correct, if you take into consideration the fact the term of this Parliament has not expired. But the people in the country

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: are anxious to know when an election will be held. In 1917, Sir Robert Borden organized a Union ministry which appealed to the country as the Union Government. We were told that there would be a fifty-fifty split as between Liberals and Conservatives in the Cabinet. Well, that part of the contract was never lived up to. Again, the people of the country voted for Sir Robert Borden as leader of the Union Government in 1917, and I will put this proposition to the House, as the people will put it to each one of us as their representatives: If, in 1917, Sir Robert Borden had said to the electors of Canada, "I am going to carry on for the war period, and should the war terminate before the conclusion of the parliamentary term, when that time comes, I am going to resign and my colleague-now Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen)-will then form another government and carry on during the rest of the parliamentary term,"-I submit that there would have been a much different result to the election. I know this much, that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Hon. Mr. Calder), delivered Saskatchewan to Sir Robert Borden and the Union Government holus-bolus; but if the situation had been placed before the people as I suggest in this supposition, he could not have delivered one seat under those conditions.

I am sorry to have transgressed the rule, Mr. Speaker; it was not my intention to do so. So far as the question asked by the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) is concerned, I cannot see that it has any bearing whatever on my remarks. I said nothing whatever in reference to Sir Robert Borden's illness.

I mean, the hon. member for King's, Nova Scotia. The right hon. gentleman's illness has nothing to do with my argument. The statement was made in this House yesterday by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), that this Government was elected in 1917.
TMr. Johnston.1
Well, now, to my mind that is not so. If I understand events correctly, this Government was not elected in 1917 but was manufactured here in July, 1920. Much stress has been laid on the argument regarding redistribution and full representation for Western Canada. Now, Western Canada wants her full representation in this House; there are no two ways about that.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend opposite say, "hear, hear;" it is gratifying to know that he is sometimes in the right. I say, Western Canada wants her full representation in this House; there is no doubt about that.
Possess your soul in patience.

But there are things dearer to the heart of the people of Western Canada than redistribution, and one thing of supreme importance is that the sovereign will of the people shall prevail. Redistribution is not possible at this time, but a general election is. In my opinion, a general election is past due, and should have been held in this country many months ago. In saying this I am but voicing the opinion of a vast majority of the people whom I have the honour to represent. Hon. gentlemen from Western Canada, particularly from the province of Saskatchewan, who say in this House or elsewhere that the feeling of Saskatchewan is not for a general election at this time, must keep their ears well filled. I travelled considerably over that province during the recess, and the one big question from one end of the country to the other is:	When are we to
have a general election?

The same thing in
Quebec.

Now, Mr. Speaker, the hour is very late and I have spoken much longer than I intended. In rising to speak I said there were one or two reasons why I wished to enter this debate. One particular reason was to set the Minister of Immigration and Colonization right on the Wheat Board proposition, and the other was to refute, if I could, the opinion that seems to have got into the minds of some hon. gentlemen opposite that the people of Saskatchewan were not asking for a general election at this time. Having done that, I feel that I should no longer continue to occupy the time of the House.

I
should regret very much indeed to have to speak at any length at this hour and I should therefore be very glad to have the opportunity, if the leader of the House would permit me to move the adjournment of the debate.

Very good. If my right
hon. friend refuses to accede to the request I shall have to proceed, but the House has not so far this session sat later than this, and it is only reasonable that I should ask that the debate be adjourned. If my right hon. friend does not see fit to accede to my request, I say to him that in so far as I and the rest of the hon. gentlemen on this side are concerned we are as well prepared to remain here all night as my hon. friends opposite.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not want the House to be under any misapprehension. It is not our desire or our intention to ask hon. members to sit here all night, or to refuse to accept a motion to adjourn. However, we would like to continue the debate tonight for a little time longer than apparently seems to be the intention of hon. gentlemen opposite. We have not come to the conclusion that the House should sit all night or anything of the sort, and we have not so intimated.
Is this not a reasonable hour to adjourn?

I am glad to hear^he Prime Minister's statement. It is entirely foreign to arrangement that we should at present sit late. It is now after eleven o'clock, and if I were to begin my speech now an adjournment later would have the effect of breaping up my remarks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The House might as well sit until half-past eleven.

Very well, but it will only have the effect of breaking up my remarks. I would like, Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to take a few moments in referring to the very eloquent speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie), who is not now in his seat. My hon. friend attempted to read a lecture to hon. gentlemen on this side. I would say to him, if he were in his place that he is not in the proper position-either as a retired Liberal or as a newly converted
Tory-to read a lecture to what he styles "the remnant of the Liberal party." I want [DOT] to say to my hon. friend also that although the Liberal party appreciated the hon. gentleman while he occcupied a seat in this House and supported Liberal policies and Liberal principles, the fact that he and his friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) have left the Liberal party does not mean the breaking up of that party by any means.
I would like to know in what water my hon. friend was baptized, so as to permit of the conversion he has undergone in moving from one side of the House to the other? I give him this credit: His conversion apparently was a proper one and one that has been fully carried into effect. What it cost, or where he was baptized, I do not know. It has cost the country a considerable amount, if it has not cost my hon. friend anything.
Let me explain the position which my hon. friend took from 1911 down to 1917 and compare it with the remarks he made in the House this afternoon. Let me compare the remarks which he made on the Reciprocity Agreement in the old Parliament buildings in 1911 with the speech he has favoured us with this afternoon.
Go ahead, let us hear it.

My hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) apparently accused gentlemen of the Agrarian or Progressive group of being disloyal and unpatriotic because they purchased farm machinery in United States and did not make their purchase from our manufacturers in this Dominion. May I be permitted, Sir, to read a few lines in regard to what my hon. friend thought was patriotic in 1911 when the Reciprocity Agreement was under consideration and under debate in this House. Speaking of the price of hogs and beef cattle in the Chicago and Buffalo markets in comparison with the English market my hon. friend on that occasion said this:
Let him compare Montreal and Toronto markets with Buffalo and Chicago, and he will And that the general average is higher, and markedly so, in Buffalo and Chicago during the last five year period. Now what is it we want? We want in my county the privilege of selling our cattle and hogs in Buffalo and other farm produce as well. You say: What is the use, the Buffalo market is lower. Well, if it is, are we hurt? We will then sell in the British market, and not touch Buffalo or Chicago. My hon. friend tells us that we have two markets now, the home market and the British; but when this arrangement comes into operation, we shall have three markets, and the one we have not got now, but which we want to get, is by far the largest. We will not send our products to Buffalo or Chicago unless we get

better prices than we do at home or in the Mother Country. Our western people are not going to send any cattle to Chicago unless they can get better prices there than elsewhere. If they cannot, they will send them to Eastern Canada or Great Britain. What is there unpatriotic or disloyal in that proposition? How do business men conduct their business? If the prices in Buffalo are good, they send their wares there; if not they send them elsewhere. Then why should not the Government carry on the business of this country on business lines? Why should the Government stay its hand at this juncture and deprive our people of one of the great opportunities of their lives?
Who said that?

The Minister of Militia.
He was taking the stand that it did not matter in regard to the patriotism or loyalty of the people of the Dominion if they could sell their products in the great market of the United States. It was a proper thing, he said, for our people to have that market. Yet my hon. friend now says there was nothing said by the Liberal party in this House in regard to free trade or a lower tariff. Why, in 1911 my hon. friend himself occupied page after page of Hansard in trying to impress upon the people of Canada that we should have the American market and that free trade in natural products which would result from the Reciprocity Agreement. Nothing said about free trade! Why, my hon. friend was one of the most eloquent exponents of free trade in natural products with the United States at the time the Reciprocity Agreement was before the House for consideration.
The hon. gentleman also had something to say with respect to the hon. member for St. Hyaeinthe-Rouville, (Mr. Gauthier) and he pictured an imaginary story which went back and forth at the time of the Liberal Convention in 1919. Of course that story was only a word picture of what he thought may have taken place. My hon. friend should be very well acquainted indeed, Mr. Speaker, with the tell-tale performance of going in and out from secret meetings and revealing what took place. I can say to my hon. friend that no member of the House is better acquainted with that system of carrying on than my hon. friend himself.
Now, Sir, I do not propose to follow the remarks of my hon. friend any further except to say that he was very courageous this afternoon in telling hon. gentlemen on this side that the time had arrived when they should be brought into the lime light, that their tariff planks and tariff policies should be open to inspection, that the acid test should

be applied to them in order to discover what their views, and ideas and policy were on the tariff. Let me say to my hon. friend that in his speech this afternoon-which we all enjoyed-while he told us what we on this side of the House should do and what we should not do, he never uttered a single word regarding his own tariff policy, and he dared not give it to the House. Now, if he is so courageous in challenging hon. gentlemen on this side of the House as to what they should do and what they should not do, I would say to him: the opportunity is open to him and to the Government of which he is a member, by accepting our challenge, to appeal to the people and let them decide whether they prefer his particular tariff policy or ours. After listening to the debate that has taken place on the motion moved by my hon. friend from Kings P.E.I. (Mr. Mc-Isaac), and on the amendment thereto by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), one could not help but be highly interested in following the very ingenious, if inconsistent, arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to their position in this House. My hon. friend the mover of the Address, in a carefully prepared and well delivered speech, referred to the retirement of the right hon. the ex-Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), and delivered an appreciative "obituary" oration to the political memory of the right hon. gentleman. At the same time he offered his very hearty congratulations in which I personally join-to 'Sfche right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) who leads the House at the present time on his promotion to the high office which he now holds. It seemed to me, however, that he did not instil into his remarks regarding my right hon. friend the leader of the Government that degree of hope and confidence which has characterized his speeches in the House in the past, and I thought his references to the right hon. gentlemen might very well be treated as the foreword to a book, we will say, to be written and entitled, " The Troubles of the Tory Party in the Future," in which my right hon. friend would be the outstanding character. But considering his uninspiring theme my hon. friend performed his task well, and I congratulate him very heartily.
I was deeply impressed and interested in the remarks made by my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. MacKelvie), who occupies a seat

in this Chamber for the first time. I was more particularly interested in the hon. gentleman, because, as he told the House, he was born in the province of New Brunswick and was a resident for some years in my constituency, and members of his family are still there with whom I am Very intimately acquainted. Consequently I had that much greater personal interest in my hon. friend's speech. I regret to a certain extent that he turned out to be such a very high protectionist, because that is not the teaching he received in his former county of Westmoreland, as he very well knows. But before he concluded his speech we discovered why he was such a high protectionist, for he was straightforward and frank in regard to his position. He said in so many words, "The reason I am a protectionist is because the late government of the right hon. the ex-Prime Minister put a duty of thirty cents a box on apples which is just that much protection for apple growers in the Okanagan valley." It reminded me somewhat of the story of the juryman who acquitted a man charged with sheep stealing. When asked how they reached such a conclusion they said, "We got a piece of the mutton." My hon. friend is a high protectionist because he gets a very good "piece" of protection on apples.
After the motion had been duly moved and seconded, Sir, we had an amendment moved by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. That amendment, if carried would, as everyone well knows, mean a general election. My hon. friend quoted a large number of authorities, constitutional and otherwise, in reference to the requirements for a general election, feeling that the time was ripe and the people of the Dominion were demanding an opportunity to pass judgment on the Government. I am bound to admit, along with my right hon. friend, that it has always been an open question and that it is very hard to find out exactly whether a majority of the people want an election or not. But when my right hon. friend answered the arguments advanced by the hon. leader of the Opposition and said, "We were elected for five years, and I am prepared to stand by the letter of the constitution and carry on for five years," I would remind him that while he has, according to the letter of the constitution the legal right to carry on for five years, yet there are two elements in our constitutional law to be considered-there is the written law and the unwritten law. The written law is the British North America Act. The unwritten law is a system of precedents, undertakings, conventions, and
understandings that are just as binding on a government or a parliament as the written law, and I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to quote one or two authorities in regard to it. First I will read what Bouri-not has to say in regard to the written and the unwritten law of the constitution in his Manual of the Constitutional History of Canada, in which the following passage will be found:
If we study the constitution of Canada we find that its principles rest both on the written and the unwritten law. In the British North America Act we have the written law, which must direct and limit the legislative functions of the Parliament and the Legislatures of the Dominion. While this Act provides for executive authority and for a division of legislative powers between the Dominion and the provinces-as we have seen in the first chapter of this work-it does not attempt to give legal effect or definition to the flexible system of precedents, conventions and understandings which so largely direct that system of administration and government which has grown up in the course of two centuries in England, and which has been gradually introduced into Canada during the past fifty years, and now forms the guiding principles of parliamentary government in the two countries.
I think every one will admit that there is just as much reason why the unwritten law-the conventions and understandings -should be observed as there is for the observance of our written constitution. There is a moral right, a moral claim, for the observance of one just as much as for the observance of the other-one is the letter of the Constitution and the other is the spirit of it. The Government that was elected in 1917 has not, in my opinion, the confidence of the people; therefore it is their moral right under the unwritten law of our Constitution to give the people an opportunity to say whom they wish to direct the country's affairs during the next number of years, or the next term of Parliament. Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
